Algeria.d: The outside hands documented here are of two kinds: a trafficking network that had reached the top of the police, and a neighbouring state's spyware. Algeria's national police chief, Abdelghani Hamel, lost his job after a 701-kilogram cocaine seizure at the port of Oran exposed the network behind it, and military and civilian courts later convicted him, along with several generals, on corruption and illicit enrichment counts rather than drug charges. Algeria published little about the trafficking case itself, so the corruption judgment is the record that exists. The other hand is surveillance. The Pegasus Project, a consortium of journalists working with Amnesty International, reported that Morocco had selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones as targets for NSO Group's Pegasus spyware, politicians and senior military officers among them. Morocco denied using it. Algeria broke off diplomatic relations with Morocco in August 2021 and named the alleged spying among its reasons, so the quarrel stands but the targeting itself was never tested in any court. The Muslim Brotherhood also has a documented presence in the country.
Algeria.imp: When the officer in charge of the national police is tied to the network moving cocaine through a port, enforcement at that port means whatever he wants it to mean, and which shipments get seized depends on who is being protected. Phone surveillance of politicians and officers works the other way round: it makes anyone in public life assume they are listened to, and that narrows what gets said, written and reported inside the country.

Angola.d: Angola's documented cases run through the state's money. Trafigura, one of the world's largest oil and metals traders, was convicted by a Swiss federal court in January 2025 of paying bribes to an Angolan official attached to a subsidiary of Sonangol, the state oil company; its former chief operating officer received a mostly suspended sentence. Trafigura has appealed, so the ruling is not final. A second route runs through the training of officials themselves: the World Economic Forum, the body behind the Davos meetings, selects people under about forty for a five-year programme of courses and meetings, and Angola's finance minister since 2019, Vera Daves de Sousa, is listed among its alumni. That is membership of a network, not an accusation. A third is religious. The Brazilian-run Universal Church of the Kingdom of God built a large following here, and after Angolan pastors accused its Brazilian leadership of racial discrimination and of pressing pastors into vasectomies, the government dissolved the church's board and removed its bishop. Oil traders, construction groups and foreign church hierarchies all have standing presence; the state's oil revenue is what makes it worth their while.
Angola.imp: Bribes paid over oil cargoes come out of the price the state gets for its own crude, and that price is most of the national budget. Schools, clinics and roads are funded from whatever is left, so for Angolans the question is never who signed the contract but why the money from it never arrives. What to watch is who holds the finance and oil portfolios, and whether a conviction in a foreign court changes anything about the contract at home.

Benin.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Benin yet. No case has been recorded here, so what follows is a best guess rather than a finding. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic chivalric and charitable order, has a recorded presence, and the French Masonic bodies — the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise — are thought likely to, as they are across francophone West Africa. Those lodges are lawful associations, and the thing worth watching is only whether ministers and judges share one. Cotton exports and the port are the other places where outside money usually arrives.
Benin.imp: An absence of recorded cases is not proof that nothing happens; often it means nobody has looked, or that courts and reporters lack the room to look. The practical cost of that gap is that there is no public finding to point at when a contract, a licence or a court ruling goes the wrong way, and nothing for a citizen to appeal to.

Botswana.d: Botswana has nothing documented on this map: no recorded case, and no organisation with a documented presence here. What follows is a guess rather than a finding. On the two measures behind the map it scores low both for documented capture and for the conditions that make capture easy, with fewer actors embedded in the state and more institutional resilience than most of its neighbours. Where pressure would be likeliest is where it appears elsewhere in southern Africa: mining concessions and the licensing around them, and policy networks funded from abroad. None of that is recorded here, and the absence may reflect scrutiny as much as conduct.
Botswana.imp: Nothing recorded is the best position a country can hold on a map like this, but it is not a clean bill of health. The question for people here is whether the bodies that award mining and procurement contracts stay open to inspection, since that is where capture begins elsewhere in the region. Where no case has ever been documented, there is also no public record to point to when something does go wrong.

Burkina Faso.d: The arrangement in force now is a military one. Burkina Faso's junta under Captain Ibrahim Traoré expelled French troops in early 2023, and in January 2024 personnel from Russia's Africa Corps — the defence ministry unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's African work — arrived and set up their first African base at Loumbila, outside Ouagadougou, starting at about a hundred men with plans for three hundred. Ghana's president alleged that a mine had been allotted to Wagner as payment; Burkina's mines minister denied it. The older layer is social rather than armed. Jeune Afrique reported that President Blaise Compaoré, who ruled from 1987 to 2014, had been a grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina and was succeeded in that office by his own foreign minister, Djibrill Bassole. Masonic membership is lawful and the reporting was never tested; what it describes is a president and his foreign minister sharing a private fraternity. French lodges and the Gulen movement, a Turkish religious network, have recorded or likely presence as well.
Burkina Faso.imp: Foreign troops who guard a government rather than a country answer to whoever pays them, and when payment is said to be in mining rights, a share of the country's gold leaves the budget without ever appearing in it. The lodge reporting points at a different cost: when the president and the foreign minister belong to the same closed society, nobody outside it can tell which decisions were actually made in the ministry.

Burundi.d: One arrangement is documented here, and it is a tobacco company working on the law that would regulate it. British American Tobacco, the world's second-largest listed tobacco firm, appears in leaked internal records reported by BBC Panorama in 2015 and analysed by the University of Bath; the analysis says payments to officials in Burundi, as in Comoros, Rwanda and Uganda, were aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws modelled on the World Health Organization's treaty. The UK Serious Fraud Office investigated and closed the matter without charges, and BAT denies the allegations, so this sits as reported rather than proven. Alongside it the map records the Atlas Network, which funds free-market policy institutes in many countries, and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic charitable order, neither with a case attached. Burundi's score for actors embedded in the state is high and its institutional resilience low, which is the condition that makes an approach to a mid-level official worth making in the first place.
Burundi.imp: A tobacco control law that is slowed or watered down shows up years later as cancer wards and household money spent on cigarettes, and nobody can point to the moment it was decided, because the decision was not to act. What to watch for is the opposite of a scandal: a bill that keeps being redrafted, a committee that keeps postponing, officials who move on before anything is signed.

Cabo Verde.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Cabo Verde. No case has been recorded here, so what follows is an estimate. The only organisation with a recorded presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic charitable order, which is not itself an allegation. The islands score low both for documented capture and for the conditions behind it, with relatively high institutional resilience. Given their position on the Atlantic shipping routes, the likeliest pressure is the one recorded elsewhere in West Africa: cocaine moving from South America towards Europe, which on this map reaches port, customs and police posts.
Cabo Verde.imp: With no documented case there is nothing for a resident to appeal to, and that cuts both ways: no scandal to answer, but no record either if a port or customs decision later looks wrong. The useful habit is watching the small offices — harbour clearance, container inspection, residence permits — because that is where the first approach is made in the countries on this map where cases do exist.

Cameroon.d: The arrangement that still operates is monetary. The Bank of Central African States, based in Yaoundé, issues the CFA franc for Cameroon and five neighbours, and the French Treasury guarantees its fixed rate against the euro; in return the member states must keep half their foreign-exchange reserves on deposit in Paris. West Africa's CFA zone dropped that requirement from 2021, but it stands unchanged for Central Africa, and a French Senate report in December 2024 called the reform incomplete. The older case is more personal. Le Monde reported that President Paul Biya had given tens of millions of francs to the Templar order OSTI and an associated body run by the Frenchman Raymond Bernard, with part of the money traced out of the state oil company SNH into Bernard's personal account. The presidency called Bernard an old friend and would not discuss the payments; Bernard was questioned in the Solar Temple inquiry but never charged. Opus Dei, the Gulen movement and the commodity trader Glencore also have documented presence, and OSTI is headquartered here.
Cameroon.imp: Half the country's foreign-exchange reserves sitting in another country's treasury means decisions about the currency people are paid in — what it buys, what imports cost — are not settled only in Yaoundé. The OSTI payments show the other direction: oil money moving out of the state company into a private account abroad, with no court ever testing it and no road or clinic built with it.

Central African Republic.d: The Central African Republic is the clearest case on this map of a state taken over rather than influenced. Russia's Wagner Group, a private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, put roughly a thousand fighters here from 2018 under a military agreement, guarding President Faustin-Archange Touadéra personally and fighting rebels alongside the national army. A Russian, Valery Zakharov, served as the president's national security adviser; the US Treasury sanctioned him as linked to Wagner, and its listing records that he also held a Central African passport. Russia's defence ministry has been folding these structures into its Africa Corps, and the country remains its largest African deployment. The money runs the other way through commodities: illicit gold exports estimated at $180 million a year, moved on military cargo aircraft registered in the country, plus a government-backed fuel monopoly, with the drug trade the smaller line. Recent reporting from Bangui describes Wagner remnants supplying tramadol, a high-dose painkiller sold under a local name meaning the cocaine of the poor, to members of the presidential guard and a youth militia, with senior security officials alleged to control the market. Nothing has been charged. Researchers assess that political and military figures, criminal actors and transnational groups have aligned to hold the country's illicit markets together. Underneath sits an older thread: President Francois Bozize was named in reporting as a Freemason initiated under the sponsorship of Congo's president.
Central African Republic.imp: When the men guarding the president are paid in gold, timber and fuel rights, the country's minerals leave without passing through a budget, and there is no line in any account where a citizen could look for them. The painkiller trade reaches further down: university research links rising consumption to a sharp increase in deaths in fights over the mining areas. What to watch is whether any of it is ever charged in a court here, because so far none of it has been.

Chad.d: Chad's documented record centres on a single trial and what it revealed about the security services. A court in N'Djamena sentenced ten people in July 2020 over a transnational network moving tramadol, the high-dose painkiller traded across the Sahel, and among them were high-ranking security and intelligence officials. Analysts who read the court documents described large sums circulating among the network's members, some of it used in attempts to corrupt the judiciary and the security services themselves. That is the difficulty the conviction exposes: with senior army and intelligence figures involved, enforcement depends on the institutions that were part of the problem. The other two entries are of a different kind. President Idriss Déby, who ruled from 1990 to 2021, was named in reporting as a Freemason, with no lodge identified and nothing tested. And his presidency announced in late 2017 that he had agreed to hand schools run by the Gulen movement — the Turkish religious network Ankara blames for the 2016 coup attempt — to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation, and to expel people connected to it. The Bank of Central African States, which issues Chad's currency, also sits on this layer.
Chad.imp: A drug network with army and intelligence officers inside it does not just move pills; it makes the courts and the security forces unreliable for everything else, because money aimed at judges in one case stays available for the next. The schools handover shows a second cost: a foreign government's quarrel decided which teachers taught Chadian children and which families had to leave the country.

Comoros.d: The case that reaches furthest here is the sale of the country's own citizenship. Under a 2008 'economic citizenship' law, Comoros sold passports in bulk to stateless people living in the Gulf, with Gulf money paying for them, in a scheme run with the Syrian-French businessman Bashar Kiwan. Prosecutors put the proceeds at about $200 million, much of which never reached the treasury. A court in Moroni sentenced former president Ahmed Abdallah Sambi to life in prison for high treason and related charges; Kiwan was tried with him. The second case is a company working on a law. British American Tobacco appears in leaked records, reported by BBC Panorama, arranging payments to officials in Comoros, Rwanda and Burundi, including payments aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws based on the World Health Organization treaty; a later University of Bath study counted hundreds of such payments across ten African countries. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its investigation without charges and BAT denied wrongdoing. A citizenship-by-investment industry still has recorded presence on the islands.
Comoros.imp: A passport scheme turns the one thing a small state can always issue into a commodity, and when the money does not reach the treasury, islanders get neither the revenue nor the services it was meant to buy, while their own travel documents become harder for other countries to trust. The tobacco payments work more slowly: a control law that never takes effect is a health bill paid by households decades later.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d: Eastern Congo is where this map records an outside state running a government rather than influencing one. The UN Group of Experts reported in June 2025 that the armed group M23, which took Goma and then Bukavu, operates under Rwandan command, that Rwandan army reinforcements backed the capture of Goma, and that officials said President Kagame decided to take both cities. The experts described a systematic effort to dismantle existing state authority: new governors installed, Rwandans placed over mining, tax, banking and border control, and customary chiefs removed. Rwanda denies directing M23. The mining economy draws the other hands. Dan Gertler, an Israeli investor and long-time friend of former president Joseph Kabila, was sanctioned by the US Treasury over opaque mining and oil deals made through that friendship; he denies wrongdoing and later handed licences back to the state miner Gecamines under a settlement. Glencore, the Swiss commodity trader, agreed to pay Congo $180 million to settle claims that it paid money intended as bribes to Congolese officials. And Erik Prince, the founder of Blackwater, was reported in 2026 to have sent men and drones to help Congo's army hold the eastern city of Uvira — a private military company hired by the state this time rather than against it.
Congo, Dem. Rep..imp: When mining, tax and border posts in a province are run by appointees of another country's army, the taxes people pay fund that arrangement and the minerals under their feet are exported through it. Further west, the deals sanctioned and settled abroad concern copper and cobalt licences sold cheaply, so the state miner collects less than it should and the revenue that would pay teachers and nurses never exists. Watch who signs mining contracts, and whether settlements abroad change anything on the ground.

Congo, Rep..d: What the record holds for the Republic of Congo is lodge membership at the top of the state, reported but never tested in any proceeding. Denis Sassou-Nguesso, the president, is reported to be Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, a body linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise. Jeune Afrique also reported that Pascal Lissouba, president from 1992 to 1997, had been initiated at a Grand Orient de France lodge in Besancon. Freemasonry is a lawful association and belonging to one is not wrongdoing; what the reporting describes is a head of state who also leads a private fraternity whose members include other officials, with no public record of who else is in the room. The commercial side of the layer is oil. The Gunvor Group, an energy trader, has documented presence, the Italian oil company Eni is thought likely to, and the Bank of Central African States issues the currency under the arrangement that keeps half of Central Africa's reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. No case has been brought in Congo on any of it.
Congo, Rep..imp: A lodge is not a crime, and the cost here is a cost of not knowing: when a president and his ministers share a private society, a citizen cannot tell whether a contract, a posting or a court ruling was settled in the ministry or at a meeting nobody records. In a country whose budget is oil money, that uncertainty covers the decisions that matter most, which is who gets a licence and on what terms.

Cote d'Ivoire.d: One entry is documented here, and it is reported membership rather than a proven transaction. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that the then prime minister, Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio, and the interior minister, Hamed Bakayoko, were Freemasons, and that a state prosecutor had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire; the same report said President Alassane Ouattara was not officially known to be a member. Lodge membership is lawful and the reporting was never tested. The concern it raises is about the offices named: the interior ministry runs the police, and a prosecutor decides which cases go forward. Around that sit organisations with recorded presence and no case attached — Opus Dei, the Catholic prelature; the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; the commodity traders Glencore and Gunvor; and the Prigozhin disinformation network, whose fake-account operations Facebook traced to targets including Côte d'Ivoire. French lodges are listed as likely. The country's institutional resilience score is among the higher ones in this file and its documented score is low.
Cote d'Ivoire.imp: When the minister who runs the police and a prosecutor who chooses which cases to charge belong to the same private society, nobody facing either of them can know whether that mattered. Nothing here has been tested in court, so what to watch is ordinary and public: whether police complaints and prosecutions move at the same speed for people with connections and people without them.

Djibouti.d: Djibouti's position is its product. China opened its first overseas military base here in 2017, a subsidiary of the state-linked China Merchants group bought a stake in the Port of Djibouti, and a US Congressional Research Service brief says Chinese institutions hold over half of the country's external debt, including a large Export-Import Bank loan. Djibouti suspended repayments in 2022 and later agreed a moratorium. US officials have warned the debt could give Beijing undue leverage; Djibouti says it will not hand over control of the port. That is leverage rather than a proven transaction. The documented transaction is older and simpler: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, admitted as part of a settlement with US authorities that it had paid high-ranking officials to win a contract with the state-owned Djibouti Telecom, in a case covering conduct in several countries that cost the company more than a billion dollars. Leaked internal Ericsson files published afterwards described corruption in at least ten countries, and the company acknowledged serious breaches of its compliance rules.
Djibouti.imp: Debt owed mostly to one country's banks changes what a government is able to refuse. If repayments cannot be met, the things on offer are the port, the land and the terms of the base, which a small country cannot replace. The telecom bribery has a plainer cost: a contract awarded because officials were paid is a contract priced for them rather than for subscribers, and the phone bills are paid by everyone.

Egypt.d: Egypt's record runs from a banking family's hold on the treasury to a mass movement that won and lost the presidency. The oldest entry is the deepest. After the Khedive Ismail's bankruptcy, Britain and France imposed joint control over Egypt's finances, and Evelyn Baring of the Barings banking family — which itself held a significant stake in Egyptian debt — became the British controller and later agent and consul-general, in practice the ruler of the country for two decades, keeping its revenues committed to its European creditors. No conflict of interest was raised at the time. The present-day thread is the Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt and for most of its history the country's largest opposition movement. Its senior figure Mohamed Morsi won the presidential election in 2012; the army removed him the following year, the cabinet declared the Brotherhood a terrorist organisation after a police-headquarters bombing claimed by a different group, membership became punishable by prison, and the courts jailed most of its leadership. The designation stays in force, and Morsi's life sentence for leading an illegal group was upheld, while a separate conviction for stealing secret documents was thrown out. Between those eras sits the Safari Club: Egypt's intelligence chief signed its 1976 charter with the services of France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran, an arrangement that flew Egyptian troops into Zaire and sold old Soviet weapons on to Somalia.
Egypt.imp: A government whose revenues are pledged to foreign creditors spends on the debt first and the country second, and Egypt's experience of that is still the reference point in arguments about lending today. The Brotherhood case cuts the other way: a banned organisation with a large membership means belonging to a group, not only acting for it, can end in prison, and the line between opposition and crime is drawn by the cabinet rather than by a court.

Equatorial Guinea.d: One arrangement is documented, and it concerns the presidency itself. Teodoro Obiang has ruled Equatorial Guinea since 1979. In autumn 2024, according to analyses including the CTC Sentinel, Russia deployed up to two hundred troops of its Africa Corps — the defence ministry unit that absorbed most of the Wagner Group's African work — to protect his presidency and to train elite units in Malabo and Bata, and Obiang officially received the Africa Corps commander in Malabo the following year. Protection for a head of state bought from another government is a service whose price is not public. Around it the map records the commodity trader Glencore, which admitted in UK proceedings to bribery of officials in Equatorial Guinea among other African states, and the Bank of Central African States, which issues the currency under the arrangement keeping half of Central Africa's foreign reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. The country's score for actors embedded in the state is among the highest on this layer and its institutional resilience among the lowest.
Equatorial Guinea.imp: Foreign soldiers guarding a president answer to the government that sent them, not to anyone living in the country, and their presence raises the cost of any domestic challenge to the man they protect. The oil revenue that pays for arrangements like this is the same revenue that would otherwise fund water, clinics and schools, and there is no published account of what the protection costs.

Eritrea.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Eritrea. No case has been recorded, so what follows is an estimate rather than a finding. The only organisation with a recorded presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic charitable order, which is not an allegation in itself. The country's scores run the opposite way from its empty case list: among the highest here for actors embedded in the state and among the lowest for institutional resilience. That combination is usually why nothing is documented. With no independent press, no open court record and no auditor publishing findings, arrangements that exist leave no trace a map like this can use.
Eritrea.imp: An empty record here should not reassure anyone. Where no court publishes judgments and no newspaper can investigate, people have no way to learn who is deciding what in their name, and no document to point at when a licence, a conscription order or a confiscation goes against them. Silence of this kind is a feature of the system rather than evidence about it.

Eswatini.d: Eswatini has nothing documented on this map — no recorded case and no organisation with a documented presence — so what follows is a guess. Its score for actors embedded in the state is moderately high and its institutional resilience low, a combination that elsewhere on this map goes with capture that is never recorded. In a small monarchy with a concentrated economy, the likeliest pressure is commercial: concessions, public procurement, and the handling of foreign money arriving for development or investment. None of that is documented here, and the absence may say more about what gets published than about what happens.
Eswatini.imp: Where no case has ever been documented there is also no record to appeal to. The practical consequence is that decisions about land, licences and public contracts are taken without a public trail, so a bad one cannot be traced back to who made it or who paid for it, and there is nothing a journalist or a court could later test.

Ethiopia.d: The arrangement here with the widest reach was not aimed at Ethiopia's government at all but at the building it hosts. China paid for and built the African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa, and Huawei supplied most of its computer and network equipment; Le Monde reported in January 2018, confirmed by the Financial Times, that the AU's own IT staff had found the building's data being copied each night to servers in Shanghai, and that microphones were found hidden in walls and furniture. The AU replaced the servers and declined Chinese offers to set up the new ones. China called the report preposterous, Huawei said its equipment was not the source, and no public evidence of a deliberate backdoor has been produced. The second thread is religious and domestic: Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed converted to Pentecostal Christianity after the war with Eritrea, attends and sometimes preaches at the Ethiopian Full Gospel Believers' Church, and formed the party that governs today. Also present on this layer, with no case attached, are the Tony Blair Institute, which places advisers inside governments, and Family Watch International.
Ethiopia.imp: Eavesdropping on the African Union's headquarters means the continent's own negotiating positions on trade, debt and borders were available to one of the governments sitting across the table. Closer to home, a prime minister who preaches in his own church raises a question people answer differently depending on their faith: whether the state is neutral between them, and whether a complaint from the wrong congregation gets the same hearing.

Gabon.d: Gabon is where the presidency and the Masonic grand mastership were the same job for more than forty years. Omar Bongo, initiated in 1953, was president from 1967 until his death in 2009, and he founded two Masonic bodies, one affiliated with the Grand Orient de France and the other with the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise, holding the grand mastership of both until he died. The French grand master then installed Bongo's son Ali as grand master of the Gabonese lodges, and Ali Bongo became president the same year, keeping the Masonic post until after his overthrow in the 2023 coup. Reporting also puts a commander-in-chief of police at the head of a Gabonese lodge, with ministers and the head of the national security council attending Ali Bongo's installation. The practice did not survive the coup unchanged: the Grand Lodge of Gabon gave the grand mastership to a provincial governor instead of the new head of state, who reportedly declined it, and the Grand Orient de France's own grand master met the coup leader in Libreville a month later and offered support to his transitional council. Lodge membership is lawful; what the record describes is an overlap between a private fraternity and the offices that run the police, the security council and the state.
Gabon.imp: When the same man leads the state and a private society that includes his ministers and his police chief, promotion and protection can run through the society rather than the ministry, and someone outside it has no way to know when that happened. For people dealing with the police or the courts, the open question is whether their case was decided on its facts. The test after a change of government is whether the overlap ends or simply moves.

Gambia.d: Both documented arrangements here date from Yahya Jammeh's presidency, which ended in 2017, and both handed an outsider a monopoly. Westwood Company, which held the exclusive licence to export rosewood, was co-founded by the Swiss national Nicolae Bogdan Buzaianu and Jammeh himself, according to the Swiss organisation TRIAL International, which filed a criminal complaint for pillage with the Swiss attorney general. The Gambia exported nearly $163 million of rosewood to China in three years although its own rosewood was almost gone by 2011; most of the timber came from Senegal's Casamance region, where logging funds armed groups. The second arrangement is financial. OCCRP reported that the Lebanese businessman Mohamed Bazzi, designated by the US as a key Hezbollah financier, was among Jammeh's closest associates and received monopolies including the fuel supply, while another designated trader paid for half of the state telecoms firms Gamtel and Gamcel. OCCRP estimated that more than a hundred million dollars from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia party and armed group. Neither case has produced a Gambian conviction.
Gambia.imp: An export monopoly held jointly by a president and a foreign partner means the timber left without anyone able to object, and the forests it came from, mostly across the border, are gone. A state telephone company half-sold to a designated financier means subscribers' bills funded something they never chose. The thing to watch after a change of government is whether the licences and shareholdings are unwound or quietly renewed.

Ghana.d: Ghana's documented entries are mostly about who sits in lodges, and they are unusually open about it. At his parliamentary vetting in January 2025, George Opare Addo was asked directly whether he was a Freemason, said yes, named his lodge, and was confirmed as minister for youth development. The parliamentary leader who put the question had himself said a year earlier that he is a Freemason and a Catholic, and the Grand Lodge of Ghana honoured the Asantehene, the Asante king, for twenty-five years in Freemasonry, with the national security and transport ministers taking part as members. None of that is unlawful and none of it is concealed, which is what separates Ghana from most countries on this layer. The older case is a drug one: seventy-seven parcels of cocaine landed from a vessel and disappeared, a recording surfaced of a senior police officer meeting suspects at his home, and a committee of enquiry led by a Supreme Court judge found the police account unsatisfactory. The officer returned to duty. The Tony Blair Institute and Airbus are also recorded here with no case attached.
Ghana.imp: Open membership is easier to live with than hidden membership: when a minister names his lodge at a public hearing, anyone can ask later whether it affected a decision. The cocaine case shows the cost of the opposite. Parcels that leave official custody are evidence that no longer exists, so the network behind them is never charged, and the officer in the recording goes back to work with the same powers over the same people.

Guinea.d: The clearest case here concerns one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits. In 2008 the government took two Simandou blocks from Rio Tinto and gave them to BSG Resources, controlled by the Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz. A Geneva court convicted Steinmetz of corruption over bribes paid to Mamadie Toure, a wife of President Lansana Conte, to obtain the rights, and Swiss appeal courts upheld the conviction; he denies wrongdoing. Drugs reach the presidential family in the other documented case. Ousmane Conte, the head of state's son, was arrested by the junta that took power after his father's death, confessed on state television to involvement in the cocaine trade — it was never clear whether the confession was coerced — and was designated a kingpin by the US Treasury while held in a Conakry prison. No verdict from a competent court ever followed, which is the pattern along the West African corridor: the admission exists, the judgment does not. Reporting also placed President Alpha Condé over the Grande Loge de Guinee, untested, and Gulen-linked schools were handed to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation.
Guinea.imp: Iron ore rights signed away for a bribe cost a country the one deposit it could have built a generation of public spending on, and the conviction that followed happened in Switzerland rather than Guinea, so nothing was returned here. When a trafficking case against a president's son ends without a verdict, the message to the next network is about which families are safe to work through.

Guinea-Bissau.d: Guinea-Bissau is the case on this map where an entire senior military command stood accused of the same trade at once. The country has been a transit point for South American cocaine heading to Europe since the mid-2000s. In April 2013 the US Drug Enforcement Administration took former navy chief José Americo Bubo Na Tchuto in a sting at sea; he pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine. An indictment unsealed weeks later charged the army chief of staff, General Antonio Indjai, who had led the previous year's coup, with offering to store cocaine for Colombia's FARC and to sell the group surface-to-air missiles, and the air force chief was charged in the same operation. Neither was ever surrendered, and both stayed in Bissau. Earlier, the president and the army chief of staff were killed within hours of each other, during the period when the UN's drugs office described the country as at risk of becoming Africa's first narco-state; no prosecution followed either killing, and the link to the trade is an assessment rather than a court finding. The most recent entry is the plainest: the head of the judicial police said 975 of 980 kilograms seized had disappeared from official custody and that police and security personnel were suspected of taking it. One officer was arrested. The country had tried no drug case since 2005.
Guinea-Bissau.imp: When the navy, army and air force commands are all charged with moving cocaine, there is no part of the security apparatus left to investigate it, and the cases that matter are tried in another country's courts or not at all. For people here that shows up as armed forces answering to a trade rather than a government, coups that follow the money, and seizures that vanish before they can become evidence.

Kenya.d: Kenya has the fullest record in this file, and it runs through almost every route on the map. Election work is the most organised. Cambridge Analytica, the British political-data firm, ran Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 presidential campaigns, rebranded the party and wrote its manifesto, as its own managing director described on undercover film before the company closed; in the 2022 election the Israeli hacking outfit known as Team Jorge showed reporters access to the Telegram account of the winning campaign's digital strategist, who confirmed it had been compromised. Drugs reach the courts themselves. Two Mombasa brothers running a heroin organisation pleaded guilty in New York, and their obstruction count was an admission that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police officers over two years to block their extradition; none of the officials who took the money has been named or charged in Kenya. A sitting member of parliament who had headed the national anti-corruption agency and then been made assistant transport minister with responsibility for container arrangements was designated a drug kingpin by the US; he denies it and a police inquiry absolved him. Religion and foreign states supply the rest: an Opus Dei numerary governed the central bank for eight years, President William Ruto is building a church in the State House grounds, and Turkey has had Gulen-linked refugees returned from Nairobi, a transfer Kenya's own foreign ministry confirmed.
Kenya.imp: Judges and prosecutors who have taken money from a trafficking network do not become reliable again for anyone else's case, so the cost falls on every litigant who never hears about it. Campaign firms that write a manifesto and target voters by personality data change what people are told in an election without anyone knowing who paid for it. And refugees handed back to the government they fled tells anyone living here on protection how little that protection is worth.

Lesotho.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Lesotho. No case has been recorded, so what follows is an estimate. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic charitable order, is the only organisation with a recorded presence, which is not an allegation. The country scores low for documented capture and middling for the conditions behind it. Where pressure would most likely appear is where the money is: water sold to its neighbour under a long-running transfer scheme, the garment factories that supply foreign brands, and the procurement around both. None of that is documented here, and nothing in the record says it happens.
Lesotho.imp: With nothing documented there is no case for anyone here to follow and no published finding to cite when a tender or a licence looks wrong. The useful habit in a country this size is watching the handful of large contracts that dominate the budget, because where capture does appear elsewhere on this map, it starts with one big procurement rather than many small ones.

Liberia.d: Liberia holds both the worst and the best documented responses on this map. The newest case is the worst. After the country's largest recorded cocaine seizure, close to four tonnes bound for Europe, the police inspector general said senior government officials were involved in trafficking, and the national police charged the head of its own Major Crimes Unit along with another official, naming a deputy commander responsible for security at Roberts International Airport as an active participant; a former vice-president was separately indicted on trafficking counts. The best is older. When South American and West African traffickers approached senior Liberian officials to buy safe passage for multi-tonne shipments, those officials reported the approaches and worked with the US Drug Enforcement Administration instead, producing extraditions and convictions in New York. The DEA called the cooperation unprecedented, which is a measure of how rare it is. Underneath both sits the country's old Masonic order: President William Tolbert was its grand master, lodge membership was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the ruling party, and most high officials were Masons by the 1970s. Samuel Doe's 1980 coup killed Tolbert and much of the Masonic leadership; Doe banned the order, then lifted the ban and was initiated himself.
Liberia.imp: An airport security commander working for traffickers means every other check at that airport is decoration, and the drugs that move through it fund the networks that corrupt the next set of officers. The older case shows the alternative is possible: officials who refuse an approach and report it can produce convictions, though those happened in a foreign court. Watch whether the current charges reach trial here, or stop at the charge.

Libya.d: Libya has two governments and both draw on the same subsidised fuel. Fuel is bought at international prices, sold at home for a fraction of that, and resold abroad; the International Crisis Group's assessment is that the racket helps keep the peace between rival elites in Tripoli and Benghazi because both tap the unofficial income. The Security Council has an instrument to interdict suspect cargoes, but it works only if the designated Libyan contact signals a shipment, and no signal has arrived in years. Foreign fighters are the other constant. UN monitors counted up to 1,200 Wagner Group fighters supporting Khalifa Haftar's eastern forces, with Syrians flown in by Wagner and landmines around Tripoli that drew US sanctions; a Pentagon report named the United Arab Emirates as the main funder, and Russia's Africa Corps began replacing Wagner in 2024. A UN panel found that Erik Prince, Blackwater's founder, broke the arms embargo in an operation to supply aircraft and personnel to Haftar; Prince denies it. Inside the state, a serving coast guard commander at Zawiya was sanctioned by the Security Council over fuel smuggling and migrant trafficking, detained in Libya, and released without conviction.
Libya.imp: A fuel subsidy resold abroad means Libyans queue for petrol bought with their own oil revenue and sold to someone else, and the men running it are the ones who would have to stop it. Foreign fighters paid by outside governments make the fighting someone else's decision to continue. And a coast guard commander sanctioned for trafficking people is the officer migrants at sea are supposed to be rescued by.

Madagascar.d: One arrangement is documented, and it concerns a presidential election. The Russian investigative outlet Proekt and the BBC reported that fifteen to twenty Russian political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin worked in Madagascar's 2018 presidential race and dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner, Andry Rajoelina. One candidate said they gave him cash; a former prime minister said he was promised two million dollars. Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate and the BBC found no evidence he took Russian money, and Prigozhin's representatives denied any link. Working several candidates at once is the signature of the method: whoever wins, the people who ran the campaign have a relationship with the winner. Also recorded here are the Wagner Group and the wider Prigozhin disinformation network, whose fake accounts Facebook removed after tracing operations aimed at eight African countries, Madagascar's election among them. French lodges are listed as likely. Nothing has been charged in Madagascar.
Madagascar.imp: Paid foreign strategists working most of the field at once means the campaign a voter sees was shaped by people with no stake in the result except access to whoever wins. Nothing was unlawful on the face of it and nothing was charged, so the only defence is knowing it happened. What to watch is who funds and staffs campaigns, and whether disclosure rules reach advisers brought in from abroad.

Malawi.d: One case is documented and it reaches the top of the government. Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau reported in June 2022 that the police and the Malawi Defence Force had awarded sixteen contracts worth over $150 million between 2017 and 2021 to five companies linked to Zuneth Sattar, a UK-based businessman. President Lazarus Chakwera said eighty-four people were named in the report, withdrew all delegated powers from Vice-President Saulos Chilima, and the former police chief and the lands minister were arrested. Chilima denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in 2024. What the case shows is the shape of the arrangement rather than a verdict: a single supplier holding a run of police and army contracts, and an anti-corruption body able to document it but not, on this record, to finish it in court. British American Tobacco is listed as likely to be present as well, as it is across the region where leaf tobacco is grown and tobacco control laws are drafted.
Malawi.imp: Police and army procurement is the money that buys vehicles, radios and uniforms, and when it goes repeatedly to one connected supplier the state pays more for less of it, which is felt as police who cannot reach a village and soldiers without working equipment. The thing to follow is whether the contracts were cancelled and the money recovered, not whether names were published.

Mali.d: Mali's government is held up by a foreign army. Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry unit that took over most of Wagner's African work after Prigozhin's death, became the only Russian force in the country when Wagner announced its departure in June 2025, with about two thousand Russian troops remaining and several Wagner commanders moving across. Human Rights Watch and Le Monde have reported killings of civilians by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps members since. The arrangement was built from inside the state: the US Treasury sanctioned Mali's defence minister, Colonel Sadio Camara, saying he planned and organised Wagner's deployment and travelled repeatedly to Russia to finalise it, along with the air force chief of staff and his deputy. Drugs run alongside it. A Boeing 727 flown from Venezuela was unloaded at a desert strip at Tarkint and burned; investigations pointed to protection by local officials and armed groups, the arrests in Bamako produced no senior conviction, and the aircraft's owners were never established. Cocaine seizures across the Sahel rose from a yearly average of thirteen kilograms before 2020 to well over a tonne afterwards, and the UN found the proceeds moving into gold and real estate, with armed groups in Mali among the beneficiaries. No prosecution followed.
Mali.imp: Soldiers hired from another government fight the war they are paid to fight, and the reported killings of civilians fall outside any court a Malian family can reach. Drug money moving into gold buying and property pushes up the price of both for people on ordinary wages, and it arms the groups they are supposedly being protected from. Watch whether any Sahel state prosecutes a laundering case; none has yet.

Mauritania.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Mauritania. No case has been recorded here, so what follows is an estimate. Four organisations have recorded presence with no case attached: the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the Gulen movement, the Muslim Brotherhood and the Brussels NGO Fight Impunity. The likeliest pressure is the one the region's record points to. Mauritania sits on the Sahel corridor where cocaine seizures jumped sharply after 2020, the country alone accounting for tonnes by mid-2023, and where UN investigators found the proceeds moving into gold and property. Nothing in Mauritania's own record names an official.
Mauritania.imp: A transit country with no documented case is not a country without a problem; usually it is one where the seizures are recorded and the networks behind them are not. The cost for people here is indirect and real: money from the trade bids up gold and housing, and the officials who would have to act on it are the ones nobody has examined.

Mauritius.d: One case is documented and it was decided by a development bank rather than a court. The African Development Bank debarred the Danish power-plant builder Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor for twenty-one months, finding on the balance of probabilities that it had paid members of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station of the Central Electricity Board, the state utility. A debarment stops a company bidding for bank-funded work; it is not a criminal finding, and no Mauritian prosecution is recorded. Alongside it the map lists the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, with documented presence, and the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise and the Indian organisation Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh as likely. Mauritius's institutional resilience score is among the higher ones in this file and its documented score low, which is the pattern of a place where the few cases that surface are found by outside institutions rather than domestic ones.
Mauritius.imp: Payments made during a power station tender show up later as electricity that costs more than it should, or a plant that does not run as promised, and the bill is spread across every household on the grid. A debarment abroad refunds nothing. What to watch is whether the state utility's tenders are published in enough detail for anyone outside the bank to check them.

Morocco.d: Morocco's most recent case put politicians in prison for drugs. A Casablanca court sentenced twenty-nine people in June 2026 after a two-year trial, among them a former head of a regional council, who drew twelve years, and two former members of parliament from the governing party, who drew ten each. The case began with testimony from a jailed Malian trafficker who said his Moroccan political associates had seized his assets after his arrest, and it covered tonnes of cannabis resin moved across North Africa alongside Latin American cocaine; one defendant was acquitted and appeals remain open. Religion runs through the state in a different way. Ahmed Toufiq, a historian who has said a meeting with the sheikh of the Boutchichiya, Morocco's largest Sufi order, set him on the Sufi path, has been the king's minister for Islamic affairs since 2002, serving under five prime ministers; a leaked letter of his warned the order about abuses during a dispute over its leadership. The Justice and Development Party, historically linked to the Muslim Brotherhood but never an official branch, led the government for a decade before losing almost all its seats. Morocco also closed Gulen-linked schools after Turkish requests, and its intelligence chief was one of five who signed the Safari Club charter in 1976. NSO Group, the maker of Pegasus spyware, has documented presence here.
Morocco.imp: When a regional council president and sitting-party legislators are convicted of moving cannabis and cocaine, the local permits, land decisions and policing in their areas were being made by people with another employer. The convictions matter because they are rare, and what to watch now is the appeals. A minister whose authority over mosques outlasts five prime ministers decides which preaching is allowed, which touches daily life more directly than most ministries do.

Mozambique.d: Mozambique's defining case is a debt its own parliament never saw. Three state companies borrowed around $2 billion from Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB for tuna fishing and maritime security projects with the shipbuilder Privinvest, backed by state guarantees hidden from parliament and the IMF. Credit Suisse bankers took kickbacks, and US prosecutors said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and officials. When the hidden loans surfaced in 2016 the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated two million people were pushed into poverty. Mozambique's Constitutional Council later declared the loans void, Credit Suisse pleaded guilty to wire fraud in the US and forgave part of the debt, and a Brooklyn jury convicted former finance minister Manuel Chang, with prosecutors saying Privinvest had paid him seven million dollars. Underneath that sits a heroin corridor researchers describe as running for three decades on a tight integration between ruling party figures and traffickers, with near-zero seizures as the evidence of it; the principal figure was designated abroad as a trafficker while remaining a prominent businessman at home, and no family member was ever charged in Mozambique. Russian networks tied to Prigozhin also targeted the 2019 election with fake accounts Facebook removed.
Mozambique.imp: Two million people pushed into poverty is what a hidden debt looks like from the ground: a currency that collapses, prices that jump, donors that stop paying for clinics and schools, and a repayment schedule outlasting the government that signed it. The convictions happened in New York and Zurich. What to watch here is whether any Mozambican official besides the finance minister is tried, and whether loan guarantees now reach parliament before they are signed.

Namibia.d: One matter is documented here and it is still before the courts. Leaked files published by WikiLeaks in November 2019, together with the account of the company's former Namibia manager, showed Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, paying people close to Namibia's government for horse-mackerel quota. Fisheries Minister Bernhardt Esau and Justice Minister Sacky Shanghala resigned the day after publication and were arrested with four associates, the group the press called the Fishrot Six. They are charged in Namibia with racketeering, corruption and money laundering, Iceland opened its own investigation into Samherji, and the company denies paying bribes and blames its former manager. The case is unusual on this map in two ways: the documents came out of the company rather than from a prosecutor, and the Namibian courts took it up rather than leaving it to a foreign jurisdiction. The Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School, a party cadre school, also has documented presence, and the Afrikaner Broederbond is listed as likely.
Namibia.imp: A fishing quota is a right to take fish out of the sea, and when it is sold for bribes the catch and the jobs that come with it go to a foreign fleet instead of local boats and processing plants. Namibians lost both the fish and the wages. The test is the trial itself: charges that are still unfinished years later are the normal fate of cases like this, and a verdict would make Namibia an exception.

Niger.d: Niger's junta changed who guards it. After the July 2023 coup the government ended military cooperation with the United States and France, and Russian Africa Corps troops arrived in Niamey the following April, stationed at Air Base 101 before American forces had finished leaving it; estimates put them at two to three hundred, working mostly in intelligence, training and surveillance. That is a government protected by another state's soldiers. The drug record is thinner but telling. A local mayor was arrested with more than two hundred kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, a case used in investigative-journalism training as the example of why a seizure is only a beginning: the work is unravelling the network behind the office, not recording the arrest. No outcome is documented. Niger sits on the Sahel corridor the UN's drugs office calls a natural stopover between South America and Europe, and reporting on it carries physical risk to journalists. Gulen-linked schools were handed to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation, and a former president was named in reporting as a Freemason without any lodge being identified.
Niger.imp: Soldiers from abroad sitting on the main air base are a shield for the government rather than the border, and the country's security becomes a matter settled between two capitals. A mayor caught with cocaine and no recorded outcome tells the next official what the risk really is. For people in the corridor towns, that means roads and checkpoints policed by men whose income may depend on what passes through them.

Nigeria.d: Nigeria's constitution bars members of secret societies from elected office and from the public service, and commentators name the Ogboni fraternities, the Freemasons and AMORC among the societies at issue. That rule made a 1999 election petition against president-elect Olusegun Obasanjo possible, though the tribunal dismissed it. The documented arrangements, though, are mostly commercial. A US diplomatic cable published by WikiLeaks records Shell's executive vice-president for Africa telling the US ambassador that the government had forgotten Shell had seconded staff to all the relevant ministries, and that the company therefore knew what was being done inside them; Shell rejected the claim. A British Virgin Islands company, P&ID, signed a gas-processing deal, never built the plant, and won an arbitration award that grew past eleven billion dollars before a London judge set it aside, finding it had bribed a government lawyer and used Nigeria's leaked privileged documents. Glencore pleaded guilty in the US and the UK to bribing officials in Nigeria and four other African states. Eni and Shell were charged in Italy over the OPL 245 oil block payment that reached a former oil minister's company, and were acquitted. Alongside those, a BBC investigation suggested money went to a confraternity linked to Black Axe to 'protect votes' in a state election, with government roles as the reward; the organisation denies the link.
Nigeria.imp: An arbitration award built on a bribe would have taken a sum larger than several federal ministries' budgets out of the treasury, and it took a foreign court to stop it. A company with its own staff inside the ministries that regulate it gets to see the file before the public does. And when a confraternity is paid to protect votes and rewarded with jobs, state posts in that region are filled by people who owe their position to an election operation rather than to any voter.

Rwanda.d: What is documented here is advice rather than money. The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London-based non-profit that places advisers inside governments and reports work in more than forty-five countries, has supported a strategy and policy unit and a government action coordination unit in Rwanda, and worked on the Imihigo performance-contract system; in Kenya it supported a similar presidential delivery unit. Its largest donor is the foundation of Larry Ellison, the American software billionaire, which gave it more than fifty million pounds in a single year. Nothing unlawful is alleged. The arrangement is that staff paid by a private foundation sit inside the offices of a head of state and help design how government work is measured. Also recorded here without a case are Opus Dei, NSO Group, the maker of Pegasus spyware, and British American Tobacco, which appears in the leaked records of payments aimed at tobacco control laws in Rwanda and three neighbours — payments BAT denies, in an investigation British prosecutors closed without charges.
Rwanda.imp: Advisers funded from outside and placed in a president's office help decide which results a government counts as success, and nobody voted for them. That is not corruption, and the practical question is narrower: whose priorities the targets reflect, and whether a citizen can find out who wrote the plan their hospital or their school is measured against.

Sao Tome and Principe.d: Nothing is documented on this map for São Tomé and Príncipe. No case has been recorded, so what follows is an estimate. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the only organisation with a recorded presence, which is not an allegation. The islands have the lowest score in this file for actors embedded in the state, and a low documented score to match. Where pressure would most likely appear is where it has in comparable small island states: offshore oil licensing, port and shipping arrangements, and the handling of donor money, all decided by a very small number of officials.
Sao Tome and Principe.imp: A very small administration means a handful of signatures decide the things that matter, which makes capture cheap when it happens and hard to see. With no case on record there is nothing for residents to point to, so the practical safeguard is whether licences, concessions and donor grants are published at all.

Senegal.d: The relationship that shapes most of Senegal's record is not foreign at all. The Mourides are a Sufi brotherhood centred on their own holy city, Touba, which has run with wide autonomy from the state since 1928; their leader, the Khalife general, has been courted by presidents for decades. Abdoulaye Wade went to Touba the day after his 2000 election and put Mourides in his government, and President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, sworn in in April 2024, called on Khalife Serigne Mountakha Mbacke within a fortnight, returned repeatedly, and pledged state help with Touba's water and sanitation before the Grand Magal pilgrimage. None of that is unlawful; it is a standing arrangement in which a religious authority with millions of followers is party to state decisions. Foreign hands appear in smaller ways: Senegal closed more than a dozen Gulen-linked schools attended by about three thousand children after Turkish requests, and Turkey's Maarif Foundation opened its own; a sitting president accepted a million-dollar peace prize funded by the Unification Church; and a governing-coalition deputy was arrested in a cocaine operation, had his immunity lifted, and saw the case end without a verdict.
Senegal.imp: A brotherhood that can deliver votes and a state that pays for its city's water are in a trade, and what it costs is settled outside any ministry a voter can petition. The schools case is sharper: three thousand children changed schools because of a quarrel in another country. And a legislator arrested in a drug operation whose case stops without a verdict tells every police officer what happens when the suspect sits in parliament.

Seychelles.d: What is documented here is a registration rather than a government. The crypto exchange KuCoin, registered in the Seychelles as PEKEN Global Limited, was fined $297 million for failing to run effective anti-money-laundering controls and to report suspicious transactions, while its executives were separately indicted in the United States over banking-secrecy and unlicensed money-transmission offences. The exchange served customers in countries where it was not licensed, from a jurisdiction that let it incorporate. That is the Seychelles' role on this map: a company registry whose products are used elsewhere, rather than officials bought at home. No Seychellois official appears in the case. The islands' institutional resilience score is one of the higher ones in this file and their documented score is low, and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the only organisation with recorded presence.
Seychelles.imp: Selling incorporation is a legitimate business until the companies registered are the ones used to move money nobody can trace, and then the cost lands on people in other countries whose savings or stolen funds pass through them. For residents the risk is financial: a registry that attracts enforcement abroad can lose correspondent banking, which is what makes ordinary cross-border payments work.

Sierra Leone.d: The current case concerns who is being sheltered. Jos Leijdekkers, sentenced in absentia in Rotterdam to twenty-four years for smuggling cocaine, was identified by Reuters through facial-recognition matching at a New Year mass two rows behind President Julius Maada Bio in the president's home town; three sources told Reuters he is married to Bio's daughter, and Dutch prosecutors said he had lived in Sierra Leone for at least six months. Reuters reported that he has high-level protection. The government said the president did not know him and that it was investigating, and the immigration chief was dismissed after footage showed him with Leijdekkers. The older cases are about an airport. A twin-engine aircraft carrying around seven hundred kilograms of cocaine landed at Lungi marked with Red Cross insignia, and the prosecutions that followed reached airport and security personnel alongside the foreign crew, described in US congressional testimony as historic for the region, the comparison being Guinea-Bissau, which had tried no drug case in years. The minister responsible for transport and aviation was dismissed after proceedings indicated he had given the aircraft landing clearance; the dismissal was administrative and the allegation was never tried.
Sierra Leone.imp: A convicted trafficker living alongside the president's family, with immigration officials pictured beside him, means a fugitive's safety here depends on connections rather than law, and so, by implication, does anyone else's exposure. The Lungi convictions show the other possibility: a case that actually reached court, which is why it is still cited. The test now is whether the current matter produces anything beyond a dismissal.

Somalia.d: One entry is documented, and it is a foreign government's quarrel settled on Somali ground. Schools run by the Gulen movement — the Turkish religious network Ankara blames for the 2016 coup attempt — had been handed to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation by June 2017 after talks through the Turkish foreign ministry, as happened in Guinea, Niger and Sudan in the same period. Turkey is a substantial presence in Somalia, and the transfer is recorded as a government designation rather than an allegation of bribery. Also present without a case attached are the Muslim Brotherhood and the security companies Erik Prince has run since founding Blackwater. Somalia's conditions score is among the highest in this file for actors embedded in the state and among the lowest for institutional resilience, which is the combination that usually means arrangements exist and no record of them does.
Somalia.imp: Children changed schools because of a dispute between a foreign government and a movement, and the new schools answer to the ministry in Ankara that funds them. More broadly, in a state with little capacity to document anything, the absence of further cases is not reassurance: whoever is making decisions here leaves no record a citizen could consult, and no court that would hear a complaint about it.

South Africa.d: The main route in here runs through the state-owned companies and the tax service. Eskom, which supplies the country's electricity, and Transnet, which runs the ports and freight railways, buy on a scale that makes a bribe worth paying, and several foreign firms have now admitted paying one: a German software company, a Swiss-Swedish engineering group and two American consultancies, which between them have paid out hundreds of millions of dollars in US settlements. The inquiry chaired by Chief Justice Raymond Zondo, which heard more than 300 witnesses, found the same thing from the other side: that ministers and the heads of state companies were acting for the Gupta family, businessmen close to then-president Jacob Zuma who are said to have offered the finance minister's job to the man who was then deputy. The tax service was a particular target, because it is the part of the state that investigates where money comes from, and Zondo found a consultancy had helped take it apart. Organised crime sits inside the police rather than outside it. A national police commissioner who was also president of Interpol was convicted of taking a trafficker's money, a colonel sold police firearms to Cape Town gangs, and allegations made in 2025 about a syndicate reaching the police minister are now before a commission of inquiry. Behind all of it is a long habit of government by private society: every prime minister from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society, and Milner's young Oxford appointees ran the Transvaal administration after 1902.
South Africa.imp: The money is the point. Bribes on power-station and rail contracts are paid out of the price of electricity and freight, and the state firms that paid them carry debts the public services. A weakened tax service collects less, so there is less for clinics and schools. When a building contract carries a cut for a 'business forum', the clinic costs more and is finished later, or never. Watch who the state's biggest buyers hire, and whether inquiry findings ever reach a courtroom.

South Sudan.d: Two things are documented here, and both touch the presidency directly. When President Salva Kiir's government detained ministers loyal to his rival in March 2025, Uganda sent special forces into the capital, Juba. Uganda's army chief said publicly that the army 'recognises only Salva Kiir' and that any move against him would be a declaration of war against Uganda. Uganda's parliament later endorsed the deployment, while South Sudan at first denied the troops were there. So part of the answer to who governs comes from another country's barracks. The second runs the other way, from money into office. Benjamin Bol Mel, a businessman close to Kiir whom the United States sanctioned for corruption in 2017, was named one of the vice presidents in February 2025 and deputy head of the ruling party, before a decree removed him from both posts in November. The numbers behind this country are unusual: very little is documented, but the reading for actors already embedded in the state is high and the reading for institutions that could resist them is near the floor. That is what the map registers when oil revenue, a ruling party and a small circle of businessmen are hard to tell apart. A commodity trader, a Catholic military order and a free-market network are recorded as present, with no finding against them.
South Sudan.imp: A government that depends on foreign soldiers for its own safety owes them something, and that debt is paid in oil, contracts and silence rather than at an election. When a businessman under corruption sanctions can be made vice president and unmade by decree nine months later, there is no settled rule about who controls public money. For people here that shows up as unpaid salaries, unbuilt roads and no office that has to answer a complaint.

Sudan.d: Sudan is in a war between its army and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary grown out of older government militias, and the outside hands here mostly belong to states supplying one side or the other. UN monitors reported 'credible' evidence that the United Arab Emirates was flying weapons to the RSF several times a week through northern Chad; the UAE denies it and says the flights carried aid. Russia came in earlier and through gold: a mining company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, who later founded the Wagner Group, was sanctioned by the United States in 2020 for helping Omar al-Bashir's government try to crush the protests that brought him down. Washington has also sanctioned the current finance minister and an Islamist militia fighting beside the army, which it says Iran's Revolutionary Guards trained and armed. The older layer still shapes the state. Bashir took power in 1989 in a coup organised with an Islamist movement in the Muslim Brotherhood tradition, and for thirty years that movement staffed the ministries, the courts and the security services. After his fall a committee set out to remove those appointments; in 2021 the High Court ordered dismissed judicial staff back to work and the committee refused to accept the ruling. Both sides of that argument are still in the fight.
Sudan.imp: War decides everything else here. Weapons arriving by air keep a front line moving through people's neighbourhoods, and gold that leaves untaxed pays for more of them. Thirty years of appointments made for loyalty left courts and ministries that cannot settle a dispute between armed men, and a drug industry has set up in that gap. For most people the cost is displacement, no working court and no state office that answers to them.

Tanzania.d: Little is documented here, and what there is points in two directions. The clearest is a training arrangement. The Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School at Kibaha, built with a $40 million grant from the Chinese Communist Party's own party school and taught in part by its theoreticians, took its first class in 2022. It is a joint project of the Chinese party and six governing parties in southern Africa, Tanzania's CCM among them. Nothing illegal is alleged; the interest is that the people who will run six states are being taught how to run a party by a party that does not lose elections. The other is drugs. In 2017 the president read out in public a list of alleged traffickers that included a regional commissioner and other public figures, and ordered arrests. Few cases were completed and most of those held were released, so the map records the episode as a head of state's assertion rather than as a finding. Otherwise the known footprint is small: a Catholic prelature and the schools of a Turkish religious movement are recorded as present, and an arms manufacturer and a tobacco company are listed as likely but undocumented. Tanzania's scores are among the lowest on the map.
Tanzania.imp: Cadre training abroad is not felt directly, but it shapes what a governing party treats as normal: how it handles a critical newspaper, a protest, a close election. The drugs list cut the other way. Names were read out in public and then nothing was proved, which leaves the accused without a hearing and the trade without a prosecution. What to watch is whether the courts finish what announcements start.

Togo.d: One arrangement is documented here and it is recent. President Faure Gnassingbé and Vladimir Putin signed a defence agreement in November 2025 covering intelligence sharing, arms sales, joint exercises and the right for Russian ships to dock at the port of Lome. Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry force that took over from the Wagner Group across Africa, is reported to have landed officers in January 2026, with roughly 300 to 350 soldiers in Lome and at northern bases by the middle of that year, and a sanctioned cargo ship unloaded vehicles at Lome in July 2026 for Russian forces in Mali. Three opposition parties have asked for a public debate about foreign troops on Togolese soil. That is the pattern worth watching rather than any single scandal: a small state on the Gulf of Guinea becomes a port and a staging ground for an outside army operating in the Sahel, under an agreement the opposition says was never argued out in public. Two spyware and influence-operations firms are also recorded as having had a presence here, and two French masonic bodies are listed as likely but undocumented. Nothing in the record has been tested by a court or an inquiry.
Togo.imp: A foreign force that trains and supplies the army becomes a party to how the government handles its own opposition, and this deal was made without the public argument three parties asked for. A port used to move another country's military cargo also attracts that country's enemies. The first effect for people here is political: a government with outside military backing has less reason to answer to voters at home.

Tunisia.d: What the map records in Tunisia is a movement that won power and is now being prosecuted. Ennahda grew out of the Muslim Brotherhood tradition, though it says it has no organisational tie to the Egyptian Brotherhood. After winning the 2011 election that followed the uprising it led the government for two years, supplying two prime ministers, with the party leader's son-in-law as foreign minister. The direction has since reversed. The party's leader, Rached Ghannouchi, speaker of parliament from 2019 to 2021, has been in prison since April 2023; in February 2025 a court added 22 years for 'plotting against state security' in a case built around a media company, and a former foreign minister and a former prime minister were given 34 and 35 years in their absence. Ennahda calls the cases political. The map keeps both facts next to each other: a religious movement did take over the state, by election, and the state now in power is jailing its leadership in trials its opponents say are not real trials. Other recorded presences, a transnational Islamist party, a private forum of senior officials and business figures, and an Israeli influence-operations firm, carry no findings against them here.
Tunisia.imp: When a party that has governed is removed by court verdict rather than at an election, nobody can tell whether the courts are enforcing the law or clearing the field, and the next government inherits that doubt. People who voted for Ennahda have little representation; people who feared it have no public record of what it actually did. What to watch is whether any of these trials is heard in open court with a defence.

Uganda.d: The outside hands recorded here are mostly religious, and they appear in the making of law. David Bahati, who chairs Uganda's national prayer breakfast and is tied to the American political prayer network known as The Fellowship, first floated the Anti-Homosexuality Bill at a Ugandan prayer breakfast, by one journalist's account; he has sat as a state minister since 2021. When a harsher version passed in 2023, carrying life imprisonment and in some cases death, a Ugandan activist named the president of Family Watch International, an Arizona lobbying group with UN consultative status, as having lobbied for it. The World Bank halted new lending to Uganda over the law. Both links are reported rather than established by a court or inquiry. The other case is surveillance.
