The Wall Street Journal reported in 2019 that technicians from Huawei, China's largest maker of telecoms equipment, working inside police headquarters helped the cyber unit get into the encrypted messages of the opposition politician Bobi Wine. The paper found no evidence that Huawei's executives in China or the Chinese state directed it, and Huawei denies the report. A Catholic prelature, a Turkish religious movement's schools and a spyware vendor are also recorded as present.
Uganda.imp: A criminal law written with foreign lobbying behind it is still enforced by Ugandan police against Ugandan people, and a lending freeze over it falls on clinics and roads rather than on the lobbyists. If the engineers who maintain the phone network also help police read messages, nobody who criticises the government has a private conversation, not just the one politician in the reported case. Watch who gets access to police systems, and on what paper.

Zambia.d: One arrangement is documented here, and it concerns the place of a church inside the state. Zambia's constitution has declared the country a Christian nation since 1996, and in September 2016 President Edgar Lungu turned a religious-affairs desk into a full Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs, giving the post to a cleric he had appointed as a nominated member of parliament. She held it until 2021; after that year's election the next president folded the ministry into a department of the vice-president's office. The ministry is gone and the constitutional clause remains. The rest of what the map records here is presence rather than wrongdoing: Huawei, the Chinese telecoms equipment maker; the political consultancy Cambridge Analytica; and Brazilian and other Pentecostal church networks. A masonic body, the long-collapsed BCCI bank and a tobacco company are listed as likely present but undocumented. Zambia's scores are low across the board, which on this map means few outside forces have been shown to have a hand inside the government, not that none do. A ministry that one president can create and the next can abolish is the thing to keep an eye on.
Zambia.imp: A ministry for religion decides which congregations get recognition, airtime and public money and which do not, which is a real advantage handed out by the state to one set of believers. Zambians of a minority faith or none had no say in it and no way to appeal. That one president could create the ministry and the next abolish it is itself the problem: the rule changed with the man holding the office.

Zimbabwe.d: The clearest case here runs from sanctions into the cabinet. Kudakwashe Tagwirei built Sakunda Holdings through fuel trading and a state 'Command Agriculture' contract worth about $3 billion, paid in Treasury bills. The United States sanctioned him in 2020, accusing him of misappropriating public funds and supporting senior officials; Britain followed in 2021, and in October 2026 President Mnangagwa appointed him a cabinet minister. He denies the allegations. The direction is the point: being named abroad as a problem has not cost him standing at home, it preceded promotion. Gold is the other route. An undercover investigation recorded intermediaries, one of them an ambassador-at-large, offering to wash cash through the state gold refinery and export it as bullion, which turns cash into a commodity with an invoice. A commission was appointed and the practice continued. Russia's contribution has been cheaper: about forty observers from a body presenting itself as independent African election monitors attended the 2018 election, and journalists later traced its organisation to people and structures around Yevgeny Prigozhin. A masonic body, the defunct BCCI bank and the Rhodes Trust are listed as likely present but undocumented.
Zimbabwe.imp: When public money runs through one businessman's companies and he then joins the cabinet, there is nobody left to audit the contract. Gold leaving through the state refinery with clean paperwork is revenue the treasury never sees, so teachers and hospitals go unpaid while the metal is exported. Foreign observers who certify an election nobody trusts take away the one tool voters have for contesting a result. Watch who the state's sole buyers and refiners are.

Afghanistan.d: Afghanistan's record has two layers that never quite separate: a drug economy that paid provincial officials and police commanders, and a foreign state with a militant group inside the government. The Haqqani network, a militant faction within the Taliban, was described in 2011 by the top US military officer as acting as a veritable arm of Pakistan's ISI, its military intelligence service. Pakistan denies it. Since the Taliban took Kabul in 2021 that network holds the capital's security and its leader sits as interior minister. UN monitors who report each year on al-Qaeda say the group keeps close ties with the Taliban leadership and a presence in several provinces, and that the Pakistani Taliban draws strong support from elements inside it; the Taliban reject the reports. The older damage is financial. Kabul Bank, the country's largest private bank, paid the salaries of soldiers, police and civil servants, and was run as a fraud: about $935 million went out in insider loans, most of it to a handful of people and their companies, among them brothers of the president and the first vice-president. Neither brother was charged. The chairman and chief executive were jailed and the state took the bank over. The opium findings, by contrast, stayed in official assessments rather than reaching courtrooms, which the record treats as the finding.
Afghanistan.imp: A bank that pays the army and the police, emptied by its own shareholders, means wages that may not arrive and a public that pays for the rescue. Where police commanders tax the opium crop, a farmer's protection costs money and complaining about it goes nowhere. And when the interior ministry is held by a group a foreign intelligence service is said to direct, who polices Kabul is being decided somewhere other than Kabul.

Armenia.d: Armenia has almost nothing on this map, and the one live record is contested in both directions. Samvel Karapetyan is a Russian-Armenian billionaire whose Tashir Group ran Electric Networks of Armenia, the company that distributes the country's electricity. It is the only distributor, which makes its owner a political figure whether he wants to be or not. He backed the Armenian Church in its quarrel with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and in June 2025 he was detained over public calls to seize power, then charged with money laundering. Parliament passed amendments allowing the state to take over the grid company. His lawyers call the charges unfounded; critics read the case as a government clearing a wealthy opponent out of the way before the 2026 election. No trial result has been reported. The Order of Malta, a Catholic lay order, has a recorded presence, and Russia's state-funded Russkiy Mir Foundation, which promotes Russian language and culture abroad, is listed as likely here but undocumented. On the evidence gathered so far, the pressure on Armenian institutions comes less from any organisation placing people inside them than from one owner holding a utility the whole country depends on, and a government willing to take it.
Armenia.imp: Whoever ends up owning the wires decides what households pay and how reliably the lights stay on, and that question is being settled by arrest and emergency legislation rather than by a regulator. The risk cuts two ways for people here: a businessman able to lean on the state through the grid, and a state able to seize a company by charging its owner. Either way the decision happens above them and they get the bill.

Azerbaijan.d: Azerbaijan is unusual here in that more of what is documented is the country reaching outward than anything reaching in. It is the home of what has been called caviar diplomacy, the practice of cultivating members of European assemblies with gifts and hospitality. The state oil company, SOCAR, is the instrument closest to hand, since the economy rests on oil and gas, and it turns up on both sides of the ledger. In 2014 schools and university-preparation centres linked to the Gulen movement, a Turkish religious network that Ankara later declared a terrorist organisation, were taken over by an education company in which SOCAR holds shares, after Turkey's prime minister asked for help against the movement. Financial viability was the reason given. Ten years later, when Azerbaijan hosted the United Nations climate talks, the summit's chief executive, a deputy energy minister, was secretly filmed by campaigners posing as investors while discussing possible oil and gas deals in the run-up to the conference. The summit's president had previously been an executive at SOCAR. Critics said the recording showed a breach of the code of conduct for hosting the talks. In both records the state oil company is doing work that a ministry would normally do.
Azerbaijan.imp: When the company that sells the country's oil also runs schools and supplies the people chairing climate talks, there is no separate authority to appeal to. Pupils lost their teachers overnight because of a dispute between two governments. And the rules a climate summit exists to negotiate, which matter to anyone living with heat, drought or flood, were being handled by officials who had gas to sell on the side.

Bahrain.d: Nothing is documented on this map yet of an outside force operating inside Bahrain. The one record runs outward rather than inward: Bahrain obtained an Interpol wanted notice for a footballer who had fled the country and had refugee status in Australia, and he was arrested on arrival in Thailand before the notice was withdrawn. What is likely inside the country is a guess. The Muslim Brotherhood and the Order of Malta are recorded as present, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards and the militias they fund are thought to reach into Bahrain, given the long contest between Iran and the Gulf monarchies. None of that is established here.
Bahrain.imp: For now the practical cost is hard to name, because nothing has been established. What the one record does show is that a Bahraini can be arrested on the far side of the world on the strength of a request from home, which is a real constraint on anyone who leaves. If outside leverage is at work inside the country, the lack of an independent court or a free press means residents would be unlikely to hear about it.

Bangladesh.d: Two different kinds of outside force show up in Bangladesh, and neither resembles the other. One is the yaba trade, methamphetamine pills coming over the Myanmar border, which bought protection inside the state. The member of parliament for Cox's Bazar, the district almost all of it passes through, appeared on the government's own list of traffickers. He was convicted in 2018 of concealing wealth and jailed for three years, while the trafficking allegations themselves never reached a trial. The crackdown that followed produced hundreds of deaths in police custody or in so-called crossfire, and a station chief in Teknaf and several colleagues were sentenced to death for killing a retired army major who had filmed them. The drug economy carried on. The other kind arrived down a wire. In February 2016 hackers inside the central bank's network sent fraudulent payment instructions to its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; $81 million went out, most of it to the Philippines, and much of that has never come back. Security firms and US agencies attribute the theft to a unit under North Korea's military intelligence, and US prosecutors charged a North Korean programmer. The army has also said it stopped a coup attempt by officers it linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a group banned here that campaigns for a caliphate.
Bangladesh.imp: The parliamentary case shows what trafficking protection does to a border district: the trade stays, the policing lands on small dealers and sometimes on whoever gets in the way. Families of people shot in crossfire got no hearing. And the central bank theft took money from the national reserves, which is what pays for imported fuel, food and medicine, so the loss is spread thinly across everyone rather than carried by anyone able to complain.

Bhutan.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Bhutan: no case, and no organisation with a recorded presence. It is the lowest score on the whole map, which is partly a measure of how little has been recorded about a small and little-reported country rather than proof that nothing happens. Anything said about what is likely is a guess. The routes a small state usually offers are a single large infrastructure or energy contract, and the weight that much bigger neighbours carry with a small foreign service. The map's own reading of local conditions here is middling rather than clean.
Bhutan.imp: With nothing established, there is nothing here that can honestly be said to cost people anything. The fair position is that no one has looked closely and published what they found. What would be worth watching is the handful of places where a small state is most exposed: a large foreign-funded project, a loan with conditions attached, and who is advising ministers on both sides of it.

Brunei.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Brunei. The one organisation with a recorded presence is the network of Chinese police overseas service stations, offices abroad that several governments have investigated as a channel for pressuring Chinese emigrants to return home. No case is attached to it here. What is likely is a guess. An oil and gas state with a small administration and an absolute monarchy offers few of the openings this map usually records, since there are few elected offices to buy, but it concentrates whatever leverage exists around energy contracts and the small number of people who negotiate them.
Brunei.imp: Nothing established means nothing that can honestly be charged to anyone's account here. The cost people may carry is of a different kind. A Chinese national living in Brunei who is leaned on to go home has no public case to point to, and in a state with no elected legislature there is no forum where an awkward question about an energy contract would be asked out loud.

Cambodia.d: Cambodia's arrangement is the online fraud economy, and it reaches the top of the state. Compounds hold trafficked workers under debt bondage to run investment scams by phone and message, and US and British sanctions give political protection as the reason the compounds operate in the open. One designated figure is a sitting senator. The clearest case is Chen Zhi, born in Fujian, who took Cambodian citizenship, built one of the country's largest conglomerates, held an honorific title and served as an adviser to Hun Sen and two other national leaders. In October 2025 US prosecutors indicted him over a fraud empire run from the compounds and seized a record quantity of bitcoin; three months later Cambodia arrested him, revoked his citizenship and sent him to China. Money is the other half of it. Huione Group, a Phnom Penh financial conglomerate whose payment arm counts the prime minister's cousin as a shareholder and director, was found by US Treasury investigators to have laundered more than $4 billion, including proceeds of North Korean hacking and of scam operations; the central bank pulled its licence. Around all this sits a casino business that UN researchers describe as a parallel banking system, hundreds of licensed and unlicensed houses along the Mekong moving value that leaves no bank record, often on the same premises as the fraud floors upstairs. The older pattern had the same shape with drugs: a two-star general arrested with heroin and manufacturing equipment was released within weeks, and that is still the highest-ranking Cambodian drug case to reach a court.
Cambodia.imp: The people hurt most are the workers held inside the compounds, many of them trafficked from other countries, and the strangers worldwide talked out of their savings. For Cambodians the cost is a police force and a licensing system that protect the business instead of policing it, and a banking system other countries now treat as suspect, which raises the price and the paperwork of ordinary transfers for everyone who has nothing to do with any of it.

China.d: China is the one country here where the main direction of travel is the state into everything else. Company law requires any firm with three or more Communist Party members to set up a party organisation inside it, and by 2018 the party reported such a body in 73 percent of private companies, with the largest state firms writing the party's role into their charters. At ByteDance, which owns TikTok, there is an internal party committee, a state fund holds a board seat in its main Chinese subsidiary, and the company admitted that staff had used app data to track journalists reporting on it. The reach extends into international institutions. A serving vice-minister of public security was elected president of Interpol, the police cooperation body, then vanished on a trip home and was later jailed for bribery, and Interpol deleted a wanted notice China had sought for an exiled Uyghur leader. Money moves the other way too: an American bank ran a programme hiring around a hundred relatives of officials and state-company executives who could steer business its way, and settled with US regulators. The drug record is almost entirely outbound, with chemical companies in Wuhan, Hebei, Shandong and Hong Kong indicted or sanctioned for shipping fentanyl precursors to Mexican buyers and mail-order customers, usually paid in cryptocurrency. With triads the older record is ambiguous: a public security minister once said patriotic triad members deserved respect, and a Chongqing police chief was executed for protecting gangs.
China.imp: Inside China, a party body in your workplace means the line between an employer and the state is thin, and what a company knows about you may not stay with the company. Journalists found that out when their movements were pulled from an app. Abroad, the weight lands on exiles, for whom a wanted notice through an international police body can mean arrest at a border over conduct no court would recognise as a crime. The precursor exports kill people on other continents.

Cyprus.d: Cyprus's record is about what a small jurisdiction sells. From 2007 to 2020 the country sold citizenship to investors, and with it a European Union passport. In 2020 a broadcaster published leaked files and then undercover footage in which the Speaker of the House and a sitting member of parliament appeared willing to help a fictional Chinese investor with a money-laundering conviction obtain one. Both resigned and the scheme was closed. A state inquiry led by a former judge found that more than half the passports granted had been granted unlawfully; four men were sent to trial and one was cleared. The other case is a bank. FBME was registered in Tanzania and run out of Cyprus, and US Treasury investigators named it a primary money-laundering concern over accounts used by organised crime and sanctioned parties. Cyprus wound the bank down, and its owners spent years in arbitration against the designation. Freemasonry, the Order of Malta and the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of politicians and business figures from North America, Europe and Asia, all have a recorded presence, with no case attached to any of them. In both documented records the product is access, to a banking system or to a European passport, and the checking of who was buying it was done lightly.
Cyprus.imp: A passport scheme run this way hands rights across the whole European Union to people a court has already convicted, and Cypriots who gained nothing from the sale carry the consequences in closer scrutiny of their own banks and transfers. When a bank the local regulator licensed is shut down from Washington rather than Nicosia, depositors learn how little their own supervisor was doing, and they learn it after the money is frozen.

Georgia.d: Georgia's single documented record concerns one man and a question about which country he serves. Bidzina Ivanishvili made his fortune in Russia in the 1990s, founded the Georgian Dream party that now governs, and as its honorary chairman nominates the prime minister: a private person holding no office who chooses the head of government. In December 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned him for undermining Georgian democracy and advancing the interests of the Russian Federation. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia sanctioned him too, and the European Parliament describes him as having personal and business links to the Kremlin. He denies acting for Russia, and no court has tested the question; a sanction is an executive finding, not a verdict. Around that, the recorded presences are the kind found almost anywhere, a French masonic grand lodge, the Order of Malta, schools linked to the Gulen movement, with no case attached. The Atlas Network, a federation of free-market think tanks that places policy advocates close to governments, is listed as likely here but undocumented. What the one record describes is not an organisation placing members inside the state but a single fortune made abroad standing behind the party in power.
Georgia.imp: Where a party's funder nominates the prime minister, an election decides less than it appears to, and voters have no way of putting a question to the person actually choosing. The sanctions name him personally, but the weight falls on Georgians. The United States, three Baltic states and the European Parliament now treat the governing party as working to someone else's benefit, which narrows what the country can expect from any of them.

India.d: The largest documented presence in India is not a foreign one. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation founded in 1925, is the body the governing party grew out of, and its people fill the government. The prime minister was a full-time RSS organiser before the movement seconded him to party politics, a count in 2020 found 38 of the 53 ministers from his party had RSS roots, and the vice-president has been associated with the movement since his teens. The RSS publishes no membership rolls. Second is the business of pharmaceutical chemicals. Indian firms have been indicted and sanctioned for shipping fentanyl precursors to Mexican cartels, in some cases mislabelled on the shipping papers, and investigations traced dozens of Indian suppliers exporting opioid pills to West African countries that had never approved the drug. Regulators suspended permissions and inspected the plants named; exports of the same opioid then rose. Elected politics carries its own load, since candidates must declare pending criminal cases and 251 of the 543 members elected to the lower house in 2024 did so. One man won the same state assembly seat repeatedly, much of that time from prison. Foreign firms appear where the contracts are large, in a helicopter deal cancelled over alleged bribes whose Italian executive was later acquitted, and a fighter-jet purchase a French judge is still investigating. New York prosecutors have charged the founder of a large Indian conglomerate over bribes to state officials; he denies it.
India.imp: When the movement that trains the governing party's ministers keeps no membership list, voters cannot tell who in the cabinet answers to whom. When nearly half the lower house has criminal cases pending, a complaint against a local strongman goes to institutions he may sit above. And the pharmaceutical exports land on people who never had a vote here at all, in West African street markets supplied with pills that neither country approved for sale.

Indonesia.d: Indonesia's deepest record is also its oldest. In the late 1950s the Ford Foundation, an American philanthropy, paid for economists from the University of Indonesia to take doctorates at Berkeley; after Suharto took power in 1966 he made them his economic team, and they ran the planning agency and the finance ministry for the next fifteen years, bringing inflation down sharply and opening the country to foreign investors. Nothing about it was hidden, and it still shapes who is considered qualified to run an economy here. Foreign companies show up where procurement is large. A US agrochemical firm had a consulting company pay a senior official at the environment ministry while that ministry was assessing its genetically modified cotton, and settled with American prosecutors; the head of the state airline was jailed for eight years over bribes that prosecutors traced to two European aircraft and engine makers. Religious organisations sit inside politics openly rather than by stealth: the supreme leader of Nahdlatul Ulama, the country's largest Muslim organisation, became vice-president in 2019, while the government stripped Hizb ut-Tahrir of legal status in 2017 and warned that civil servants who stayed members would lose their jobs. Pemuda Pancasila, a paramilitary group founded in 1959 that took part in the killings of 1965 and 1966, was formally part of the ruling party for two decades and still does extortion and protection work alongside local politics. Drug cases reach high: a two-star general days from commanding the Jakarta police was convicted of having seized methamphetamine replaced with alum and sold on.
Indonesia.imp: Economic policy written by people trained and paid for abroad meant the terms on which Indonesia opened to foreign capital were set inside a small circle, and that circle, not the voters, decided what the country owed and to whom. A bribe at the environment ministry means a crop safety assessment was bought. And where a paramilitary group collects parking fees and protection money with official tolerance, small traders pay a second tax that no budget records.

Iran.d: In Iran the outside force is mostly an inside one that grew until it was both. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the state's ideological military force, runs a construction business: its engineering arm controls more than eight hundred registered companies, working in dams, tunnels, oil and gas fields. In 2009 a consortium backed by Guards-linked foundations bought control of the Telecommunication Company of Iran, which runs the fixed-line network and the largest mobile operator, the network the state uses to filter what people say. A Guards unit said it left telecoms in 2018. The drug courts are live. Defence lawyers describe the revolutionary courts that try drug cases as security-dominated, moving fast against small defendants while leaving trafficking networks untouched. One attorney who handled more than seventy such cases compiled a report on two named Tehran judges and submitted it with the case files; lawyers who press such cases report being turned on themselves. With no independent forum, none of it can be tested. Older records belong to another era: the head of the Shah's secret police signed a five-service intelligence club's charter in 1976, and one of the Shah's prime ministers was Grand Master of Iran's masonic lodge. A clerical society purged in 1983 is reported to have later placed members in the judiciary and government staffing offices.
Iran.imp: When the army owns the construction industry, a bid for a public contract is judged by a competitor with guns, and the price and the delivery date are whatever it says they are. When the same force has controlled the phone network, a private call is a state record. In the courts, a person caught with a small quantity gets a fast hearing and, in hundreds of cases a year, a hanging, while the networks above them keep working.

Iraq.d: Iraq's clearest case of an outside force inside the state is written into law. The Popular Mobilization Forces formed in 2014 to fight Islamic State: around 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. A law passed in 2016 made them a branch of Iraq's armed forces, under the prime minister and paid from the state budget. One of them, Kata'ib Hezbollah, has been listed by the United States as a terrorist organisation since 2009 and staffs several of the PMF's brigades. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it takes orders from Iran's supreme leader. The commission's chairman, sanctioned by the US Treasury over the killing of protesters in 2019, remains in post. Money leaves through a separate door. In 2021 and 2022 about $2.5 billion was taken out of a tax authority account through hundreds of cheques written to front companies posing as oil firms owed refunds; a Baghdad court sentenced ten people, among them a former head of parliament's finance committee and the prime minister's former office chief, while several senior tax and bank officials were never charged. The drug trade is newer and growing. Captagon seizures have risen steeply, most of the traffic crossing the long border with Syria, and the state has begun drug-testing its own employees and teachers.
Iraq.imp: A soldier paid by Iraq who answers to a commander in another country means the armed forces are not under the government voters chose, and the people who shot protesters in 2019 are still on the payroll. The tax money that went out the door was the public's, and $2.5 billion is schools, electricity and salaries not delivered. The drug testing of teachers and officials is a sign of how far the trade now runs through the institutions families deal with daily.

Israel.d: What is documented in Israel is mostly domestic capture plus an export business. The long-running case is Case 4000. Prosecutors say Benjamin Netanyahu, while prime minister and communications minister, handed regulatory decisions worth large sums to the controlling owner of Bezeq, the country's biggest telecoms company, in exchange for favourable coverage on that owner's news site. He is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust, denies it, and asked the president for a pardon in 2025 while the trial was still running. The export is surveillance. NSO Group sells Pegasus, software that takes over a phone, only to governments and only under Israeli defence ministry export licences, which makes each sale a foreign-policy decision. Researchers tied its use by state clients to the surveillance of journalists and dissidents, including people around Jamal Khashoggi before Saudi agents killed him, and the US Commerce Department put the company on a trade blacklist in 2021. Two further records sit alongside. Serving police officers have been convicted of passing investigative material to crime organisations. And aides to the prime minister are under investigation over suspicion that they worked for Qatar, a case that has not been tested. Two drug makers based here also paid billions to settle American opioid claims without admitting wrongdoing, part of it in supplies of the overdose antidote.
Israel.imp: A regulator captured by the company it regulates shows up in phone bills and in what the news does not cover. Spyware sold under export licence means a journalist in another country can be read through their own phone because two governments found that useful. Officers leaking files to crime organisations put witnesses in danger and end cases before they start. And the opioid settlements buy an end to litigation rather than a finding of fact.

Japan.d: Movements with a religious or nationalist core hold the firmest grip inside Japan's government, and they hold it by supplying what politicians need: volunteers, votes and donations. Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby campaigning for constitutional revision and patriotic education, works through a cross-party league of members of parliament rather than by running candidates of its own; most of the cabinet formed in October 2025 sits in that league or in the Shinto Political League, the political arm of the national shrine association, and the prime minister has served in the first. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, ran a parallel track through campaign help and event fees until the ruling party surveyed its own 379 lawmakers and found 179 with ties to it; Tokyo courts have since ordered the church's Japanese branch dissolved over four decades of coercive donation-taking. Organised crime goes at companies rather than at ministries: brokers placing labourers into the taxpayer-funded Fukushima clean-up, a large bank ordered to improve its conduct after its loans reached gang members. The oldest lesson comes from the nuclear regulator. A parliamentary commission found that it asked plant operators what they wanted before writing safety rules, told them they need not plan for losing all power, and let the company running Fukushima put off earthquake checks for years.
Japan.imp: Rules end up written for the people in the room. The nuclear regulator's deference showed up as a plant with no plan for losing power, and the clean-up bill fell on taxpayers while gang-linked brokers took a cut of the workers' pay. Where a church supplies a campaign, the people it has taken money from find nobody in government in a hurry to act on their complaints. Watch which lobbies a new cabinet's ministers belong to.

Jordan.d: Jordan's documented problem sits on its northern border, where the amphetamine captagon moves out of Syria toward the Gulf, and the state has been pulled into it from the inside. Jordan's own State Security Court has convicted serving and former soldiers of moving pills and weapons across the frontier, which is the clearest evidence anywhere on this corridor that the protection reaches into the force doing the intercepting. The army also strikes production and storage sites inside Syria. Since Syrian production was disrupted at the end of 2024 the smugglers have changed method rather than stopped: heavy-lift helium balloons with satellite guidance and timed release mechanisms, launched from empty desert so that no local help is needed, drop their loads once across the line. Jordan intercepted more than a hundred such attempts in nine months. The other outside force here is political rather than criminal. The interior ministry banned all Muslim Brotherhood activity in April 2025 and said its assets would be seized, after arrests over an alleged weapons plot that the group denied knowing about. The Brotherhood's political arm is still the largest party in parliament, with 31 of 138 seats, and the United States designated the Jordanian branch a terrorist organisation in January 2026.
Jordan.imp: A border force with members on the smugglers' payroll is a border that leaks, and what leaks is a drug that wrecks the young people who end up taking it here and in the countries beyond. The balloon campaign means interception now depends on radar and luck rather than on checkpoints. On the political side, the largest party in parliament has been outlawed as an organisation while its members keep their seats, which leaves voters unsure what they are allowed to support.

Kazakhstan.d: Almost nothing is documented inside Kazakhstan's state on this map, and the one case on record shows a government declining to do what a foreign capital asked. After the July 2016 coup attempt in Turkey, Ankara pressed Central Asian governments to close schools founded with help from the Gulen movement, the religious network of the preacher Fethullah Gulen that Turkey blames for the coup. Kazakhstan refused to shut them. What happened instead was quieter: the foundation that sponsored 33 Turkish-Kazakh lyceums announced that it was renaming them, and no government order behind the change was reported. The pressure arrived, the schools stayed open under a new name, and no official was found to have acted on Turkey's behalf. Beyond that, the organisations recorded as present are the kinds that move among elites without needing a post in a ministry: Catholic bodies, the Order of Malta, the banned party Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Turkish nationalist Grey Wolves. The country's reading for people inside the state carrying outside loyalties is middling and its defences against them are weak, so the thin record reflects what anyone has managed to document rather than a finding that there is little to find.
Kazakhstan.imp: For most people here the practical effect so far is thin: a school changed its sign. The wider cost is that a foreign government can reach into what children are taught by leaning on a sponsor instead of on a minister, and nobody has to answer for it in public. Weak courts and a weak press mean that if something larger were arranged, the record would look much as it looks now. Watch who owns and funds schools and broadcasters.

Korea, DPR.d: North Korea is unusual on this map because the direction runs outward. The state itself is the organisation: a hacking group that steals cryptocurrency, a programme that places remote IT workers inside foreign companies under false identities, and the Reconnaissance General Bureau, the military intelligence arm that runs them, are all based here, and they appear in other countries' records rather than in this one. Nothing is documented of an outside force getting a hand on Pyongyang, which is what a closed state with no independent courts, press or opposition looks like in a dataset. The single case on the map runs the other way and did not hold up. A North Korean freighter delivered 125 kilograms of heroin to a beach in Australia in 2003, and an Australian jury acquitted the captain and senior crew of importation three years later, unpersuaded that they knew what the cargo was; the state link was never established in court. The Unification Church, founded in South Korea, is recorded as having a presence here, a legacy of its founding family's northern origins and its dealings with Pyongyang. What the scores reflect is not cleanliness but opacity: the highest possible reading for actors embedded in the state, and almost no resilience.
Korea, DPR.imp: People here have no way to find out who inside their government answers to whom, and no court that would hear the question. The cost lands mostly elsewhere: a company that unknowingly hires North Korean workers is funding the state, and a cryptocurrency theft traced here is money taken from savers abroad. For North Koreans the relevant fact is that the earnings from these operations do not reach them and cannot be audited by anyone.

Korea, Rep..d: Two churches and one conglomerate account for most of what is documented in South Korea, and the church cases are moving through the courts now. The Unification Church, founded here in the 1950s and long active in conservative politics, bought access with gifts and cash. A special prosecutor's investigation has produced prison sentences for the church's own leader, for a former first lady who accepted a diamond necklace and a designer handbag passed through an intermediary, and for a governing-party floor leader who took 100 million won before the 2022 presidential election and lost his parliamentary seat. A minister in the current government resigned in December 2025 over allegations, which he denies, that the church paid him to help an undersea tunnel project. Shincheonji, a separate church, tried a different route: prosecutors say tens of thousands of its members were signed up as members of the governing party over two years, enough to shape that party's internal votes, and its elderly founder has been indicted. The older pattern is corporate. Samsung's heir was convicted in 2017 of bribing entities tied to the president to win state backing for a merger that tightened his control of the group; he was later pardoned and now chairs it.
Korea, Rep..imp: When a church can deliver members into a party's internal elections, the people choosing candidates are not the voters that party claims to represent. When it can reach a president's household with gifts, its own donors' complaints get a slower hearing. The Samsung case cost shareholders and pension holders: a merger approved with state help reorganised the country's largest company around one family's control. Watch party membership rolls, and whose names appear on ministers' gift declarations.

Kuwait.d: What is documented in Kuwait is open politics rather than infiltration. After Iraq's 1990 invasion the Kuwaiti Muslim Brotherhood broke with the international movement and set up its own party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, known as Hadas. It won seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and occasionally placed members in the cabinet, and it was out of parliament for a time after boycotting the 2013 elections. That is a movement with religious roots contesting elections and sometimes winning, which is what parties do; the record here holds no finding that it took direction from abroad or acted against the state. Alongside it the map records the Trilateral Commission, a private forum where officials and executives from wealthy countries meet, and the Gulf networks that fund Salafi missionary work abroad, with Kuwait as a source of that money rather than a target of it. The readings here are among the lowest in the region for documented cases and for reach. The gap worth noting is between a high score for actors inside the state with outside loyalties and middling defences, which means little has been tested rather than that much has been cleared.
Kuwait.imp: The practical effect for people here is mild and mostly about money leaving. Charities and foundations funded from Kuwait shape mosques and schools in other countries, and there is little public accounting of who gives what to whom. At home, a parliament where a religious party wins and loses seats is politics working rather than failing. What would be worth watching is disclosure: who funds candidates, and whether charitable transfers abroad are reported at all.

Kyrgyzstan.d: Kyrgyzstan's documented problem is protection: men whose business depends on the state leaving them alone, and officials who oblige. The clearest trace is a criminal figure designated by the United States as a drug kingpin in 2011, then repeatedly released or lightly sentenced by Kyrgyz courts for more than a decade, until security forces killed him in 2023. The record of releases is the only documentary evidence that the protection existed. A deputy chief of customs was sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2020 over a smuggling scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country; the journalists who documented it were prosecuted or pushed out, and he settled his domestic case by repaying money and served no prison term at the time. The third case is a foreign state reaching in. Orhan Inandi, a Kyrgyz citizen who ran a network of Turkish-founded schools, disappeared in Bishkek in 2021, and Turkey's president said days later on state television that he had been captured and taken to Turkey. Kyrgyz military prosecutors then opened proceedings, not against whoever took him, but against the national security committee's own border officers who let him out of the country.
Kyrgyzstan.imp: A customs service run as a private toll gate means importers pay twice and the treasury collects once, so clinics and schools go without. When courts release the same man repeatedly, people learn that a sentence depends on who you are. And a citizen can be lifted off a street in the capital and flown abroad with border officers looking away, which is a warning to anyone else a foreign government dislikes. Watch what happens to reporters who name names.

Laos.d: One stretch of riverbank explains most of Laos's record. In 2007 the government leased a piece of Bokeo province in the Golden Triangle to a Chinese casino operator for 99 years and let his company set up and administer a special economic zone there. In 2018 the US Treasury designated that operator's group as a transnational criminal organisation, saying its casino was used to store and distribute heroin and methamphetamine coming out of Myanmar and to launder the proceeds. The UN drugs office has since linked the zone to compounds where people are held and made to run online fraud. What separates this from a state fighting crime badly is the concession itself: the government handed over the administration of territory, and the US State Department reports that confusion between Lao officials and the zone's own security hinders investigation and that no complicit official has ever been investigated, prosecuted or convicted. The casino kept operating and expanding after the designation, which is a fair measure of what a foreign sanction is worth where the host will not act. In 2025 the global anti-money-laundering body placed Laos under increased monitoring, which reaches the banks of the state that granted the lease.
Laos.imp: Inside the zone, people trafficked there to work the phones in fraud compounds are beyond the reach of Lao law, because the officials who would enforce it have no clear authority. Outside it, ordinary Laotians face heavy drug policing, with more than twenty thousand arrests in five years, while the concession at the centre of the trade stays open. A country under monitoring also finds its banks treated as risky, which raises the cost of sending money for everyone.

Lebanon.d: In Lebanon the outside forces are built into the furniture of the state. Hezbollah, a Shia party with an armed wing backed by Iran and listed as a terrorist group by more than two dozen countries, holds seats in parliament and two ministries in the government formed in 2025, and runs a unit of its own for liaison with Lebanon's security agencies; the cabinet approved the principle that only the state should hold weapons in August 2025, and the army produced a plan to disarm the militias, which Hezbollah's leader rejects. The banks are the second structure. A study of ownership found that 18 of the country's 20 major commercial banks had major shareholders linked to the political class; they lent heavily to the state and the central bank until the system collapsed in 2019 and froze depositors' savings. The long-serving central bank governor is now under Western sanctions and charged at home with embezzling public funds. Drugs run through a third layer: traffickers sanctioned abroad over captagon, a laundering network that moved money through exchange houses and used-car sales, and a military court that had twice condemned a wanted trafficker in absentia and then gave him four months once he stood in front of it.
Lebanon.imp: People here lost their savings to banks their own politicians owned, and no banker has gone to prison for it. An armed group holding ministries means the state cannot promise anyone that force is its monopoly, and a court that gives a sanctioned trafficker four months teaches that sentences depend on connections. Health and labour decisions pass through ministries held by a party answerable partly to a foreign capital. Watch who the banks' shareholders are.

Malaysia.d: Malaysia's largest documented case is a bank reaching into a government. 1MDB was a Malaysian state investment fund; bankers at Goldman Sachs arranged its bond issues with a financier, money was diverted, and officials in Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates were paid. Goldman settled with Malaysia for about $3.9 billion in 2020, one of its bankers pleaded guilty in New York and another was convicted, and in December 2025 Malaysia's High Court found former prime minister Najib Razak guilty on all counts tied to the money that reached his personal accounts and sentenced him to fifteen years; he is appealing. The second strand is the drug trade's hold on enforcement rather than on politics. The anti-corruption commission has prosecuted narcotics officers for releasing suspects and reselling seized product, in cases concentrated in Johor and the Klang valley, in a country that sits on the export route out of the Golden Triangle and runs one of the region's busiest transhipment ports. The third is a foreign government's reach: in May 2017 police detained three Turkish nationals under a security law allowing detention without trial and deported them within days, treating them as illegal immigrants once Ankara cancelled their passports.
Malaysia.imp: The money that went into a prime minister's accounts was borrowed in the state's name, and the public is repaying it. Where narcotics officers resell what they seize, a drug case becomes a business decision and the people prosecuted are whoever has no protection. And residents of any nationality learn that a security law written for emergencies can put them on a plane in two days at a foreign government's request. Watch how the 1MDB appeal goes.

Maldives.d: Nothing is documented on this map for the Maldives: no case, no organisation recorded as present, and no finding that any outside force has a hand inside the government. What follows is an estimate rather than a record. Given the country's size, its dependence on tourism and on foreign construction lending, and a long run of contested elections, the likeliest forms would be a foreign state buying influence through infrastructure loans and the contracts attached to them, and money passing through resort and property ownership. The scores here rest on general conditions rather than on evidence, and should be read as a best guess.
Maldives.imp: If this estimate is right, the cost would show up as debt taken on for projects chosen abroad rather than at home, and as property prices driven by money that needs somewhere to sit. None of that is established here. What would make the picture clearer is plain disclosure: who holds the state's loans and on what terms, and who actually owns the resort companies.

Mongolia.d: Mongolia's single documented case is a government getting in the way of a foreign operation on its own soil. In July 2018 Veysel Akcay, who managed the foundation running Turkish-Mongolian schools linked to the Gulen movement, the religious network Turkey blames for its 2016 coup attempt, was seized in Ulaanbaatar. Mongolian authorities grounded a plane at the airport and he was released the same day. Turkish exile outlets reported that Turkey's intelligence service carried out the abduction; Mongolian officials said they had no specific knowledge of one and were investigating. No Mongolian official was found to have helped. Beyond that the map records Chinese police overseas service stations, the informal offices Beijing has used to reach its own nationals abroad, as present here, and notes the Unification Church as probable but undocumented. The readings are among the lowest on the map for documented cases and for reach, with middling scores for both state-embedded actors and resilience. Nothing in the record establishes a pattern. It establishes that one attempt was made and was stopped at an airport.
Mongolia.imp: The practical point for people here is that a foreign service tried to take someone out of the country and the state's own officials blocked the aircraft. That is the system working. The exposure that remains is for residents with ties to China or Turkey, who may find that a dispute at home is followed up here. Watch whether informal foreign police offices operate, and whether extradition requests get a hearing in court.

Myanmar.d: In Myanmar the state does not so much get infiltrated as subcontracted. Armed groups are formally brought inside the structure as border guard forces and then run their own territory. The commander of one Karen force, decorated by the military government, partnered with Chinese investors from 2017 to build the compound city of Shwe Kokko, and was sanctioned by Britain and the United States over forced labour in its scam centres. In the Kokang zone on the Chinese border, the family that supplied the zone's first administrator and a member of the state assembly ran gambling and fraud operations until China took the matter over: Myanmar handed the former zone chief across the border, and a Chinese court sentenced him and his son to death. The drug economy works the same way, through militias recognised by the state in the areas producing the largest assessed volumes of methamphetamine anywhere. The other force here is religious. A Buddhist nationalist monks' association drafted texts that became the Race and Religion Protection Laws passed in 2015, covering conversion, interfaith marriage and birth spacing; the group was later ordered disbanded, but an army spokesman donated to its successor and the junta dropped the sedition case against its best-known monk and gave him a national honour.
Myanmar.imp: Whole districts are governed by whoever holds them, so there is no authority to appeal to, and people trafficked into the scam compounds there are outside any law that functions. The 2015 laws reached into private life, deciding who may marry whom and how often a woman may give birth. Myanmar also sits on the short global blacklist for money laundering, which makes every ordinary bank transfer in and out slower and dearer for people with no part in any of it.

Nepal.d: Nepal's one documented case is diplomatic pressure applied to a ruling party's internal fight. In mid-2020, as the Nepal Communist Party split over the prime minister, China's ambassador in Kathmandu met him, the president and two senior party leaders, reportedly urging them to keep the party together, and that December the Chinese Communist Party sent a delegation from its International Department, the body that handles its relations with foreign parties. Former ministers and diplomats called the meetings interference; the embassy said it only wished to see the party united. That is lobbying at the top of a governing party rather than a post inside the state, and nothing in the record shows a Nepali official acting on instruction. The map also records the Unification Church and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation based in India, as present here. Nepal's readings are low for documented cases and reach but high for actors inside the state with outside loyalties and low for resilience, so what the single case shows is one episode that reporters managed to pin down, not the limit of what happens.
Nepal.imp: When a foreign embassy is working on a governing party's internal split, the question of who leads the country is being settled partly in a room voters cannot enter. The practical cost is in what follows: infrastructure deals, loan terms and border arrangements negotiated by a leadership that owes somebody something. Watch which party officials meet which embassies, and whether party funding is disclosed at all.

Oman.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Oman: no case, and no organisation with an established presence inside the state. What follows is an estimate. Two entries are listed as likely but unproven, the long-collapsed Bank of Credit and Commerce International, which handled hidden money for intelligence services and governments across the Gulf, and Le Cercle, a private forum where security officials and politicians meet without minutes. Given Oman's role as a quiet intermediary between Iran, the Gulf states and the West, the likeliest forms would be intelligence liaison and private channels rather than criminal capture. This is a best guess.
Oman.imp: If the estimate is right, the cost to people here is opacity rather than extraction: decisions about who talks to whom, and what is traded for it, taken through channels that leave no public record. None of it is established. The things that would show it are ordinary disclosure, of who owns the companies that win state contracts and which foreign bodies senior officials belong to.

Pakistan.d: Several different kinds of outside force are documented in Pakistan, and the army appears on both sides of them. A military court convicted a brigadier at general headquarters and four majors in 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned party that had tried to recruit officers to a plan for a coup and a caliphate. The state has also acted against a foreign movement at another government's request: in 2018 the Supreme Court ordered the Gulen network banned and the schools it ran handed to a Turkish state foundation, saying Pakistan was bound by a declaration of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Money is the second strand, in the form of a Karachi exchange house group designated for laundering at multi-billion-dollar scale for drug organisations and listed terrorist groups at once, whose principal pleaded guilty in the United States. A third strand is hereditary rather than conspiratorial: families holding custody of Sufi shrines draw income and votes from devotees, and one such custodian served twice as foreign minister. And while the country was negotiating a bailout in 2019, an IMF staff member was appointed governor of the central bank the day after his predecessor was abruptly removed. Membership and office are documented; direction is not.
Pakistan.imp: When officers inside headquarters are recruited by a party that wants a coup, the institution holding the country's weapons is itself in question. An exchange house moving billions means honest traders compete against money that cost nothing to earn. A shrine custodian in the cabinet brings a devoted vote bank no rival can match on policy. And a lender's own official running the central bank blurs who is setting interest rates. Watch who gets appointed during a bailout.

Philippines.d: Churches that vote as a bloc are the steadiest outside power in Philippine government. Iglesia ni Cristo, which instructs its members to vote together and counts them in the millions, endorses presidents, vice-presidents and whole Senate slates, puts tens of thousands of people onto the main highway in Manila when one of its own is investigated, and had its executive minister appointed a presidential special envoy in 2018. Other churches place their founders directly: an evangelical church's founder served as a deputy speaker of the House, and a preacher who was called the president's spiritual adviser was arrested in 2024 on child-abuse and trafficking charges and is under US indictment for sex trafficking. The second power is the online gambling industry licensed from 2016 to serve players in China. Senate hearings tied its compounds to fraud, trafficking and torture; a mayor turned out to be a Chinese citizen and is serving life for trafficking, a former presidential spokesman faces trafficking charges over a raided hub, and the president banned the sector outright in 2024. Underneath both sits the drug war, in which between six thousand and more than thirty thousand people were killed from 2016 while the trade continued, and which the International Criminal Court is investigating as crimes against humanity.
Philippines.imp: A bloc that can deliver millions of votes gets its complaints heard faster than yours, and cases against its members move slowly. The gambling licences brought fraud compounds into Philippine towns, with people held and beaten inside them, and the shutdown moved those operations rather than closing them. The drug war killed poor people in large numbers without shrinking the trade. Watch who the churches endorse, and whose names appear on licence applications.

Qatar.d: What is documented in Qatar is a neighbour reaching in, not a force embedded inside. In late May 2017 the state news agency and government social media accounts were hacked and made to carry false quotes from the emir; within days Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Bahrain cut ties and imposed a blockade. The Washington Post, citing US intelligence officials, reported that senior Emirati officials had discussed the hacks the day before they happened, though those officials could not say whether the UAE did the hacking or paid for it. The UAE called the report false. The same period produced a second case with the same origin. Project Raven was an Emirati surveillance unit, run through a Dubai firm and staffed partly by former US intelligence operatives, which used an iPhone exploit to target foreign officials and activists, among them Qatar's emir. Three of the Americans involved signed deferred-prosecution agreements with the US Justice Department and paid fines. The map also records Fight Impunity, the Brussels non-profit at the centre of a European Parliament bribery investigation, and the Gulf religious funding networks, as having a presence here.
Qatar.imp: A forged quotation on a state website set off a blockade that cut food and travel routes for ordinary residents for years. Phone surveillance of a head of state is not a private matter either; it shapes what a government will tell its own people and what it holds back. The practical lesson is that the weak point was a news agency's publishing system, not a minister. Watch how official channels are secured and how statements are verified.

Saudi Arabia.d: The oldest arrangement documented here is financial and runs both ways. The US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation, set up in 1974 after the oil embargo, was co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi finance minister and funded almost entirely from a Saudi account held at the US Treasury; a US government audit found that it recycled oil money and steered American goods, services and technology back into the kingdom. The same era put one Saudi intelligence chief at the centre of two networks: he signed the 1976 charter of the Safari Club, a private alliance of five intelligence services, and was later a major shareholder in the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, pleading out of a US prosecution over its concealed takeover of an American bank. Inside the kingdom the direction reverses, with the state reaching into companies. From November 2017 a committee under the crown prince held princes and company chairmen at a Riyadh hotel and took settlements the government valued at about $107 billion in property, companies and cash; some of those held later said they were beaten. At the receiving end of the captagon trade, the adjudicated record consists almost entirely of executed couriers, most of them foreign nationals, and no Saudi official.
Saudi Arabia.imp: A business owner here knows that ownership can be renegotiated in a hotel room without a court, which pushes capital out and makes investment a matter of standing with the palace. The drug record falls on the poorest people in the chain: foreign couriers executed while the trade's organisers and financiers appear in no case at all. The religious funding networks based here shape mosques and schools in other countries with little public accounting. Watch who is detained and what they sign.

Singapore.d: Singapore's record divides between what it polices hard and what it hosts. The hard part is foreign political influence. In 2017 the home affairs ministry cancelled the residence of a professor at a public policy school, calling him an agent of influence of a foreign country it declined to name, and in 2024 it used a foreign-interference law to designate a Hong Kong-born businessman, the first person listed, who had attended a Chinese united front body as an overseas delegate and must now disclose his foreign links and donations. Drug money gets the same treatment at street level: dozens of men a year are convicted under a statute making it a separate offence to hold or move the proceeds of drug dealing, with prison and caning for sums a bank elsewhere would settle with a fine. The hosted part is corporate. Two of the largest offshore trust and company providers named in the Pandora Papers operate from here, administering structures for clients including sanctioned figures; one was fined by the regulator, and neither has been charged over drug proceeds. A ship-supply contractor based here also spent years bribing US Navy officers for schedules and inside information, with a civilian contracting officer in Singapore quashing an early inquiry.
Singapore.imp: The uneven part here is who pays. A courier holding drug cash goes to prison and is caned; a firm that administers the structures hiding ownership pays a regulatory penalty and keeps its licence. The foreign-interference law gives the government wide discretion to name someone as susceptible to cultivation, with little way to contest it, which touches anyone with family or business ties abroad. Watch who gets designated, and whether any firm is ever charged.

Sri Lanka.d: A Buddhist nationalist monks' movement is the force with the clearest hand on the Sri Lankan state. Bodu Bala Sena was founded in 2012 and has been accused of stirring violence against Muslims. The defence secretary, the president's brother and later president himself, opened its training centre as chief guest in 2013, and in 2021 a president appointed its general secretary, the monk Gnanasara, by gazette to chair a task force drafting proposals for a single legal code for the country. The justice minister said he had not been consulted, and the Bar Association said the task force would take over work belonging to parliament and the ministry. The courts have since unwound part of this. Gnanasara had been jailed for contempt in 2018 and pardoned by a president in 2019, was jailed again in 2024 and 2025 over statements about Islam, and in September 2026 the Supreme Court declared the pardon arbitrary and invalid, sending him back to serve the rest of his sentence. Elsewhere the record is thinner. A trafficker's arrest abroad produced photographs of him at a party with police officers and politicians, and the inquiry that followed ended when he was killed in police custody.
Sri Lanka.imp: When a monk accused of inciting hatred is handed the pen for a national legal code, Muslim and Tamil families have reason to read it as a threat rather than a reform. A pardon that lifts a contempt sentence tells courts their orders are provisional. And an inquiry into officers photographed with a trafficker that ends with the trafficker dead in custody leaves those officers unexamined. Watch presidential pardons and task force appointments.

Syria.d: Syria is the case where the drug trade was the state's own business rather than something done to it. Western and European governments designated three of the president's cousins, his brother as commander of the Fourth Armoured Division, the manager of that division's revenues and a sitting member of parliament over the manufacture and export of the amphetamine captagon; one coastal facility was assessed as producing 84 million pills in a single year. The EU described the trade as a regime-led business model, and those findings are executive, not judicial. Alongside it, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force advised and commanded with Assad's forces from 2012, with Hezbollah fighters in combat roles, until the government fell in December 2024 and Iran pulled its commanders out. What has followed is dispersal rather than an ending: production moved from state facilities to Sweida province, held by local armed factions, in smaller and scattered operations harder to reach by border enforcement. A Damascus court sentenced the deposed president and his brother to death in absentia in August 2026 for murder, torture and crimes against humanity, not for the drug trade, while both remain in Russia, which refuses extradition. Human Rights Watch questioned whether those trials were fair.
Syria.imp: A state that manufactures a drug for export does not police it, so the harm lands on users across the region and on Syrians drawn into the work of making and moving it. When the government fell the trade did not: it broke into pieces held by armed factions, which is harder to stop and no safer for the people living nearby. Trials held in absentia against men protected abroad settle nothing. Watch whether any court hears the trafficking charges.

Taiwan.d: Taiwan is pressed mainly from one direction. China's united front system works by winning people over rather than planting agents, and the sums are small: money reaches a minor party chairman, a city council candidate through a Hong Kong bank account, or the village and ward chiefs taken on trips to Zhejiang paid for by a Chinese city government, where officials urge them to back a particular party. Since the Anti-Infiltration Act gave prosecutors a tool, courts have been convicting steadily — a retired official of the cabinet who tried to recruit military personnel, former party aides who passed on the president's travel schedules. The Interior Ministry is now asking the Constitutional Court to dissolve the Chinese Unification Promotion Party, founded by a former Bamboo Union triad leader; police counted 98 organised-crime cases linked to its members since 2010, which is where political infiltration and gangland business meet. A second kind of pressure is commercial rather than political: engineers inside TSMC passed the company's 2-nanometre process secrets to the Taiwan unit of the Japanese equipment maker Tokyo Electron, and a court jailed them. Taiwan's name can also be borrowed from outside — the pager brand Gold Apollo had licensed it to a Budapest company that turned out to be a Mossad front.
Taiwan.imp: What is being bought here is elections, cheaply: a modest payment to a candidate, a free trip for the local official who tells a village how to vote. The cost is that you cannot tell whose money is behind a campaign until a prosecution says so, years later. In the chip plants, decades of work walk out in a file, and the jobs built on that work are less secure for it. Watch who funds local candidates and who pays for delegations to China.

Tajikistan.d: What gets inside the Tajik state comes across the Afghan border. Heroin moves north through the country toward Russia and Europe, and the officials who control the crossings are part of the route rather than an obstacle to it. The record reaches surprisingly high and then stops. Tajikistan's ambassador to Kazakhstan was arrested in Almaty in 2000 with 86 kilograms of heroin in his car; the deputy interior minister was murdered the following year, and prosecutors argued at trial that he was killed for refusing to pay for a consignment. Estimates a decade later put drug money at up to 30 percent of the national economy. Below ministerial level prosecutions do happen — border guard officers at the Vakhsh checkpoint on the Afghan frontier were sentenced in 2012, the longest term going to the checkpoint chief, in whose office investigators found a stock of hashish — but that is the rank at which the record stops, and most seizures are of small dealers. A separate kind of reach is diplomatic. In 2015 President Emomali Rahmon decreed seven schools linked to Turkey's Gulen movement closed, overruling a cabinet decision from 1994 that had let them operate, and handed them to the state as schools for gifted children.
Tajikistan.imp: A border run as a business means the goods that pay best move freely, while the people living near the crossings do not get a police force that works for them. When a large share of the money in the economy may come from one illegal trade, prices, land and politics all bend around it. Convictions stop at checkpoint rank, so there is nobody above that to complain to. Watch which officials get posted to border and customs jobs.

Thailand.d: In Thailand the hand inside the state belongs mostly to the drug trade on the Myanmar border and to the protection business that grows around any illegal market. A sitting senator was indicted in 2023 on trafficking and laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok and sanctioned by the United States over support for the junta; the narcotics board seized more than 400 million baht of property from his homes, and the case runs from production in Shan State into the upper house. The same year the deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over an alleged protection relationship with an online gambling network, in a case that split the police leadership in public. Both remain charges rather than verdicts. Bangkok is also a place where cases die: the administrator of AlphaBay, then the largest darknet drug market, was arrested there in July 2017 and died in custody a week later, which ended the prosecution before any of the evidence was tested. A lawful kind of connection runs alongside all this. The World Economic Forum picks people under about forty for its Young Global Leaders programme, and its 2025 class included Paetongtarn Shinawatra while she was prime minister; the Constitutional Court removed her from office that August.
Thailand.imp: Protection money is paid by the people buying it and recovered from everyone else. A police unit working for a gambling ring is not available for anything else, and a senator under indictment still votes on laws. Cases that reach this high tend to stall, so the practical lesson people draw is that rank is a defence. Watch whether the trafficking counts survive to trial or quietly get dropped, which is what has happened before.

Timor-Leste.d: Timor-Leste's documented case is one operation with a long tail, and it is about oil. In 2004, two years after independence, the Australian Secret Intelligence Service planted listening devices in the government building in Dili to learn what the new country would settle for in talks over the Timor Sea gas fields. The treaty that followed limited Timor-Leste's claims to the seabed. It came out because a former ASIS officer, known in court only as Witness K, told Timor-Leste's lawyer Bernard Collaery; Australia raided both men in 2013. Timor-Leste took Australia to the International Court of Justice, which ordered Australia in 2014 not to interfere with its legal communications, and to the Permanent Court of Arbitration. A new boundary treaty in 2018 replaced the old one and split revenue 80 to 20 in Timor-Leste's favour. Australia then prosecuted the two men who had disclosed the bugging: Witness K pleaded guilty to a secrecy offence and the case against Collaery was dropped. Nobody was prosecuted for the operation itself. Beyond this the map records only listed presences — Australian intelligence, the Cold War propaganda agency Aginter Press, the Order of Malta — with no second case attached to them.
Timor-Leste.imp: A government that cannot keep its own cabinet room private negotiates at a disadvantage, and here the disadvantage was measured in oil and gas revenue for one of Asia's poorest countries: the difference between the treaty signed after the bugging and the one that replaced it fourteen years later. The men who made the operation public faced criminal charges; the officers who carried it out did not. Watch where the revenue under the new boundary actually goes.

Turkiye.d: Turkey is both a target and a source, and its largest arrangement is a reversal. The state now treats the Gulen movement — a religious network that spent decades placing graduates in the police, courts and army — as a terrorist organisation, and has removed its suspected members at a scale no other country has attempted. The judicial council dismissed 2,745 judges, about 36 percent of those then serving, on a single day in July 2016, the day after the failed coup; police and military dismissals followed in the tens of thousands and public-sector dismissals in the hundreds of thousands. The state also took the money: 784 companies were handed to the TMSF, the state deposit-insurance trustee, and most were later returned. Courts have moved both ways. The Ergenekon and Sledgehammer trials jailed officers, politicians and journalists for alleged coup networks, then collapsed — the appeals court found no evidence Ergenekon had existed, and experts found the Sledgehammer documents named a navy ship that did not yet exist on their supposed date. The government now blames those prosecutions on Gulenists inside the police and judiciary. Underneath sits the older layer. The 1996 Susurluk crash put a deputy Istanbul police chief, a sitting MP and a Grey Wolves gunman wanted for murder and trafficking in one car; the parliamentary inquiry concluded that state bodies had used the Grey Wolves, and produced almost no convictions. Turkey exports too: its state religious directorate, the Diyanet, employs imams abroad and gave parliament intelligence reports from them on Gulen followers in dozens of countries.
Turkiye.imp: Purges on this scale mean the judge hearing your case, or the officer policing your street, may hold the post because the previous holder was removed on a security list rather than for anything a court tested. Companies were seized and some handed back, which makes ownership itself a political matter. When a conviction can be annulled years later over forged evidence, no verdict quite settles. Watch who fills a dismissed judge's seat, and whether a seized company is returned or sold.

Turkmenistan.d: The one arrangement documented in Turkmenistan runs through schools. Turkish schools linked to the Gulen movement, a religious network that built its reputation on education, opened across Central Asia in the 1990s, taught the children of officials and professionals, and were for years the respectable route to a foreign language and a university place abroad. Turkmenistan closed or nationalised most of them in 2011, years before Turkey's own break with the movement. What followed went beyond closure. After a wave of detentions in late 2016 of people with some Gulen connection, 18 men were convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and membership of a criminal organisation, according to a joint statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee. Because the trials were closed, what the men were said to have done inside the state cannot be checked from outside. That is the shape of the record here. The country scores among the worst anywhere on the conditions that let outside forces embed in a state, and almost nothing about who is actually inside it is documented, which reflects how little information leaves the country rather than an absence of pressure on it.
Turkmenistan.imp: Closed trials mean a family can be told a relative has 25 years and never learn what for. Parents who had sent children to the best schools available found that choice turned into a liability. For everyone else the lesson is that association is enough, which is how people stop joining things at all. There is no public record to appeal to, so watch instead for what outside human rights organisations manage to get out of the country.

United Arab Emirates.d: The Emirates work in two directions at once. Inward, Dubai is where money made elsewhere is placed. The documented machinery is mundane: exchange and hawala houses designated by the US Treasury for moving funds for sanctioned and trafficking networks, free-zone companies whose real owners are visible only to the zone authority, a gold refining trade where an auditor found that nearly half of one major refiner's business in a single year was cash for gold, including bullion handed over by customers who produced no paperwork, and shell structures in Dubai and the British Virgin Islands used to employ the operatives of a sanctioned Balkan trafficking organisation. The country sat on the Financial Action Task Force grey list from 2022 to 2024, and correspondent banks around the world priced in the risk, which is how a listing bites without a single prosecution.
