The registries were reformed rather than opened. Outward, the state buys standing in international bodies. Through a foundation it gave Interpol donations reported at about 54 million dollars, roughly the combined dues of every other member country, and a senior Emirati interior ministry officer was then elected Interpol president; French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a torture inquiry into him over complaints from detainees, and he denies the allegations. The same approach put the chief executive of the state oil company ADNOC in the chair of the COP28 climate talks, with leaked briefing papers that carried commercial talking points for his meetings with foreign governments.
United Arab Emirates.imp: If money can move through a place while nobody outside can see who owns the company moving it, the proceeds of a cocaine route or a sanctioned regime arrive looking like ordinary trade, and the honest trader competes against them on price. Standing bought with donations means an international policing body can end up useful to a government that wants its critics abroad pursued. Watch the beneficial-ownership rules, and who appears as the local sponsor on a free-zone company's filings.

Uzbekistan.d: The documented story in Uzbekistan is one family and one market. To sell mobile phone service in the country, foreign telecoms companies paid the president's daughter. Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of the late Islam Karimov, controlled companies that took payments in exchange for licences and radio frequencies, and the firms involved later settled foreign-bribery cases with American, Dutch and Swedish authorities; Telia alone paid about 965 million dollars, and Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at 869.3 million. No spycraft was needed and nothing had to be hidden about where power sat: the regulator and the ruling family were effectively the same address, so a company that wanted a licence paid the family and booked it as a consultancy or a stake. The afterlife matters as much as the bribe. Karimova was convicted at home twice and remains in prison, Switzerland dropped its own trial in 2026, and the penalties were paid to foreign treasuries rather than to Uzbekistan. Beyond the telecoms cases the map records Chinese police overseas service stations as present in the country, with the Gulen movement, Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Grey Wolves listed as likely but undocumented.
Uzbekistan.imp: Uzbek phone customers paid for the bribes in their bills, and the money that came back as penalties went to the treasuries of other countries. A market opened by payment ends up with the wrong number of competitors in it, at the wrong prices, for years afterwards. The prosecutions happened abroad, which is the usual shape of these cases: the country where the bribe was taken is the last to get anything back. Watch who holds the licences now.

Vietnam.d: Two quite different things are documented in Vietnam. One is police officers working for the drug trade. Two former members of a Hanoi district drug investigation team were indicted for shielding a Laos-Vietnam network that moved 137 kilograms, and a senior officer in Viet Tri was sentenced to life in 2025 for financing a 12,000-tablet purchase he intended to convert into a staged arrest. Vietnam executes traffickers at those quantities, which is the measure of what the officers were protecting. The other is the state's own use of the language of infiltration. In October 2016 the Ministry of Public Security designated Viet Tan, a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles in 1982 and based in the United States, a terrorist organisation, saying it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments dispute the designation, the US government has said there is no evidence the party is a terrorist group, and Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of belonging to it. Opus Dei is also recorded as present in the country, and the drug firm Novartis and the telecoms firm Ericsson as likely but undocumented.
Vietnam.imp: A drug squad that sells protection decides who gets arrested, and at these quantities an arrest can end in an execution, so an officer's choice is somebody's life. On the other side, a designation that outside governments say has no evidence behind it means a person can be imprisoned for belonging to a party rather than for anything they did. Watch what the actual charge is when someone is prosecuted for membership.

Yemen.d: In Yemen the outside hands are the ones holding the war. The documented case shows how directly it works: the Southern Transitional Council was formed in 2017 with Emirati help to pursue a separate southern state, and in April 2022 it was given a place on the Presidential Leadership Council that governs in the internationally recognised government's name, with its leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi becoming a vice-president. A foreign-sponsored separatist movement was installed inside the state it wants to leave. It did not hold. After a council offensive in December 2025 and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive, al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE and was removed from the council, and a delegation in Riyadh announced the movement's dissolution, which its UAE-based spokesman rejected. Around that single record the map lists presences rather than cases: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Quds Force and its allied militia network, Hezbollah, the Muslim Brotherhood, and DarkMatter, the Emirati cyber-operations firm. Yemen scores among the worst anywhere on the conditions that let outside forces embed, and far less is documented than that implies, because in a war almost nothing can be investigated.
Yemen.imp: When a vice-president's position comes from a foreign capital, the people in the south get a government whose survival depends on a sponsor rather than on them, and the sponsor can take it away again, which is what happened within four years. Armed groups follow whoever is paying their salaries this year. The practical cost is that no authority lasts long enough to deliver water, courts or wages, and the fighting restarts wherever the sponsors disagree.

Australia.d:
Australia's live problem is a foreign state working through donors and community groups. Intelligence advice led the government to cancel the residency of a property developer who had given millions to both main parties and chaired a body described as a peak organisation for groups tied to the Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department; a state anti-corruption commission later traced 100,000 dollars in cash delivered to a Labor head office back to him, disguised as staff donations. A Melbourne community leader became the first person convicted under the 2018 foreign interference law, for using ethnic associations to reach an acting immigration minister. India's foreign intelligence service had officers expelled after an operation that cultivated politicians and a state police service.

The commercial side is larger. The big accounting firms sit on both sides of tax law: a partner hired to advise the Treasury on new anti-avoidance rules passed confidential plans to dozens of colleagues, after which the firm sold its government consulting arm for a dollar; no charges have been reported. Casinos and banks have paid the largest civil penalties in the country's corporate history for failing to monitor junket money and cash deposits. A 99-year lease of the port of Darwin to a company whose owner has Party ties is still contested; both main parties have promised to return it to Australian ownership and the company is now in arbitration.

Older ground: outlaw motorcycle gangs reached into a construction union on state projects, and a Sydney bank staffed with retired US intelligence officers collapsed in 1980.
Australia.imp: Donations that buy access change which communities get heard and which policies get drafted. When an accounting firm advises the Treasury on closing tax loopholes and then tells clients where the gaps are, the revenue lost is money not spent on services. Casino and bank penalties are paid by shareholders, not by the people whose drug money moved through the tills. Watch donation disclosure, and who government hires to write its rules.

Fiji.d:
The one documented arrangement in Fiji is a policing one, and part of it is still in place. Under a 2011 police cooperation agreement signed while the country was under military rule, China's Ministry of Public Security attached officers to the Fiji Police Force, two at a time from 2013, and posted a police liaison officer to its embassy in 2021. Fijian officers train in China. In 2017 Chinese police working with local officials arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China, which is the kind of operation such an arrangement makes possible: a foreign force reaching people on Fijian soil through Fiji's own police.

In March 2024 the home affairs minister said Fiji had asked China to withdraw the embedded officers but would keep the agreement itself, reviewing it every six months. The officers go; the framework stays.

Nothing else is documented inside the Fijian state. A South Korean church is recorded as present, and the Indian nationalist volunteer organisation RSS is thought likely to be active among Fiji's Indo-Fijian population, though no case has been established.
Fiji.imp: When a foreign police force can work through your own, the people most exposed are residents from that country's diaspora, who can be picked up and flown home without an extradition hearing. For everyone else, a force trained and equipped abroad answers partly to someone outside the country. Watch the six-monthly reviews, and whether the text of the agreement is ever published.

Kiribati.d:
Kiribati's documented case is a continuing one: up to a dozen uniformed Chinese police officers work alongside the Kiribati Police Service on six-month rotations, which the acting police commissioner has confirmed. They do community policing, teach martial arts and provide IT support for a crime database. That is ordinary-looking work, and it puts a foreign ministry inside the service that holds local records and decides who gets arrested.

How it came about is straightforward. Kiribati switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019 and asked Beijing for policing help in 2022; the officers followed. The ministry sending them, China's Ministry of Public Security, runs police and internal security at home rather than foreign aid, and training carries working methods with it.

Nothing else is documented. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic charitable order that keeps its own diplomatic service, is recorded as present. Kiribati is a small state with a small administration, which is part of why a single offer of equipment and training can change how an entire service works.
Kiribati.imp: A crime database built and maintained with foreign help holds the names of people that foreign government may have its own interest in. Training shapes how officers handle crowds, suspects and critics. For people in Kiribati the practical questions are who can see police records and who answers if an officer oversteps. Watch whether the rotations are reported to parliament and what the database is used for.

Marshall Islands.d:
The documented case here is a straightforward purchase of a law. Two China-born businesspeople who had bought Marshallese passports paid tens of thousands of dollars to officials, among them members of parliament, over about four years, to get a statute passed creating a semi-autonomous Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region: a zone inside the country with its own administration, on an atoll whose people were displaced by nuclear testing. Both pleaded guilty in a New York court and were sentenced, the longer term 42 months.

The US State Department then barred a former president and a sitting member of parliament from the United States over those bribes. The former president denies taking them.

Two things make the arrangement work. The buyers already held Marshallese passports, bought rather than inherited, so they had standing before they started paying. And the prize was not a contract but a law, which is harder to undo than a deal. Nothing else appears on the map: no foreign intelligence service, no criminal network inside the police, no lender or company shown writing policy. The case was brought by prosecutors abroad, not at home.
Marshall Islands.imp: When a legislature can be paid to carve out a special zone, the people living on that land lose any say over who governs it, and here that land belongs to a community already displaced once. The check came from a court in another country, which is a thin kind of protection to rely on. Watch who holds bought passports, and whether special-zone bills come back.

Micronesia.d:
Micronesia's entry rests on an allegation made by its own outgoing president. In a thirteen-page letter in March 2023, David Panuelo accused China of political warfare, meaning bribery, threats and pressure on officials, aimed at keeping the country aligned with Beijing, or at least neutral, in any war over Taiwan. He wrote that he had considered switching recognition to Taiwan. China rejected the claims, and nothing in the letter has been tested by a court or an inquiry.

That is the whole documented record, and it is worth being plain about what kind of record it is: a head of state's account, not a finding. It is on the map because of what Micronesia has that outsiders want, which is a vote on recognition and in international bodies. Recognition is the lever, and both Beijing and Taipei pull it.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with its own diplomatic service, is also recorded as present. No criminal network and no foreign agency inside the state has been documented.
Micronesia.imp: If officials are being paid or pressured over a foreign-policy choice, voters are not the ones making it. The letter shows a second cost: suspicion that cannot be settled, because there is no inquiry to settle it. Watch whether parliament examines the claims, and whether gifts and travel taken by officials are disclosed.

Nauru.d:
Nauru's documented record is about phosphate and about detention, the two things outsiders buy here. Australian federal prosecutors charge a Queensland phosphate trader with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians over several years to win rock deals; the case has been delayed repeatedly. In a related prosecution a Sydney businessman pleaded guilty to paying over 120,000 dollars to a Nauruan member of parliament and a minister, and was jailed.

The second thread is the money Australia pays contractors to run its offshore asylum centre on the island. A 2023 newspaper investigation found subcontracts worth millions going to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, including suspect payments to the justice minister and about 2.6 million dollars to a company of a man who later became president. The reporters were careful to say they were not claiming the payments were bribes, and the minister denies wrongdoing; the same investigation said Australia's home affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations since 2010.

Both threads run the same way. One export and one foreign customer, and a government small enough that a few people hold both ends.
Nauru.imp: Nauru's income comes from phosphate and from hosting Australia's detention centre, so money reaching a few officials can decide what the whole country lives on. For the asylum seekers held there, the contractors running the camp were chosen in a process reporters traced back to the leaders' own circles. Watch whether the bribery case ever reaches trial, and whether the detention contracts are published.

New Zealand.d:
New Zealand's record is mostly about policy institutes and private networks rather than crime. Several ministers came to office out of free-market think tanks: a finance minister of the early 1990s belonged to the Mont Pelerin Society, a long-standing international society of free-market economists, and the current deputy prime minister worked for conservative institutes in Canada in the same network before entering parliament. A later prime minister appears on the World Economic Forum's young-leaders list. Membership and office are documented; no inquiry has found that any of these bodies directed a government decision, and the distinction matters.

The sharper case concerns China. Two members of parliament, one from each main party, left at the 2020 election after intelligence agencies raised concerns. One had been a Communist Party member and had taught at People's Liberation Army institutions that trained intelligence linguists. Neither was charged, and neither departure was explained to voters at the time.

The money side is a casino. The country's largest operator settled with the financial intelligence unit over failing to monitor high-value play, and faced the same complaint about its Australian casino. New Zealand pays the highest methamphetamine prices in the world, and the casino floor is where that cash surfaces.
New Zealand.imp: When ministers arrive from policy institutes funded by business, the ideas reaching cabinet have already been filtered somewhere outside the election. That is lawful, and it is worth knowing. The casino failures bite more directly: unmonitored high-value play is how drug money gets cleaned, and the harm lands on the households the drugs came from. Watch who funds the institutes, and whether gambling operators now check sources of funds.

Palau.d:
Palau's documented case involves an organised-crime figure rather than a state. Wan Kuok-koi, known as Broken Tooth, is the former head of Macau's 14K triad; the US Treasury sanctioned him in 2020 and said he sits on a Chinese Communist Party United Front body. Reporting by OCCRP found that he visited Palau in 2018 as a guest of the government, and that a former postmaster general and a former state governor were listed as directors of his Palau Hongmen association, registered in early 2019 to plan a casino zone on the island of Angaur.

The president of the day opposed the casino, the association applied to dissolve, and the effort stopped there. The reporters did not establish that the Chinese state directed it.

What this shows is the shape of an approach rather than its success. A small island state is offered a casino development; local notables are put on the paperwork so the venture reads as domestic; and the people behind it come from a trade that needs somewhere to put money. Hong Kong and Macau triads are thought likely to be present more widely, but nothing further is documented.
Palau.imp: A casino zone on a small island brings in money that needs cleaning, and the jobs and rents it creates make the arrangement hard to undo later. Former officials lending their names to the registration is what makes it look local. For Palauans the question is who vets a foreign investor before land is committed. Watch company registrations and who sits on their boards.

Papua New Guinea.d:
Papua New Guinea's documented cases divide between a bank and the police. In 2014 the government borrowed about 1.2 billion US dollars through the Swiss bank UBS to buy shares in an oil company, against cabinet advice and before parliament had approved it; the treasurer who objected lost his job. A commission of inquiry heard that the state lost around 432 million dollars while the bank took fees and interest, found the loan unlawful, and recommended barring UBS from the country for a decade. The prime minister of the time was later charged with giving false evidence to that inquiry.

The police side is less resolved. After a light aircraft loaded with cocaine crashed on a makeshift runway outside Port Moresby, the police commissioner said publicly that there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary and promised to remove them. The Australian-based organisers were convicted and the pilot jailed; the officers alleged to have enabled the night flights were not charged.

A third thread is Australian. The contractor paid hundreds of millions to run Australia's asylum centre on Manus Island is the subject of an allegation by its own former director that money routed to a businessman close to senior officials included a bribe. The company's former chief executive denies any improper payment.
Papua New Guinea.imp: A loan that cost the state hundreds of millions is money that did not reach clinics, roads or schools, and it was taken before parliament agreed to it. Where officers help move cocaine, the people who lose are the communities it passes through and anyone who reports what they see. Watch whether the inquiry's recommendations are acted on, and whether any officer is ever charged.

Samoa.d:
Nothing is documented on this map for Samoa yet: no case of an outside force inside the government, a company or an international body. A South Korean church is recorded as present, and that is the whole entry.

On the pattern of its neighbours, the likely approaches are pressure and inducements tied to diplomatic recognition, offers of policing or infrastructure help from a larger state, and ordinary lobbying of a small administration by foreign contractors. That is a best guess drawn from what is documented elsewhere in the Pacific, not a finding about Samoa.
Samoa.imp: An absence of documented cases is not proof that nothing happens; it can also mean nobody has looked. For people in Samoa the protections that would show it are the mundane ones: published contracts, declared gifts and travel for ministers, and an auditor who reports to parliament. Watch for any new policing or security agreement with an outside government, and ask to see the text.

Solomon Islands.d:
The Solomon Islands holds the clearest documented case in the Pacific of a foreign government's money reaching legislators. In 2019 China agreed to fund a discretionary fund run by the prime minister's office, as Taiwan had done before it, so the old practice continued with a new donor. At a livestreamed parliamentary budget hearing the prime minister's own secretary said China had provided about 2.49 million US dollars spent in 2021, and that 39 of the 50 members of parliament received payments in two tranches that November and December. The prime minister survived a no-confidence vote weeks later; the opposition leader said the money was keeping him in power, which his office denied.

The recognition switch itself was contested. Members of parliament told reporters that both Beijing and Taipei had offered them money to sway the vote, riots followed, and anger over the switch fed the violent unrest in Honiara two years later.

Policing came next. China sent a police advisory team after those riots and signed a security agreement letting Honiara request Chinese police and military personnel. In 2025 Chinese public-security police began a local pilot of a community-surveillance model, suspended after objections. A critic of the relationship became prime minister in 2026 and promised a review.
Solomon Islands.imp: A fund that pays most of the legislature turns a no-confidence vote into a question of who is paying. Constituents cannot tell whether their member is representing them or a donor abroad. The policing side reaches further: a surveillance model from another country was tried on Solomon Islanders until local objections stopped it. Watch whether the security agreement is published and whether the discretionary fund is audited.

Tonga.d:
Tonga's one documented case is about a national fund and an outsider given authority over it. Tonga sold passports to Hong Kong residents before 1997 and put the proceeds into the Tonga Trust Fund. An American financial adviser, Jesse Bogdonoff, whom the king appointed court jester in 1999, moved the fund into a firm that invested in life-insurance policies bought from the terminally ill. The firm went bankrupt in 2002 and about 33 million dollars was gone, roughly 40 per cent of a year's state revenue. Tonga sued him and he settled in 2004 without admitting fraud.

This is not infiltration by a network. It is a very small treasury exposed to one adviser with no institution checking him, and a title from the palace standing in for a mandate. The money itself came from selling citizenship, a trade that draws people who want a document rather than a home; the passport-sale industry is the other presence the map records here.

Nothing else is documented: no foreign intelligence service, no criminal group inside the police, no lodge or church placing members in office.
Tonga.imp: Losing close to half a year's state revenue means money meant to outlast the passport sales bought nothing at all, and a settlement with no admission leaves no finding anyone can point to. For Tongans the live question is who now decides where public funds are invested and who gets to see the statements. Watch whether the trust fund's holdings are reported to parliament.

Tuvalu.d:
Nothing is documented on this map for Tuvalu. No outside force is recorded inside its government, its companies or an international body, and no organisation is listed as present.

On the pattern of its neighbours, the approaches most likely to be made are inducements tied to diplomatic recognition, offers of policing or infrastructure assistance from a larger state, and ordinary lobbying of a very small administration by foreign contractors. That is an inference from what is documented elsewhere in the Pacific, not a finding about Tuvalu.
Tuvalu.imp: With no documented case, the honest answer is that nobody can say what is or is not happening here. The things that would show it are mundane: published agreements with foreign governments, declared gifts and travel, and accounts an auditor can examine. Watch for any policing or security pact, and ask whether its text is public.

Vanuatu.d:
Vanuatu is at an early stage of the arrangement several of its neighbours already have. China has sent police advisers since 2023. In September 2025 Vanuatu's internal affairs minister met China's Minister of Public Security in Beijing; China donated police equipment worth about 720,000 New Zealand dollars, including motorcycles and drones, and both sides said they were discussing a wider policing partnership.

That is the whole documented record, and the detail worth holding onto is which ministry is doing the giving. China's Ministry of Public Security runs police and internal security at home, including the surveillance of its own citizens. Equipment and training carry working methods with them, and the force receiving them is the one that polices protests and keeps records on people.

No agreement has been signed and published, so what is on the map is an approach rather than an outcome. Nothing else appears: no foreign intelligence operation, no criminal network inside the state, no church or lodge placing members in office.
Vanuatu.imp: Donated motorcycles and drones are useful, and they also set what a police force is able to watch. If a partnership is signed, its terms will decide who can be called in, who sees police data and what happens when a foreign officer oversteps. For people in Vanuatu that is worth knowing before it is agreed rather than after. Watch for the text of any policing pact.

Albania.d: Albania is one of the few states to have admitted in law that its own institutions were captured, and then tried to clear them out. A decriminalisation law adopted in 2015 bars people with serious convictions, at home or abroad, from elected office and makes candidates declare their records; several MPs and mayors have lost their seats under it, one of them over an Italian drug-trafficking conviction, and hundreds of state employees left their jobs. A parallel EU-monitored vetting of every judge and prosecutor, running since 2017, has removed or forced out roughly half of those assessed, mostly on unexplained wealth. What was being cleared out is the cannabis and cocaine trade. Saimir Tahiri was interior minister until 2017; after Italian police arrested his cousin in a cannabis case in which wiretaps mentioned the minister, he was convicted of abuse of office, though the trafficking and organised-crime charges were dropped. The money is still arriving. In 2026 the special prosecution seized over 100 million euros, tracing cocaine proceeds into land deals along the coast and into high-rise towers under construction in the capital, and its seizure order refers to meetings with senior state officials whom it does not name. A separate hand is Iran's: a 2022 cyberattack shut down government online services, and Albania broke off diplomatic relations over it.
Albania.imp: Half the judiciary gone means a case you file may outlast the judge hearing it, and those who remain were vetted on their bank accounts rather than their rulings. Cocaine proceeds in coastal land and Tirana towers set what a flat costs, and the buyer competing with that money is on an Albanian salary. Watch whether the senior officials the seizure order mentions but does not name are ever charged.

Andorra.d: Andorra's position is unusual in that one of its two heads of state is a foreign official by right of office. Under the 1993 constitution the president of France is ex officio a co-prince alongside the Bishop of Urgell, a role Emmanuel Macron has held since 2017. Acting alone the French co-prince appoints a member of the Constitutional Tribunal and of the Superior Council of Justice and must agree to treaty texts; jointly with Andorra's head of government he appoints the head of government, calls elections and signs laws into force. None of this is covert, and it is written into the constitution. The contested part of the record is a bank. In March 2015 the US Treasury's financial crimes unit named Banca Privada d'Andorra a primary money-laundering concern, saying senior managers had knowingly handled transactions for third-party launderers working for criminal organisations and moved the money through US correspondent banks. Andorra took the bank over the next day and wound it up within the week; clients had to prove their own funds legitimate to recover them. The Treasury then withdrew the finding, Spanish courts dismissed money-laundering cases against the bank, and in July 2025 an Andorran court sentenced eighteen executives, the former chief executive to seven years. They are appealing.
Andorra.imp: Depositors learned that a bank can be shut in a week on a foreign regulator's notice, and that getting their own money back meant proving where it came from. Some clients named in the case have never been convicted of anything, and the US finding that triggered it was later withdrawn. In the constitutional arrangement, a French election changes who signs Andorran laws. Watch the appeals, since the convictions and the withdrawn finding point in opposite directions.

Austria.d: Austria's neutrality and Vienna's role as a diplomatic and banking hub make it a place where other states operate. Russia is the most documented. The Freedom Party signed a five-year cooperation agreement with United Russia in late 2016, and its ministers sat in the federal government from 2017 to 2019; the agreement lapsed at the end of 2021 when a later party leader declined to renew it. Karin Kneissl, foreign minister during that period, was appointed by the Russian government to the board of the state oil company Rosneft in 2021, resigned the following year and now lives in Russia. The sharpest case is a conviction: in May 2026 a Vienna court found that Egisto Ott, a former officer of Austria's domestic intelligence service, had spied for Russia through the fugitive Wirecard executive Jan Marsalek, searching police databases for people Moscow wanted located, passing on a journalist's home address and handing over phones from the interior minister's office. Turkey operates through religion instead. Austria's 2015 Islam law bans foreign funding of religious bodies, and in 2018 the government closed mosques and put under review the residence permits of about 40 imams employed by the Austrian branch of Turkey's state religious directorate. The Cold War left its own deposit: a secret anti-communist paramilitary force whose founder later became interior minister, and more than 80 US arms caches hidden on Austrian soil without the government being told.
Austria.imp: A governing party with a standing agreement with the ruling party of another state makes it hard to say whose interest a cabinet decision serves. When an intelligence officer sells database searches, anyone recorded in those systems — a journalist, an exile — becomes findable by the government they fled. Where mosques are staffed and paid from abroad, a congregation's religious life runs on another country's politics. Watch which parties sign foreign cooperation agreements, and who employs the imams.

Belarus.d: Belarus is the plainest case on the map, because both governments describe the arrangement openly. After the disputed 2020 election left Alexander Lukashenko without a credible mandate, Vladimir Putin promised him a 1.5 billion dollar loan, and what followed was less infiltration than a transfer of control. In February 2022 Russian forces launched part of the invasion of Ukraine from Belarusian territory. A referendum that same month removed the constitutional ban on nuclear weapons being based in the country and allowed permanent Russian bases. Russia supplied nuclear-capable Iskander-M missiles the next year, Putin said warheads had been delivered, and he has said Russia keeps control of them. There is no court case here and no denial. The arrangement sits in treaties, joint presidential statements and a constitutional amendment, which is what separates it from the covert work recorded elsewhere: a dependency created by a loan to a government that badly needed one, then written into law. Beyond it the map lists the Order of Malta as present, with the Russkiy Mir Foundation and Interpol as likely but undocumented.
Belarus.imp: Belarusians voted in a referendum that put foreign nuclear weapons on their soil and foreign bases there permanently, and the weapons are not under their own government's control. A country used as a launch point for a war becomes a target in it. Because none of this is secret there is nothing to expose; the only open question is whether a future government could unpick treaties and a constitutional amendment. Watch the basing arrangements.

Belgium.d: Belgium holds two things that attract outside hands: the European Union's institutions and the port of Antwerp. In Brussels the approach is usually a payment or a favour to someone who can move a position inside the European Parliament. The Qatargate investigation began when police found bags of cash at the home of a parliamentary vice-president in December 2022; prosecutors allege that Qatar and Morocco paid to shift Parliament's positions, with money passing through a Brussels human-rights NGO run by a former MEP who had chaired the Parliament's human rights subcommittee and who later signed a plea deal. The Huawei case has the same shape with a company in place of a state: prosecutors allege that gifts, travel and football tickets bought signatures on a 2021 letter opposing curbs on foreign 5G equipment, at up to 15,000 euros for the author and 1,500 for each co-signer. Parliament has also used the sanction it controls, withdrawing the access badges of Amazon's lobbyists after the company skipped hearings on workers' rights. Foreign states listen as well as pay: Snowden documents showed the NSA bugging EU missions and Britain's GCHQ breaking into Belgacom, the majority state-owned telecom. At Antwerp, through which the largest cocaine volumes in Europe move, what gets recruited is port workers, customs staff and police, because container reference codes, gate access and scanning records are the things worth buying, not the cargo. The Cold War left a stay-behind network that a Senate inquiry documented in 1991 and a far-right group with gendarmes and State Security informants inside it.
Belgium.imp: Rules that bind hundreds of millions of people get written in a building where a signature on a letter had a price list, so the law you live under on 5G, tobacco or vaccine contracts was shaped partly by who had access — and in the Pfizer case the Commission could not produce the messages that made the deal. At Antwerp, a job at a container terminal is something traffickers recruit for, and a justice minister needed protection after a kidnap plot. Watch lobby registers and immunity votes.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d: Bosnia is the one country here where a foreign official holds legal power over the state by agreement. The Office of the High Representative was created by the 1995 Dayton peace deal and answers to the Peace Implementation Council of foreign governments; since 1997 its Bonn powers have let it impose binding laws and remove officials, and by 2004 it had dismissed 139 of them, 58 on a single day. Germany's Christian Schmidt has held the post since 2021, and Russia, China and some Bosnian politicians call his appointment illegitimate and have pressed at the UN to close the office. The pull in the other direction runs through Republika Srpska, the Serb entity. Its police signed a cooperation agreement with Russia's interior ministry on intelligence and counter-terrorism, and its long-time president Milorad Dodik met Putin repeatedly from 2022, received a Russian state order, was sanctioned by the United States for obstructing the peace agreement, and was then delisted in October 2025, a day after meeting Russia's foreign minister; a Bosnian court has banned him from politics for six years. Underneath both sits organised crime: twenty-three people were arrested in Sarajevo in 2024 over trafficking and laundering for a kingpin already sentenced in the Netherlands, and Europol said corrupt officials who facilitated the network were among them.
Bosnia and Herzegovina.imp: Politics here is conducted toward audiences abroad rather than at home. A law can be imposed by an envoy nobody elected, and a politician can be sanctioned, delisted and barred from office inside a year depending on which capital is acting. Voters end up with leaders whose standing rests on foreign decisions rather than on them. The trafficking case shows the ordinary cost underneath: customs and police posts available for hire. Watch whether the officials arrested in 2024 are tried.

Bulgaria.d: Bulgaria sits on the Balkan smuggling route, and the documented problem is the institutions that control its chokepoints. The largest single Magnitsky action the United States has ever taken against one country named Bulgarian officials and business figures, several of them in customs and border roles, over networks that included smuggling protection. Bulgarian prosecutions largely did not follow, which is the recurring feature of the record here: the finding is made abroad and nothing happens at home. The second mechanism is leverage over judges rather than payment of them. Martin Bozhanov, known as the Notary, is alleged to have collected compromising material on judges and prosecutors and used it to pressure them; a former prosecutor general was questioned in the case, which remains under investigation and has never been tested in court. Russia's reach is recorded but unproven. Nikolay Malinov, a former MP who led the country's largest pro-Russia organisation, was charged in 2019 with collecting state secrets for a Russian state think tank, travelled to Moscow while on bail and was given the Order of Friendship by Vladimir Putin, and a Sofia court acquitted him of all charges in May 2026. Huawei, United Russia's party-cooperation network and a Russian state institute are among the other presences listed without cases.
Bulgaria.imp: If the people running customs protect smugglers, every honest importer pays more and the state collects less duty than the law provides for. Judges who can be shown their own files decide cases accordingly, and from outside you cannot tell which judges those are. Foreign sanctions name people whom Bulgarian courts never try, so the question is never settled either way. Watch whether a domestic prosecution follows the next designation.

Croatia.d: Croatia's documented case is a single transaction at the top of government over a single asset. MOL is Hungary's state-influenced oil company and INA is Croatia's national one. Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive in exchange for handing MOL management control of INA. The case has had a long career: convicted in 2012, quashed in 2015, convicted again in 2020, confirmed by the Supreme Court in 2021. Hungary has not handed over the executive said to have paid, and MOL denies there was a bribe. That asymmetry is the part worth noticing — the official who took the money has been convicted, while the company said to have paid it has never been tried, because the two men sit in different jurisdictions and one government will not cooperate. Around that one case the map records presences without cases: Opus Dei, the Order of Malta, the Trilateral Commission and the Finnish arms maker Patria, with Tradition Family Property and the Ordo Iuris legal institute listed as likely but undocumented.
Croatia.imp: Control of the national oil company changed hands because of a payment, which means the terms Croatians got for an asset they collectively owned were set by what one executive was willing to pay one prime minister. The conviction took nine years and two trials to stick. The man said to have paid is beyond the reach of Croatian courts, so the lesson available to a company is that paying across a border is safer than taking. Watch the extradition requests.

Czech Republic.d: The Czech record is mostly about owners, advisers and foreign money in media. Andrej Babis owns Agrofert, a farming, food and chemicals group that receives EU farm subsidies; a European Commission audit published in 2021 concluded that he still controlled it while serving as prime minister, despite having placed it in trust funds under a conflict-of-interest law. He is prime minister again, took back sole ownership in late 2025 and moved the shares into a new trust in February 2026, saying the conflict is resolved. China's route in was an adviser. Ye Jianming, formerly deputy secretary-general of a Beijing friendship body used for overseas contacts, was made an economic adviser to President Milos Zeman while his oil conglomerate CEFC was buying Czech assets; he was detained in China in 2018 and Shanghai state investors took the company over. Russia's route was a media outlet: in March 2024 the government placed Voice of Europe and the Ukrainian oligarch Viktor Medvedchuk on its national sanctions list after the security service said the network was financed from Russia and run from Czech territory, with payments reported to politicians in several European countries. The oldest entry is a bank. In March 1939, after Germany occupied Prague, the Bank for International Settlements transferred 23 tons of Czechoslovak gold to the German Reichsbank, with the Bank of England's governor approving it without consulting his own Treasury.
Czech Republic.imp: When the prime minister owns a company drawing farm subsidies, every subsidy decision is open to the question of whom it was for, and the answer keeps changing with the trust paperwork. A presidential adviser who worked for a foreign state's friendship body sits where privatisation and investment decisions get discussed. The 1939 gold transfer is the long reminder that an institution can act against the country whose money it holds. Watch the subsidy audits.

Denmark.d: Denmark's record is mostly about what its own institutions let others do. The clearest case is Operation Dunhammer. The Defence Intelligence Service allowed the US National Security Agency to tap internet cables running through Danish intercept stations, and an internal review completed in 2015 found the NSA had used that access to listen to the German chancellor, her foreign minister and the leader of the opposition, and reportedly to senior figures in Sweden, Norway and France. The defence minister was told in 2020; the intelligence chief and three other officials were suspended, and Danish broadcasters made the findings public in 2021. An ally's hand reaches Danish territory too: Danish intelligence has reported that Americans ran an influence campaign in Greenland. Money is the other channel. Danske Bank pleaded guilty in the United States and forfeited 2 billion dollars over roughly 200 billion euros of non-resident money that passed through a single Estonian branch — laundering infrastructure rather than anything drug-specific, since the same channel serves any proceeds that need distance from their origin. The Cold War left a stay-behind network code-named Absalon hidden inside military intelligence, disbanded after Italy's disclosures. At the lawful end of the record, King Frederik X is listed among the alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme.
Denmark.imp: A Danish listening station was used to monitor the leaders of neighbouring countries, which required cooperation rather than a breach, and Danes learned of it six years after their own service did. An Estonian branch of a Danish bank became the route for other people's dirty money, and the forfeiture was paid to the United States, not to the countries the money came from. Watch what oversight the intelligence service now answers to.

Estonia.d: What gets a hand inside Estonia comes through two doors: a church that answers to Moscow, and a banking system small enough that one branch can matter to the whole of Europe. On the religious side the state is the one pushing back. The Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate has about 150,000 faithful; in 2024 the government refused to renew the residence permit of its head, calling his support for Russia's war a security risk, parliament declared the Moscow Patriarchate a supporter of Russian aggression, and in 2025 it tightened the churches law to cut foreign control. Those measures stay in force. The money side is older and now largely closed. Estonian banks once held large numbers of non-resident clients, customers with no real business there, and the Estonian branch of Denmark's Danske Bank was the channel through which about $2.9 billion of Azerbaijani money moved in 2012-2014, some of it reaching European politicians who then spoke for Azerbaijan. Supervisors withdrew the licence of Versobank, a small licensed bank, for long-running anti-money-laundering failures, and the non-resident channel shut with it. What remains is quieter and lawful: Estonia's prime minister and its economy minister appear on the lists of private forums, Bilderberg and the Davos forum's Young Global Leaders, where officials and executives meet off the record.
Estonia.imp: The religious decision is the one people feel directly. A church with Estonian congregations has had its leader removed and its foreign ties cut by law, which touches ordinary worship and not only security. The banking years cost something else: supervisors closed a bank and the whole non-resident channel with it, and a small country's financial reputation was spent moving other people's money. Worth watching are the conditions attached to the next banking licence, and who vouches for a client list.

Finland.d: Almost nothing on Finland's record is a foreign service buying its way in. What is documented is a government whose senior figures move through private networks run from outside the country, and one old episode of officers acting against their own state's obligations. The present-day part is membership. The Davos forum picks people under about forty each year for its Young Global Leaders network, and the official curriculum vitae published by the Office of the President lists Alexander Stubb as a member of it since 2009; he also appears on the Bilderberg participant lists for 2024 and 2025 as a sitting head of state, as does former prime minister Sanna Marin. Bilderberg is a private annual meeting of politicians, executives and academics, with no public record of what is said. Selection by the organisers is not a finding of influence, and no forum has found that these networks steered Finnish policy. The older background is domestic. After the 1944 armistice with the Soviet Union, officers of the operational department of Finnish Military Headquarters began hiding weapons around the country, and thousands of people took part. The scheme was exposed to the Allied Control Commission in 1945, and under a retroactive law passed in 1947 some 1,488 people were convicted, most sentenced to a few months.
Finland.imp: Little of this reaches daily life in Finland. What it touches is who the people in office already know before they take office: a president and former prime ministers who have spent years inside networks that meet without a public record, so the thinking behind a position can form in a room nobody can read back. The weapons-cache case left a different mark, in a mass of ordinary people questioned and convicted under a law written after the fact.

France.d: France is both a target and a base. Interpol, Airbus, Dassault and two of the country's main Masonic bodies are headquartered here, and French state networks reached well beyond its borders: the Service d'Action Civique, a Gaullist militia set up by de Gaulle's Africa adviser Jacques Foccart, ran that African business from the Élysée until the government dissolved it by decree in 1982, after its Marseille leader and his family were murdered by an SAC commando. What keeps repeating is movement between finance and the top of the state. Georges Pompidou went from general manager of Banque Rothschild to prime minister in 1962; Emmanuel Macron was a partner at Rothschild & Cie before becoming an Élysée aide, economy minister and president. No court or inquiry has found that the bank directs French policy, and the claim that Macron is the Rothschilds' president is a version of a long-running antisemitic conspiracy theory. Consultancies take a similar route into the ministries: a Senate inquiry called the state's use of consultants since 2017 sprawling and opaque, and prosecutors are still pursuing McKinsey over its French tax. Industry sits close to the bodies meant to police it: a Paris court convicted the drug firm Servier over the pill Mediator and fined the national medicines agency for ignoring warnings. Foreign states work at the margins, with Azerbaijani money reaching Council of Europe parliamentarians and a Russian bank lending nine million euros to the Front National. France answers with bans: it dissolved the Grey Wolves by cabinet decree in 2020, and that ban stays in force.
France.imp: The cost shows up as a rule not enforced in time. Mediator stayed on sale for more than three decades while the agency that could have withdrawn it sat on warnings, and patients paid for that with damaged heart valves. When a minister smooths the path for one company, its competitors and the people who work for it get rules written around someone else's business. Worth watching: who audits consultants' contracts, and where a regulator's staff go when they leave.

Germany.d: Germany carries more documented cases than any other country on this map, and they come from every direction at once. Foreign services work on parliament and on industry. A German citizen who worked as an aide to a member of the European Parliament is serving four years and nine months for working for China's Ministry of State Security, and three people are on trial in Düsseldorf over ship engines, sonar and lasers gathered for the same service. Russia's reach runs through people rather than offices: the chief operating officer of Wirecard, a payments company that collapsed after admitting 1.9 billion euros did not exist, was named by investigators as a Russian intelligence asset and lives in Russia; a former chancellor took the chair of the Russian state oil company Rosneft, and the Bundestag closed his ex-chancellor's office over it. Turkey and Iran reach in through religion. DITIB, the German branch of Turkey's state religious authority, runs about 900 mosques with imams paid as Turkish civil servants; prosecutors investigated some of them for reporting on Gülen followers, dropped the case for lack of evidence, and the interior ministry cut DITIB's federal funding. The Islamic Centre Hamburg was banned outright in 2024. The quieter route is the revolving door: a Goldman Sachs Germany co-head became state secretary and later finance minister, and the current chancellor chaired BlackRock's German arm before returning to politics. The older roots sit underneath: the CIA ran Radio Free Europe from Munich, and the stay-behind network the foreign intelligence service operated was dissolved only in 1991.
Germany.imp: The costs land in particular places. A payments company was allowed to grow while the financial regulator banned short-selling of its shares and filed complaints against the journalists reporting the fraud, and the people holding the shares paid for that. A tax claim against a Hamburg bank was dropped after its co-owner met the city's mayor, and a second claim was collected only when the federal ministry intervened. Watch whether a regulator's first move is at the firm or at its critics.

Greece.d: Two things dominate Greece's record: creditors sitting inside the state's finances, and an army and police organised from within. In 2001, as Greece entered the euro, Goldman Sachs arranged currency swaps for the public debt agency that worked as a hidden loan of about 2.8 billion euros, outside the figures Greece reported under EU rules. They came to light in 2010, by which time the fees and the state's obligation had both grown. The people who handled the rescues came from the same world: the central bank governor of the euro-entry years became prime minister of an unelected government in 2011 to secure the second bailout, and the investment bank Lazard advised on the 2012 bond swap and was rehired in 2015. A restructuring adviser sees a government's whole balance sheet. The older background is the officer corps. IDEA, a secret society of army officers formed in 1945, supplied several leaders of the April 1967 coup, and its members took key posts under the colonels, convicted of high treason in 1975. A NATO stay-behind unit seized the Defence Ministry during the coup; the defence minister confirmed in 1990 that the Greek branch ran until 1988. That history carries into the police, where reported ties to Golden Dawn preceded the 2020 conviction of the party's leaders for running a criminal organisation.
Greece.imp: Greeks paid for the hidden swaps twice: in the fees and the growing obligation, and again when the debt came due and the rescues arrived with conditions attached to pensions, wages and public services. The police side costs people differently. Where officers are close to a party that attacks migrants and the left, a complaint goes nowhere and an assault is not investigated. Worth watching is who advises the finance ministry on debt, and who pays that adviser.

Hungary.d: Hungary's documented record is thin, and what is in it points to a government that opens the door rather than one broken into. In February 2024 the interior minister and China's minister of public security agreed a policing arrangement that lets Chinese officers patrol alongside Hungarian police in tourist areas and at large events. The ministry denies that Chinese police stations operate in the country, although a human-rights group had listed two in Budapest. The direction is unusual: other European governments on this map have been closing such outposts rather than inviting the officers in. Russia appears through a single prosecution. A Hungarian member of the European Parliament for the nationalist party Jobbik was accused of spying on EU institutions for Russia, lost his parliamentary immunity in 2015, and was sentenced in absentia to five years by Hungary's top court in 2022; he lives in Russia. Beyond those two cases the map records organisations as present without a case attached to them, among them Opus Dei, the Order of Malta, the Trilateral Commission, the Mont Pelerin Society and Israel's foreign intelligence service, and lists the Russian influence network around Viktor Medvedchuk and the conservative legal institute Ordo Iuris as likely here but not documented.
Hungary.imp: The patrol agreement means a Chinese family in Budapest may meet officers of the state they left, in the company of Hungarian police, with no clear way to refuse. For everyone else the cost is quieter: a government that treats policing as something to trade with a foreign power spends credibility its own police need when they ask the public for help. Worth watching is whether the agreement is published in full, and what happens to anyone who complains about it.

Iceland.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Iceland: no case of an outside force getting a hand on its government, its companies or its courts. Two organisations are recorded as present, the Mont Pelerin Society, a network of free-market economists whose members have held office in other countries, and Samherji, an Icelandic fishing company headquartered here. The likeliest openings are the ordinary ones for a small, open economy: a single large export industry close to the ministries that regulate it, and banking and shipping routes that carry other people's money. This is a best guess, not a finding.
Iceland.imp: With nothing documented, there is no rule here that went unenforced and no case that died. What would be worth watching is specific and dull: who sits on the boards of the large fishing firms and who they know in the fisheries and finance ministries, whether a company under investigation abroad gets the same scrutiny at home, and whether company records show who really owns what.

Ireland.d: Ireland's record splits between a Catholic lay order that once sat inside the cabinet and today's lighter forms of outside contact. The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic fraternal order with its headquarters in Ireland, had members at the top of the inter-party government formed in 1948: the Taoiseach, John A. Costello, and his justice minister, Seán MacEoin, were both Knights, and MacEoin is reported to have assured the Order's supreme council that efforts would be made to prevent conflict between church and state. Members also held civil service posts, including Dublin City's chief planner. These accounts rest on two biographies rather than on a court or an inquiry, and membership of a lawful order is not wrongdoing. What is current is softer. China's Fuzhou city police ran one of its unofficial overseas service stations from a street in Dublin, the kind of office used to pressure people wanted by China into going home, until the Department of Foreign Affairs ordered it closed in 2022. And heads of government here appear on the Davos forum's Young Global Leaders list, a sitting Taoiseach named to it in 2018 and the Tánaiste to the 2025 class. Selection by the organisers is not a finding that anyone's decisions were directed.
Ireland.imp: The older arrangement had a measurable cost. A health scheme for mothers and children was opposed from inside government, which meant care that was not provided. The newer forms cost less and are harder to see: for a time a foreign police force could lean on people living in Dublin from an office on an ordinary street, and leaders arrive in office with contacts made in a private forum. Worth watching is whether a closed station reopens under another name.

Italy.d: Italy's exposure is less about a foreign spy service than about the short distance between public office and groups already inside the country. Three of them recur. The mafias — Cosa Nostra in Sicily, the 'Ndrangheta in Calabria, the Camorra around Naples — do not lobby. They place their own people in town halls, hiring offices and public-works tenders, and they pay the officials who award contracts. Italy answers with a law of its own: when a prefect's inquiry finds a council conditioned by a clan, the cabinet can dissolve it and send commissioners to run the town, and 402 such decrees have issued since 1991. Second are the secret lodges and associations. A membership list seized at a factory in Arezzo in 1981 held ministers, 195 military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services; the law passed the following year dissolved that lodge and banned associations working secretly on public bodies, and it stays in force, with prosecutions still brought under it. Third are the Cold War structures: the stay-behind network a prime minister disclosed to parliament in 1990, built against an invasion that never came and caught up instead in domestic bombings. Beside all this runs ordinary foreign reach — a party cooperation pact with Putin's United Russia that renews unless cancelled, joint street patrols with Chinese police that the interior ministry ended, and the UN food agency in Rome, where both the leadership election and an industry partnership are contested.
Italy.imp: When a clan sits inside the council, the rubbish contract, the transport job and the building permit go by permission rather than merit, and residents pay twice — in the price of the work and in the service they do not get. Where senior police, judges or intelligence chiefs share a private membership with the people they are meant to investigate, cases stall without anyone having to order it. Watch which councils are dissolved and which firms are barred from public contracts.

Latvia.d: Latvia's exposure runs mostly one way — toward Russia — and it arrives through institutions that look domestic. Until 2022 the Latvian Orthodox Church was a self-governing branch of the Russian Orthodox Church, whose patriarch in Moscow is close to the Kremlin. Parliament amended the law to cut that tie and now requires the president's office to be told when bishops are appointed; no other Orthodox church has recognised the new status, so the question of who holds authority is still open. The second route is personal. A long-serving Latvian member of the European Parliament was shown by leaked emails to have been reporting to officers of Russia's FSB, the domestic security service; the state security service opened a criminal case and searched her property, and the Parliament penalised her for breaking its conduct rules. The third is money. Latvian banks and crypto services became a transit point for funds leaving Russia and the darknet, and the decisive action has come from Washington rather than Riga. A US designation of one Latvian bank as a money-laundering concern triggered a deposit run and the bank liquidated itself within weeks, with no trial anywhere. A crypto exchange designated later shared its infrastructure with an earlier one — the same operation under a new name.
Latvia.imp: A bank that collapses on a foreign designation takes its depositors' arrangements with it, and the money that passed through was somebody else's stolen tax revenue. Where a church's chain of command runs to another country, congregations find internal disputes settled by people who answer elsewhere. A legislator working for a foreign service votes on the sanctions, energy and security files that decide what residents pay. Watch the bishop appointment notices and the security service's open cases.

Liechtenstein.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Liechtenstein yet. No case has been recorded here, and the only organisation with a known presence is the Order of Malta, a Catholic chivalric body. What is likely follows from what the country does. It is a small financial centre with a banking, trust and foundation industry very large relative to its population, so the plausible route in is money rather than politics: foreign clients using its banks, foundations and company structures, and the lawyers and formation agents who build them. That is a best guess from the country's profile, not a finding about anyone.
Liechtenstein.imp: For now nothing on this map has been shown to cost people here anything. The risk that comes with a financial centre is indirect: the money handled is largely other countries' tax revenue and other countries' crime proceeds, so when a scandal breaks the cost arrives from outside — blacklists, lost correspondent banking, treaty demands — and falls on the whole small economy rather than on whoever arranged the structure.

Lithuania.d: The one case that reached the top of the Lithuanian state is two decades old and still shapes how these questions are read there. A Russian businessman who ran a helicopter firm in Lithuania reportedly gave about 400,000 dollars to a presidential campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by the president's own decree. The Constitutional Court found the president had broken his oath, parliament removed him in 2004 — the first European head of state to be impeached — and the European Court of Human Rights later held that barring him from parliament for life went too far. Nothing comparable has been documented since, and the country's current exposure is infrastructure rather than office. An encrypted messaging network used by criminal groups ran partly from servers here until French and Dutch investigators read its traffic for three months and closed it. More recently, prosecutors elsewhere traced the revenue of a retail drug trade in Iceland into Lithuanian property: the selling happens at one end of Europe and the money settles as flats and land at the other, which is the part hardest to see from inside the country. The documented record here is thin rather than absent.
Lithuania.imp: A president installed with help from a foreign donor owes that donor something, and a citizenship decree is the visible payment. When laundered money buys housing, the people competing for the same flats pay the inflated price without ever learning why. And an encrypted network hosted locally means the country's servers carry other countries' violence. Watch campaign-finance disclosures, and watch who buys property with money that has no local source.

Luxembourg.d: Luxembourg's documented record is small, and the two entries are about secrecy rather than politics. The country was the registered home of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, whose operating centre was in London and which regulators in several countries closed together in 1991. The registration and the business were deliberately in different places, so no single supervisor ever saw the whole bank — which is the thing worth understanding about a small financial centre: the paperwork lives in one jurisdiction and the decisions in another. The other entry is a criminal trial. Two former officers of the gendarmerie's mobile brigade went on trial in 2013 over eighteen bombings in the mid-1980s that hit power pylons and similar targets. Their defence argued the attacks were the work of NATO's stay-behind network, the secret wartime-reserve structures set up across Western Europe, and a recording of a prime minister, a justice minister and the intelligence chief speculating about exactly that was played in court. The prosecutor told the court that most of the pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended, and although officers were later referred to trial for false testimony, nobody has been tried for the bombings.
Luxembourg.imp: When a bank is registered in one country and run from another, depositors discover only afterwards that nobody was supervising the whole of it. And a bombing case that stops because the evidence has gone missing leaves the public with a police force it cannot check: the question of whether officers planted the bombs stays formally open, which is a cost paid in trust rather than money. Watch what the false-testimony referrals produce.

Malta.d: Malta's exposure comes from what it sells, which is licences. The island licenses online betting companies, small banks and crypto exchanges, and until recently sold citizenship and residence to investors; in each case the whole of the control is the due diligence done before the licence is granted. Italian investigators found mafia groups collecting bets and washing money through Malta-licensed gaming firms, and the gaming authority suspended licences after the arrests rather than before them. A small licensed bank lost its licence only once its owner had been arrested abroad, and Malta's failure to act on earlier warnings was among the findings that put the country on an international watch list. The deeper case reaches the prime minister's office. A businessman who was a director of the company built to supply Malta's gas power station also owned a company in Dubai from which, on leaked papers, the prime minister's chief of staff and the energy minister expected payments. The journalist investigating those companies, Daphne Caruana Galizia, was killed by a car bomb in 2017. He is charged with commissioning the murder and, separately, with corruption over the power project alongside the two officials, both of whom resigned. A public inquiry found the state had created an atmosphere of impunity.
Malta.imp: A licence granted without real checks makes the people of a small country guarantors of other people's crime: the gaming firm, the bank or the passport scheme carries Malta's name abroad and the island carries the consequences, from grey-listing to the cost of borrowing. On the power station, the electricity bill was set by a contract that officials had a private interest in. Watch who is being licensed and whose signature approved it.

Moldova.d: Moldova is the clearest case on this map of a state captured from the inside and then unpicked in its own courts. Between 2010 and 2014 Russian companies were made to 'guarantee' invented debts that Moldovan district judges then ordered paid, moving a very large sum out of Russia through a Moldovan bank and on through Latvia; prosecutors later charged judges who had validated the debts. In the same years about a billion dollars, equal to twelve per cent of the country's annual output, was drained from three Moldovan banks through loans repaid with further loans and routed through shell companies abroad. The businessman widely described as controlling the government and its parliamentary majority at the time fled in 2019, was arrested in Greece, extradited, and in 2026 sentenced to nineteen years. Russian money is the live route now: a party financed with undeclared Russian funds was ruled unconstitutional, and the governor of the autonomous region of Gagauzia, elected as that party's candidate, is serving seven years over the financing. A separate strand shows the state doing another government's work — the intelligence service seized seven Turkish teachers from a school network Ankara treats as hostile and put them on a plane, which the European Court of Human Rights found unlawful and unnecessary.
Moldova.imp: A billion dollars missing from three banks is repaid by everyone: the loss went onto the public books, so pensions, roads and clinics were funded with what was left. Where judges can be hired to validate fake debts, nobody's property claim is safe in those same courts. And a security service that deports people on a foreign government's request offers no protection to anyone that government dislikes. Watch the asset recovery and who funds the next campaign.

Monaco.d: Monaco's unusual feature is that the outside force inside it is a friendly neighbour, by treaty. France is responsible for Monaco's defence, key judicial posts are held by French magistrates proposed by Paris, the police are commanded by a French officer, and the head of government is appointed after the prince consults the French government — until a constitutional change in 2002 he had to be a French citizen chosen from a French list. A French senior civil servant has held the post since July 2025. None of this is hidden, which is why it sits differently from the rest of the map. The other two entries concern money and sport. World athletics' governing body is based here, and its former president was convicted in Paris of taking money to delay doping cases against Russian athletes, with part of one deal meant to fund a presidential campaign in Senegal. And a Russian billionaire resident who owns the local football club was made a formal suspect over courting Monegasque officials, including a former public prosecutor, on the strength of messages taken from his lawyer's phone; the case was dismissed and then closed in 2025 once the courts ruled the phone data had been obtained unlawfully.
Monaco.imp: Residents of a state whose judges, police commander and head of government are chosen with another country's agreement have little say over the institutions that decide their cases. For everyone else the cost is the sports federation: an athlete who did not dope lost a place to one who paid to compete. Watch whether influence-peddling cases that collapse on evidence rules are ever rebuilt on lawfully gathered material.

Montenegro.d: In Montenegro the state and the cocaine trade have been staffed by some of the same people, and the proof arrived from outside the country. When European police cracked the encrypted phone service Sky ECC and passed the messages to Podgorica, the transcripts produced charges against the former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and a state security officer, all over protection of one of the clans running a Kotor-based smuggling network. Separate indictments name a former president of the Supreme Court, two former police directors and the mayor of a coastal town. The most senior conviction so far is of the judge who led the Supreme Court until 2020: a court in Podgorica sentenced her to ten years in 2026 for using her position to shield a cigarette and narcotics smuggling ring run by her son, who received a similar term and then absconded from house arrest. The third entry is of a different kind. The sitting prime minister was selected for the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses for people under about forty. That is a membership, not a finding of wrongdoing, and it belongs here as a channel rather than an offence.
Montenegro.imp: If the chief prosecutor and the head of the Supreme Court are working for smugglers, there is no point at which an ordinary complaint can be heard honestly, and the cases that do get built depend on foreign police handing over the evidence. Smuggling money also sets property prices along the coast. Watch whether appeals hold the sentences up, and whether anyone still in office, rather than only former officials, is charged.

Netherlands.d: The Netherlands carries two different kinds of pressure at once. The first is the port. Rotterdam is a main European entry point for cocaine, and the way in is not the fence but the payroll: terminal planners and IT contractors have been convicted of handing over container release codes and shifting boxes in the stacking system so extraction crews can find one among millions. The same trade has reached the legal system — a defence lawyer convicted of relaying her imprisoned client's messages through the privileged channel between counsel and detainee, a police employee prosecuted for leaking protected information, and the murders of a crown witness's brother, his lawyer and a journalist. Dutch banks have settled laundering cases for hundreds of millions, usually with no individual charged. The second pressure follows from The Hague being the seat of international justice. Russian military intelligence officers were caught in a car outside the chemical weapons watchdog with equipment to steal its network logins, and reporting describes Israeli intelligence pressuring and surveilling International Criminal Court prosecutors over years. Quieter channels sit alongside: Chinese 'overseas service stations' the foreign ministry ordered shut, a Chinese-owned chipmaker whose governance the economy ministry seized and then suspended, memos showing two large companies lobbied for a tax change during coalition talks, and a private annual conference founded by the King's grandfather at which the King and serving ministers still appear.
Netherlands.imp: Corruption at the port is paid for in the violence that follows the cargo — the shootings, the threatened witnesses, the lawyers who need guarding — and in a justice system that has to be hardened against its own staff. A bank that pays a settlement and charges nobody passes the cost to its customers and keeps the practice. When foreign services can reach into the courts at The Hague, the people waiting on those cases wait longer. Watch who is prosecuted beside the institutions that settle.

Norway.d: Norway's documented record is two entries, and both concern the state's own apparatus rather than anyone reaching in from abroad. The older one is the stay-behind network, the secret reserve structure set up across Western Europe after 1945. In 1978 police found weapons and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested the businessman holding them, who said Norwegian intelligence had supplied the guns. The defence minister then stated that the network answered to nobody outside the country and had no CIA connection — a flat denial of the foreign coordination that equivalent structures elsewhere in Europe turned out to have. Two decades earlier the intelligence chief had already complained to NATO about related activity by officers at its Norwegian headquarters. The recent entry is a police one. The officer who ran Oslo's narcotics section for years was convicted of aggravated corruption and of helping import around fourteen tonnes of hashish together with an informant he had himself been running, and sentenced to twenty-one years; the Supreme Court refused his appeal. It is the most senior conviction of its kind in Scandinavia, and it came out of the Norwegian system rather than from leaked foreign evidence, which is what separates this record from several further south.
Norway.imp: When the head of a narcotics unit is importing the drugs, every arrest his section made is open to doubt, and the people he charged have grounds to ask who really decided. For the older matter the cost is what citizens cannot check: a secret armed structure that a minister described in terms the records elsewhere contradict. Watch whether the state publishes its stay-behind files, and who audits the handling of police informants now.

Poland.d: The clearest pattern in Poland is a legal advocacy group moving its own people into the state. Ordo Iuris, founded in 2013, is a conservative Catholic legal institute headquartered in Poland. Its co-founder and former board chair was made deputy foreign minister for legal and treaty affairs in 2015; appointed to the Supreme Court in 2019 with no previous judicial experience, he was then entrusted by the president in 2020 with the duties of acting First President of that court. The same institute drafted a near-total abortion ban that parliament rejected in 2016 after nationwide protests.
