A sitting member of the lower house has been reported as a supernumerary of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members keep ordinary jobs and homes, and he now vice-chairs the parliamentary inquiry into the previous government's use of spyware. Membership of a lawful organisation is not wrongdoing and none of these appointments has been found unlawful; what the map records is the route. Separately, prosecutors charged a senior Huawei employee in Poland and a cybersecurity expert who had worked for the internal security agency with working for Chinese intelligence, alleging the executive pursued contracts that would give the company a view into state and local government data systems. Both plead not guilty, and the Warsaw trial is closed to the public.
Poland.imp: When the people who drafted a law are also the officials and judges who apply it, the public loses the step where an outside eye checks the text — and the text at issue here decided whether a pregnancy could be ended. A trial held behind closed doors over telecoms contracts means nobody can see what a foreign company was alleged to be buying. Watch who is appointed to courts without judicial experience, and what the spyware inquiry publishes.

Portugal.d: Portugal's record runs from a dictatorship's export business to a bank that took part of the state down with it. Aginter Press was set up in Lisbon in 1966 under Salazar's Estado Novo and presented itself as a news agency; it trained its members in bombing and sabotage, and an Italian magistrate investigating the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing told his parliament that Aginter instructors had taught Italian neo-fascists to use explosives. Its papers were found after the 1974 revolution, once its organisers had left the country. What carries into the present is the banking relationship. Banco Espírito Santo was run by a family close to power since the Salazar years, and its chief was nicknamed 'the owner of all this'; the bank collapsed in 2014. In the case known as Operation Marquês, prosecutors charged a former prime minister with receiving undue payments, some of which they link to that group, alongside the banker on corruption and money-laundering counts. A judge threw most of it out in 2021, an appeal court reinstated it in 2024, and the trial opened in 2025 with all defendants presumed innocent. The current pressure is offshore: cocaine now arrives by mid-ocean transfer between the Canaries and the Azores and lands on remote coastline in small craft, which is what happens once the ports are watched.
Portugal.imp: A bank wound into the state leaves the public holding the losses while the case against the people who ran it takes a decade to reach a courtroom, and the delay is itself part of the cost — witnesses age, charges lapse. On the coast, landings by small boat put the trade into fishing villages with no police presence rather than into guarded terminals. Watch what the Marquês trial actually decides, and where the landings move next.

Romania.d: Romania's documented record on this map is thin, and it rests on reporting rather than court findings. In 2019 a magazine, citing anonymous Masonic sources, named the then interim interior minister, who was also deputy prime minister, and the head of the Gendarmerie as Freemasons who had not listed the membership in the interest declarations the magazine said the law required. The minister neither confirmed nor denied it; the head of the government chancellery, a former foreign-intelligence officer, said he had been a Mason and no longer was. Membership of a lawful fraternal body is not wrongdoing, and the undeclared part — which is what the entry turns on — has never been tested anywhere but in that one publication. The other entry is a current prosecution over money rather than office: invoices for services never performed were passed between France and Romania to launder 306 million euros of drug and tax-evasion proceeds, cutting the taxable income at the same time, so one false document did both jobs. Several networks are recorded as present here without a documented case, among them Azerbaijan's hospitality lobbying and the Moldovan group behind that country's bank theft. The thin record describes what has been documented, not an assurance that little happens.
Romania.imp: An interior minister and a gendarmerie commander who do not declare a private membership leave the public unable to tell, in any particular decision, whether something else was in the room. False invoicing on this scale takes money twice over — once as laundered crime proceeds and once as tax never paid, which is schools and hospitals not funded. Watch whether interest declarations are enforced, and what the cross-border laundering case recovers.

Russia.d: Russia hosts this and exports more of it than anywhere else. Inside the country the state and private wealth are hard to pull apart: the US Treasury, sanctioning Bank Rossiya over Crimea, called it 'the personal bank for senior officials', its shareholders drawn from the president's circle. The usual deal runs backwards: rather than a firm buying an official, an official's connections decide who owns the firm. An American investor in a shareholder fight over a Russian bank was arrested by the FSB on fraud charges and convicted; the conviction was vacated years later. A presidential decree now lets the state take 'temporary management' of assets owned by companies from countries it calls unfriendly, and the federal property agency took Danone's Russian business and Carlsberg's brewery, with politically connected managers installed. Outward, the instruments are money, religion and information: a state-funded foundation for Russian culture, a media network the Czech government sanctioned for paying European politicians, the Orthodox Church, and crypto exchanges and mixers that cash out ransomware and darknet proceeds from Moscow, where a foreign designation changes little. Russia also works inside international institutions: a WADA inquiry found the sports ministry and the FSB running a doping cover-up, and Interpol has stopped Russian police sending wanted-person alerts directly to other countries. Organised crime is the older thread: a gang in a Krasnodar village operated for years under local police protection before killing twelve people. One claim in circulation, that a Jewish banking house financed the Bolsheviks, is an antisemitic myth; the bank's own records show it refused them money.
Russia.imp: For a foreign company here, ownership can change by decree rather than by sale, and a criminal case can be the weapon in a business dispute rather than the remedy for one. Where local police are protecting a gang, complaints go nowhere until the bodies appear. Outside Russia the bill arrives as ransomware payments, laundered proceeds moving through exchanges that stay open, politicians whose positions were bought, and athletes who lost places to competitors whose samples were swapped.

San Marino.d: San Marino is a small republic inside Italy with its own banks and its own building permits, and the one case documented here turns on that combination. Licences to run a bank, granted by a government of a few dozen senior figures, are worth a great deal to anyone who wants to move money; permission to build on a small mountainous territory is scarce in the same way. In the 'Conto Mazzini' case prosecutors said construction and banking entrepreneurs paid Sammarinese politicians for exactly those two things, with the cash drawn from an account at a local bank opened in the name of Giuseppe Mazzini, the nineteenth-century Italian nationalist. Twenty-one former political figures went on trial for criminal association to launder bribes, among them two former state secretaries, which is what San Marino calls its ministers. Several were convicted, and an appeal court upheld most of the convictions with lower sentences. Nothing else is documented on the map here, and the republic's size cuts both ways: a handful of relationships can cover the whole state, and the same closeness made the arrangement impossible to keep quiet once prosecutors started pulling at it.
San Marino.imp: In a state this small, a bank licence or a building permit handed out as a favour is not a technicality. It decides who may build on scarce land and who may handle other people's savings, and the cost is carried by everyone whose property, rents and deposits sit inside that system. What is worth watching is who licenses the banks, who signs off construction, and whether either decision is ever reviewed by someone outside the same political circle.

Serbia.d: What Serbia documents most clearly is officers and criminals on the same payroll. The modern version runs through the interior ministry's armed units. The prime minister was shot in 2003 by a serving commander of the ministry's special operations unit, which had merged with a Belgrade criminal group holding a share of the Balkan heroin trade; twelve men were convicted and the unit was disbanded. The arrangement keeps reappearing: the prosecution of the Belivuk-Miljkovic group produced evidence that its members carried state security identification and could get into protected facilities, and a former head of the security service was later charged in connection with them. That case is running rather than finished, and the attributions are contested in Serbian politics. The background is sworn brotherhoods of army officers who chose who governed. Officers who went on to found the Black Hand killed the king and queen in the palace in Belgrade; their leader became chief of military intelligence, was court-martialled for treason and shot, and was acquitted decades later for want of proof. A rival officers' society put its own general in as prime minister when the king suspended the constitution. What those decades left is the armed part of the state behaving as a political actor in its own right, which is what the later cases keep running into.
Serbia.imp: When the unit meant to arrest traffickers is also protecting them, reporting a crime can mean handing your name to the people you are reporting. Prosecutions turn into political arguments, and witnesses have to weigh whether a conviction will survive appeal. The practical test is whether the police and the security service are audited by anyone outside them, and whether charges against senior officers reach a verdict instead of quietly lapsing.

Slovakia.d: Slovakia's documented cases are about proximity rather than proven control, and two of the three run through the prime minister's own office. A journalist, Jan Kuciak, was shot dead with his fiancee in 2018 while finishing an article about Italian businessmen running farm companies in the east of the country, named in investigations into the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia. The article showed that the prime minister's chief state adviser had co-founded a company with one of them years earlier. She and the secretary of the security council stepped aside, saying their names were being misused, and the prime minister resigned after mass protests. No court has found that his office acted for the 'Ndrangheta. The third case is a foreign service borrowing a Slovak asset: a Vietnamese former state-company executive seeking asylum was seized off a Berlin street, and a journalist later found an invoice from Slovakia's interior ministry to Vietnam's for the flight to Moscow that followed. A former Slovak president has written that the interior minister arranged the loan of the government plane. Germany expelled a Vietnamese intelligence officer. Behind both sits a small political class where advisers, party figures and businessmen already know each other, and where the records that would settle who knew what are held by the ministries involved.
Slovakia.imp: The cost here is visible in what it took to find any of this out: a reporter was killed over work that had not yet been published. When the people closest to a prime minister are also former business partners of men under mafia investigation, decisions on farm subsidies, land and contracts are made by people nobody outside can question. Worth watching is whether advisers' business interests are declared, and whether the use of state aircraft and ministry contracts is logged where the public can see it.

Slovenia.d: Slovenia carries one documented case, and it ended with the verdict wiped out. Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, won a contract to supply armoured vehicles; a Finnish broadcaster then alleged the company had paid bribes, partly aimed at the prime minister of the day, Janez Jansa. A Ljubljana court sentenced him to two years, the Constitutional Court annulled the verdict, and the case lapsed before any retrial. In Finland the defendants were acquitted on appeal; an Austrian court convicted one middleman. So the arrangement that was alleged, a defence firm reaching a head of government through intermediaries to land a procurement deal, was never established against the politician, and he has held office again since. Arms procurement is where this sort of approach tends to surface in a small state: the orders are large against the size of the budget, the equipment is specialised enough that price comparison is difficult, and the deals pass through brokers in third countries, which is where the one conviction landed. The organisations with a documented foothold in Slovenia are otherwise the familiar lawful ones, including Catholic institutions, a transatlantic policy group, and Azerbaijan's lobbying network in European assemblies. Presence of that kind is not wrongdoing on its own.
Slovenia.imp: A case that collapses this way leaves people with no finding either way. The public never learns whether the vehicles were bought on merit, the politician carries an accusation that was formally undone, and the money has been spent and the equipment delivered regardless. In a small country the useful thing to watch is who brokers defence deals, because the middlemen sit outside the state and outside most of the rules that require officials to declare an interest.

Spain.d: Two different things are documented in Spain. One is cocaine and the officials who help it through. The Galician inlets became Europe's main landing ground, worked by clans that had switched over from tobacco smuggling, and the Strait of Gibraltar is the other door: at Algeciras, the country's largest container port, trafficking networks recruit from the municipal police, the customs service and the port workforce, and officers have been sentenced for guarding a cocaine load through the strait. Around that sits a laundering industry sold as a service, with prosecutors describing groups whose actual business is cleaning other criminals' profits for a fee, through lower-division football clubs, transfer fees and shell companies. The second thing is older and lawful in form. From the late 1950s Franco appointed members of Opus Dei, a Catholic institution whose lay members follow its spiritual programme while holding ordinary jobs, to the ministries that ran the economy, and after a scandal over export credits from a state industrial bank the reshuffled cabinet had eleven members with ties to the institution. Membership is not wrongdoing, and the thread continues more faintly through a later interior minister reported to be a member and through shareholder suits over a failed bank, which Opus Dei denies. Spain also hosts the private rooms where officials meet money: ministers attended the Bilderberg meeting in Madrid, which keeps no public record of what is said. And the prime minister's phone was found infected with Pegasus, spyware sold only to governments. No state has been named for that.
Spain.imp: At the ports and the crossings, the officer meant to check a container is sometimes the one clearing it, which is why seizure figures do not track the traffic and why reporting a corrupt colleague is a real risk. For everyone else the laundered money turns up as property prices and as clubs bought with cash nobody can trace. The thing to watch is whether port access control and police postings are audited by someone outside the same local chain of command.

Sweden.d: Sweden is a strong state with thin spots rather than a captured one. Criminal networks reach it from below. A research review for a Swedish policy institute found them placing people inside government agencies, running companies in the publicly funded welfare sector, with wrongly paid welfare put at over thirteen billion kronor a year. Courts have convicted police employees of passing information from law-enforcement registers to those networks, and a security service officer of unauthorised disclosure; police reporting treats insider access to registers as a standing weakness, not a one-off. Municipalities are the softest point, because much public money is spent locally with weaker oversight. The Baltic branches of Swedish banks also processed very large non-resident flows in the same years as the Danske affair, and the regulator fined and censured them; the origin of that money has never been separated out. The older background is private rather than criminal. The Wallenberg family's foundations hold just over half the votes in Sweden's most valuable listed company while owning far less than half of it, which carries board seats across Ericsson, SEB, ABB and the defence maker Saab. That control is legal, disclosed and built on shares with unequal voting rights. Swedish prime ministers also attend the off-the-record Bilderberg meeting, in one case without appearing on the published list.
Sweden.imp: Welfare money that leaks into companies run by criminal networks is money not spent on the care it was voted for, and a leaked police register can put a witness, a victim or a neighbour in danger. Where a few foundations hold the votes in the country's largest industrial group, decisions about plants and jobs are taken by boards answerable to them. Worth watching: who is allowed to query a police register, and who audits welfare contracts awarded by a municipality.

Switzerland.d: Switzerland's place on this map comes from what is based there, not from anyone capturing the Swiss state. The headquarters list runs from the World Health Organization and the central banks' own bank in Basel to FIFA, the International Olympic Committee and the traders who move the world's oil, metals and grain, so an organisation that wants to reach global rules comes here to do it. A committee of experts commissioned by the WHO, reading documents released in US lawsuits, found the tobacco industry running an 'elaborate, well financed, sophisticated and usually invisible' effort to undermine tobacco control, working through consultants, scientists and other UN agencies; leaked company papers later showed the same campaign aimed at the tobacco treaty itself. A private American foundation is the WHO's second-largest funder, with most of its money earmarked for programmes it chooses. At the sports bodies, US indictments allege World Cup votes were paid for, and Switzerland's own attorney general left office after unrecorded meetings with FIFA's president. The country also supplied the ground for a long intelligence operation: a Swiss firm sold cipher machines to governments around the world while secretly owned by the CIA and West Germany's BND, which could read what its customers sent. Money runs through the same address, with a major Swiss bank criminally convicted over a cocaine organisation's laundering and two commodity traders over bribery. Parliament found and dissolved a secret cadre army run outside its own control; the full report on its ties to British services stays sealed until 2041.
Switzerland.imp: Rules written in Geneva and Basel reach people who never hear the arguments. A weaker tobacco treaty means cheaper cigarettes and more smokers; donations earmarked by the donor decide which diseases get attention. A government that bought cipher machines from a firm owned by two spy agencies had its diplomats' and soldiers' messages read for decades. What to watch is who funds an international body and whether that funding is tied to named projects, and whether officials meet the industries they regulate on the record.

Ukraine.d: Ukraine is pulled at from two directions at once. Russia's reach is the open one. Its state technology corporation is accused of running hidden supply channels through the management of Ukraine's main aircraft-engine maker, whose former president is on trial for treason, and parliament has banned church bodies tied to the Moscow Patriarchate, whose patriarch backs the war. The other direction is domestic: the men who own the banks and the heavy industry also hold or fund public office. The founder of the country's largest bank was governor of a region while the bank lent heavily to companies belonging to its own managers. The state nationalised it, needing a bailout of 5.6 billion dollars financed with IMF support; the United States designated him for significant corruption, and Ukrainian investigators charged him with fraud and embezzlement. Customs and border officers at the western crossings into the European Union have been charged with running contraband channels, and an investigation into the state nuclear power company alleges large kickbacks on its contracts. Wartime reconstruction adds a new layer, with a large asset manager asked to help design the framework for public and private investment in rebuilding. Through all of it the institutions exist and sometimes work: the anti-corruption bureau brings these cases, against people inside the state rather than outside it.
Ukraine.imp: A hole in a bank that the state fills is filled with tax money and borrowed money, so the repayment lands on wages and prices for years afterwards. Kickbacks at the nuclear utility come out of electricity bills in a country being shelled. When border officers run their own contraband lines, the delays and the paperwork fall on everybody else. The test is whether cases against well-connected defendants reach court and survive appeal.

United Kingdom.d:
Britain is both a target and a base. The arrangement most often tested is the quiet overlap between private fraternities and public office. Freemasonry is a lawful lodge-based society, but two Commons inquiries in the 1990s looked at how many of its members sat in police forces, on benches and in prosecution offices, and the question is still live: the Metropolitan Police now treats lodge membership as a declarable association, 397 officers and staff have declared, and the High Court refused the United Grand Lodge of England permission to challenge the rule. A similar rule for new judges came in after the inquiries and was later dropped.

Then there is the paid route. The big accounting firms second staff into the Treasury to help draft tax law and can then sell advice on the gaps; former ministers take consultancies and ring the regulators that oversee their clients; a prime minister out of office texts a serving chancellor on behalf of a finance firm. Little of it is illegal, which is what each inquiry keeps finding.

Foreign states work the same building. MI5 has warned Parliament about a solicitor acting in coordination with the Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department, and an ex-MEP for Wales is serving ten and a half years for taking money to make pro-Russian speeches.

Underneath sits older London business: a network around Cecil Rhodes's trustees and Alfred Milner that supplied War Cabinet ministers and editors of The Times, and bank houses that financed British wars, the Suez shares and the compensation paid to slave owners.
United Kingdom.imp: The cost shows up where safety and money meet. The Grenfell inquiry found the makers of the tower's cladding and insulation had deceived the testing system; 72 people died in the fire. Pandemic protective equipment was bought through a fast lane for offers referred by ministers and peers, and one supplier has been ordered to repay about 122 million pounds for gowns that went unused. Watch who writes a rule, and who is paying the firms that rule covers.

Vatican City.d:
The Holy See is a church government with a bank, and nearly every case runs through that bank. The Institute for the Works of Religion holds accounts for religious orders and Vatican offices and answers to no outside regulator. Its letters of comfort stood behind Banco Ambrosiano's lending, an Italian bank that collapsed in 1982; the Institute denied legal liability but paid about 224 million dollars to creditor banks, citing moral involvement. When Milan magistrates issued warrants for its president, Italy's highest court held that the Lateran Treaty put the bank beyond Italian jurisdiction; he stayed inside the walls and was never tried.

Since then the pattern has been internal: Vatican courts trying Vatican officials. A former head of the bank was convicted of embezzlement over property sales. A cardinal who ran day-to-day business at the Secretariat of State was convicted over a London building bought with church funds, then saw the indictment nullified and a retrial ordered for 2026. An official was jailed for leaking financial documents; the journalists who published them were acquitted.

The other thread runs outward. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order also treated as a sovereign subject of international law, with its own diplomats, had its Grand Master forced out and its constitution rewritten by the Pope, who appointed its council himself.
Vatican City.imp: Few people live in Vatican City, so the cost falls on the Catholics and religious orders whose donations and funds sit in the Institute's accounts, and on the creditors of banks that failed around it. A state that is also a church can try its own officials, and can also keep a foreign court from reaching them. Watch whether the retrial goes ahead and what the accounts now disclose.

North Macedonia.d:
North Macedonia's single documented entry is a membership rather than a case. The country's foreign minister, Timčo Mucunski, appears on the World Economic Forum's 2025 list of Young Global Leaders, a programme that selects people under forty from government, business and civil society and brings them into the network around the Forum's annual meeting. Membership is a selection by the Forum; no inquiry has found that it directed any decision he has taken. It is recorded here because the map tracks the places where officials and private money meet, not because anything improper has been established.

Beyond that the map lists the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with its own diplomatic service, as present, and treats the Gülen movement as likely but undocumented. That is the religious network Turkey calls a terrorist organisation and whose schools and followers it has pursued across the Balkans, including in neighbouring Kosovo, where six people were flown out by Turkish request.

What the record does not contain is as notable as what it does: no documented foreign intelligence operation, no criminal group inside the police or the courts, no lender or company shown writing a law.
North Macedonia.imp: A minister's membership of an international network changes nothing here on its own; what would matter is a decision taken for reasons never explained. The thinness of the record is the real condition. Neighbouring states have documented deportations and captured agencies, and nothing says this country is immune. Watch what ministers declare about travel, hospitality and outside roles.

Antigua and Barbuda.d: What the map records here is a regulator accused of being paid by the bank he was meant to regulate. Allen Stanford ran Stanford International Bank out of Antigua and was later convicted in the United States of a $7 billion fraud. An American indictment charges Leroy King, then head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, with taking more than $100,000 in bribes from Stanford to look past what the bank actually held and to help obstruct an investigation by US securities regulators. Antigua extradited King to Houston in 2019. The map carries it as a charge, not a verdict. That is the shape of the exposure in a very small state. A bank large relative to the whole economy does not need to capture a government; it needs the one official whose signature says the books are sound, and in a commission of a few dozen people that official is reachable. The other recorded presences, a Catholic military order and a Macau-based investment group, carry no findings here. Antigua's scores sit near the bottom of the map, which reflects how little has been documented rather than how little is possible.
Antigua and Barbuda.imp: An offshore bank registered here was selling certainty, and what gave it that was the stamp of a local regulator. Most of the people who lost money were abroad, but the cost lands at home as well: when a jurisdiction's supervision is shown to be reachable, the correspondent banks that small economies need for remittances and trade start withdrawing. Watch whether the regulator publishes its findings, its budget and its staffing.

Barbados.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Barbados yet. No case has been recorded of an outside force getting a hand inside its government, whether a foreign service, a company, an organised group, a church or a lender. What follows is a guess from neighbouring states, not evidence. A British masonic body is listed as probably present. The plausible routes into a small economy built on finance and tourism are an offshore bank or insurer that needs a friendly regulator, a contractor seeking a licence, and compliance decisions taken by banks abroad. The absence of cases may mean only that nobody has looked.
Barbados.imp: An empty record is not a clean bill of health; it means no court, inquiry or journalist has published anything the map can use. The practical question for people here is whether the institutions that would find such a thing exist and work: an auditor general with staff, a financial regulator that publishes its decisions, a press free to report on who got a licence. Those are what keep a record empty for the right reason.

Belize.d: The one case recorded here was never proved, and the map says so. In September 2013 the prime minister stripped Elvin Penner, his minister of state for immigration, of the post after accusations that he had sold and issued a Belizean passport to a South Korean man who was at the time in prison in Taiwan. Penner was charged in 2014 and the charges were dropped the same year for lack of evidence. He stays on the map as a disputed case rather than a finding. What sits behind it is why the country appears at all: Belize runs a passport and residence industry, and the map treats that industry as a presence in its own right. A travel document is the one thing a small state can sell that is worth a great deal to a particular kind of buyer, someone who needs a different name at a border, and the official who signs it is the whole supply chain. Belize's documented score is close to the floor while its reading for actors inside the state is middling, which on this map means the opportunity is visible and the record is thin.
Belize.imp: A passport sold off the books is a border crossing bought by someone other governments are trying to keep track of, and it devalues the document every other Belizean carries, because visa-free travel rests on trust in the issuing office. When the only case brought collapses for lack of evidence, nothing is settled either way. What to watch is whether approvals, buyers and fees in the residence programme are published at all.

Colombia.d:
In Colombia the trade went into the institutions rather than around them. The clearest measure is the legislature: roughly 30% of Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the AUC paramilitaries, who were themselves among the country's largest cocaine exporters. Above that sat the appeal layer. Two former presidents of the Supreme Court, a sitting magistrate and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking payments to shelve or steer the proceedings against those legislators. The same reach extends into the prosecution service, where a serving prosecutor was charged with holding property in her own name for a front man of the Gulf Clan.

The money is handled by separate businesses. US designations treat the launderer, the enforcement service and the trafficker as firms with client relationships, and the fronts are ordinary and dull by design: farms, coffee and meat traders, estate planners, a football club, five companies registered at one Medellin address. They are replaced about as fast as they are named. The oldest mechanism needs no company at all: dollars are sold to importers who want them and the peso equivalent is paid to the trafficker at home, so nothing crosses a border as money.

Foreign firms buy the top. President Santos acknowledged in 2017 that his 2010 campaign had taken illegal payments from the Brazilian builder Odebrecht, saying he had not known.
Colombia.imp: Laws are written and votes taken by people who owe their seats to armed groups, and the court that should correct that was bought at the top, so a victim's case can be shelved by a magistrate rather than lost on the evidence. Farms and shops in whole districts are held on paper by launderers, which means ordinary buyers compete with money that does not need to earn a return. Much of the enforcement arrives as a foreign sanctions list rather than a verdict.

Costa Rica.d:
Costa Rica carries far less of this than its neighbours, and what is documented is recent and sits in the police. The country has shifted from a consumer market to a transit route, and the cases follow the route. A former vice-minister of public security who later sat as a judge was designated by the US Treasury in 2025 for helping move cocaine from Colombia through the country, and specifically for using his contacts inside the government to find out what counter-narcotics investigators were doing. He was arrested on a US extradition request weeks after the president signed a constitutional reform permitting Costa Ricans to be extradited for drug trafficking, which is the change that made his removal possible.

A separate file reached officers stationed on the Caribbean lowland corridor. Investigators logged regular telephone contact between them and the organisation that holds the corridor, and found that some had been recruited for one purpose: to warn of raids, checkpoints and investigator movements in time for loads to be moved or hidden. Five were charged before the specialised organised crime court.

Religion enters through the ballot box rather than through infiltration. An evangelical singer turned deputy reached the 2018 presidential runoff on opposition to a court ruling on same-sex marriage, and has sat in the Legislative Assembly since.
Costa Rica.imp: The cost is that enforcement leaks. A raid the target has already been told about catches nobody, and an investigation a well-placed official can read is one the target can plan around. For people living along the Caribbean corridor, that means the traffic settles in and a police presence stops meaning protection. The extradition reform is the thing to watch, because it is what allowed one of these men to be taken out of the country at all.

Cuba.d:
Cuba is the inverse of most entries here: the state is the infiltrator rather than the target. The documented cases concern Freemasonry, a lawful fraternal order with lodges across the island. A man who became Grand Master in 2000 after government pressure admitted on state television in 2011 that he had worked for state security under a cover name, and that he had been placed in the post so the government could monitor Freemasons. A former grand official who left the country in 2023 said a state security officer had told him agents had been watching the lodges for more than forty years. When the Grand Lodge fell into a leadership dispute in 2024, after money kept in the Grand Master's safe for a Masonic retirement home went missing, the Justice Ministry, which holds the register of associations, intervened and refused to recognise the newly elected leadership.

The remaining case runs the other way. In 1989 a decorated army general and an interior ministry colonel who ran the state's hard-currency operations were court-martialled for moving cocaine through Cuban waters and airspace and shot by firing squad. The interior minister was dismissed and jailed in the same purge.
Cuba.imp: For members of an ordinary fraternal order it means the person chairing the meeting may be reporting it, and the ministry that registers the group can decide who is allowed to lead it. Independent association stops being independent without ever being banned. The 1989 executions show the other side: where the state is the only authority, the only check on officials who traffic is a purge decided from above, with no public evidence and no appeal.

Dominica.d:
Dominica's exposure runs through the sale of citizenship. The country sells passports, and researchers counted roughly 7,700 buyers by 2023, among them a former Afghan intelligence chief and sanctioned Russians. The single documented case concerns what sits above a passport, which is a diplomatic posting. Al Jazeera reported in 2019 that an Iranian businessman gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's 2014 campaign and received an ambassadorship and a diplomatic passport in return, which a witness said was handed over in Kuala Lumpur. The businessman was later jailed in Iran over oil-revenue theft. Skerrit denies any trade took place, and the account rests on journalism rather than on a court finding.

What makes a small state useful in this trade is not its own machinery but what its documents open elsewhere. A Dominican passport and a diplomatic rank are used in other countries, by people whose own papers would attract a second look. Nothing on the map yet shows an outside organisation placed inside a Dominican ministry, and the one allegation points the other way: the government is the seller.
Dominica.imp: People here get the fee income and carry the cost if a buyer turns out to be someone a foreign prosecutor wants. Banks and visa officers abroad then treat every holder of the same passport with more suspicion, which falls on ordinary travellers who bought nothing. A diplomatic post handed over as a favour also means the person speaking for the country abroad was not chosen for competence. Worth watching: who signs off on those appointments, and whether the decision is ever published.

Dominican Republic.d:
Two things are documented here, and both touch the parts of the state that handle cargo and contracts. The anti-drug agency and the armed forces have a standing problem with their own staff. Senior officials of the National Drug Control Agency were arrested while providing security to traffickers waiting on a shipment bound for Puerto Rico, a navy officer responsible for port security was accused of moving a load to Spain, and a group of officials, mostly navy, were accused of killing Colombian traffickers to take their cargo. The response has been removal rather than prosecution: more than 700 drug-agency personnel pushed out since 2009, around 200 of them suspected of trafficking. That clears a payroll without producing a verdict.

The other case is corporate. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group, admitted to US prosecutors that it had paid tens of millions in bribes here for public works. A Dominican court convicted the businessman named as the channel for the money and a former public works minister in 2021, four other defendants were acquitted, and an appeal court upheld both convictions in 2023. That makes it one of the few Odebrecht files in the region to end in a domestic conviction that survived appeal.
Dominican Republic.imp: Port and airport screening is what suffers first: when the officers on duty are the ones arranging passage, inspection stops being a check on anything. Dismissing people in bulk moves the problem rather than settling it, since an officer removed without charge can turn up working somewhere else. On the contracting side, a bribe paid for a road means the road costs more and may be built where it suits the payer rather than where it is needed.

Ecuador.d:
Ecuador's courts and police are where the pressure sits now. Decryption of a trafficker's phone produced the broadest judicial-capture case in the country's history: judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials charged with fixing cases and selling protection, with 20 of 21 defendants sentenced in November 2024 and public service treated by the court as making the offence worse. A second file in Guayas province charged judges alongside a former legislator whom prosecutors described as the power behind the provincial courts. The recurring device there was sentence reductions granted by prison-guarantee judges acting outside their competence.

The cocaine moves inside the legitimate export economy. Loads travel in fruit shipments out of Guayaquil, and prosecutions have reached exporters, port staff and customs officials. A licensed tuna fleet out of Manta was sanctioned in 2026 not for carrying drugs but for meeting the go-fast boats at sea with fuel, food and medical help while watching for law enforcement, using government-subsidised fuel to do it.

The older layer is foreign companies buying ministers: a vice-president jailed over bribes from the Brazilian builder Odebrecht, and a Geneva oil trader convicted in Switzerland of corrupting Ecuador's state oil officials. The present government has gone a different way, announcing a deal with Erik Prince, Blackwater's founder, for his contractors to support the security forces.
Ecuador.imp: Where judges have been bought, a case against a trafficker is not a risk to him, and someone arrested on good evidence can walk out on a release order that was priced. Banana and tuna firms doing ordinary business carry the cost too, in inspection regimes written for the ones that are not. Fuel subsidised by taxpayers has ended up provisioning the boats offshore. One thing to watch: the court sent its ruling back to prosecutors to investigate people named at trial but never charged.

El Salvador.d:
One arrangement is documented in El Salvador, and it runs between the prison system and the gangs. The US Treasury designated the director of prisons and the head of a cabinet unit for negotiating with leaders of MS-13 and Barrio 18 inside the jails: privileges and money for the leaders in exchange for lower homicide figures and electoral support. A US indictment of MS-13 leaders unsealed in 2023 describes the same thing from the other side, saying the meetings 'were organized by the government of El Salvador and prison officials', who gave the leaders benefits and released one man the United States wanted, and that the gang in return cut public killings and backed the governing party in the 2021 election. The government denies any pact, and nothing has been tried in a Salvadoran court.

What separates this from an officer taking money is the direction. The state is not simply being bought; it is trading with an armed group for two things a government wants, a crime statistic and a bloc of votes. The gang remains the counterparty to whatever was agreed, and the terms are not public.
El Salvador.imp: A homicide count that falls because of an agreement rather than because fewer people are killed tells residents nothing about their own safety, and it is the figure governments campaign on. Prisoners the state convicted receive privileges that victims' families were never told about. If the arrangement breaks, the violence it held down returns at a time the gangs choose, not the government's. Because no court has tested it, there is no public record of what was promised to whom.

Grenada.d:
Grenada sells citizenship and has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen, and that is where its single documented case sits. Al Jazeera reported in 2019 that an investor claimed he had paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell; Mitchell said he received fifteen thousand dollars, for travel costs. In the same reporting an American businessman said a partner of his had been offered a diplomatic post in exchange for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. None of it has been tested in court, and the record rests on an investigative broadcast and on the accounts of men with their own interests in the story.

The shape is the familiar one for small states that sell documents. What is on offer is not influence over Grenadian policy but a Grenadian title that works elsewhere: a passport, a diplomatic rank, the standing that comes with representing a country. Nothing on the map shows an outside organisation embedded in a Grenadian ministry, and the allegation runs the other way, with the government as seller.
Grenada.imp: Residents get the programme's fee income and carry what follows if a buyer turns out to be someone a foreign prosecutor wants: tighter visa treatment and more banking friction for everyone holding the same passport. A diplomatic appointment made as a favour also means the person speaking for the country abroad was chosen for what he paid rather than what he knows. The useful question is who approves those posts, and whether the reason is ever published.

Guyana.d:
Enforcement records now treat Guyana as infrastructure rather than as a run of incidents. The US Treasury published a chart in June 2025 setting out how traffickers use the country's airstrips, river craft and port clearance to move cocaine toward the United States. Alongside it came designations of the men said to run the largest domestic organisations, Colombians managing clandestine airfields, and a serving police officer accused of arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers. None of them has been tried. Cocaine has been found buried in bunkers on the airstrips and in the jungle.

The gold trade is the other documented route. Treasury sanctioned a family gold-trading firm for keeping thousands of kilograms off customs declarations and evading duty, and said it had bribed customs officers, paid for favourable treatment in court matters and bribed to win state contracts. The family denies it. The same action named a permanent secretary of the home affairs ministry for taking cash and gifts in return for contract, gun-permit and passport favours.

Behind that is an unresolved history. The country's most powerful trafficker ran an armed group that operated alongside the state during the killings of the mid-2000s. He was convicted in New York; the group's relationship to the government was examined publicly in Guyana and never resolved in a court here.
Guyana.imp: Duty an exporter does not pay is revenue the country does not get, out of the same budget that pays for clinics and police. A gun permit or a passport that can be bought means the person holding it was never checked. Where a serving officer sells safe passage, a roadblock protects the shipment instead of the public. Almost all of this record comes from foreign designations rather than Guyanese trials, so the allegations have not been tested where the people affected live.

Haiti.d:
In Haiti the armed groups and the political class are not separate things. The gangs that joined in the Viv Ansanm alliance control much of Port-au-Prince, and the man who leads the largest federation among them served in the national police until 2018. Canada sanctioned sitting and former senators in 2022 over what it called illicit financial support to armed gangs, and the US later designated a former president for trafficking activity including sponsoring and financing gangs. He denies it, and no court has heard the allegations, which is true of nearly all of this record. A UN panel of experts reported in October 2026 that former legislators are arming groups and sponsoring attacks, that at least one member of a new municipal commission in Cité Soleil is an active gang member, and that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information.

Where the state cannot act, it has hired. Haitian authorities confirmed in January 2026 that contractors from Vectus Global, the private security firm run by Blackwater's founder Erik Prince, had taken part in anti-gang raids, under a plan reported to run for ten years and to include helping collect taxes. A foreign company is now inside both the use of force and the revenue system.
Haiti.imp: People in Port-au-Prince deal with whoever holds their street, and that person may be funded by someone they voted for. The officer at the checkpoint may be the source of the weapons used against them. Because almost nothing here has reached a courtroom, the only consequence a backer faces is a sanctions listing, which does not stop the money. Tax collection passing to a private foreign contractor means the basic business of the state is being done by people no Haitian chose.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d: What St Kitts and Nevis has to sell in this field is its own citizenship, and the passport-sale industry is headquartered here rather than imported. The federation has sold citizenship since 1984: an investment in the country, and a passport that travels on it. The documented problem is who buys. In 2014 FinCEN, the US Treasury unit that tracks financial crime, warned that several Iranians under US sanctions had obtained Kittitian passports through the programme, which it said maintained lax controls, and that Iranians kept getting them even after applications from Iran were suspended. A passport is useful to a sanctioned person for the same reason it is useful to anyone: it decides which name a bank sees and which border waves you through. The programme has since been changed and the passports in question have expired, and FinCEN withdrew the advisory in February 2026. Nothing else is documented here, and the country's score is among the lowest on the map.
St. Kitts and Nevis.imp: A small country's main asset in this field is the trust other governments place in its documents, and that trust is spent by whoever gets sold one. When an advisory goes out, residents and local businesses get the extra scrutiny as well — slower banking, harder visas — over decisions made inside one government office. What to watch is who appears on the published list of people granted citizenship, and who checks them.

St. Lucia.d: Nothing is documented on this map for St Lucia yet: no case of an outside force getting a hand on the government here has been recorded, so what follows is a best guess rather than a finding. The only noted presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic standing that runs charitable work, which is not wrongdoing. Given the region, the forces most likely to appear in time are the offshore company-formation and citizenship-sale business, and cocaine transit money looking for a bank, a property deal or a construction contract. None of that is established here.
St. Lucia.imp: With nothing recorded, there is nothing yet to count as a cost to people here. The standing risk for a small island economy is scale: one bank, one law firm or one government office handling foreign money matters more than it would anywhere larger, so a single bad arrangement can affect the whole country's standing abroad. What to watch is who holds the licences, and who checks them.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d: No case has been documented here, so St Vincent and the Grenadines sits on the map without a record and this write-up is an estimate rather than a finding. The one noted presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic charitable order with diplomatic standing, and belonging to it is not wrongdoing. The country also scores low on the measure of outside actors embedded in the state, lower than most of its neighbours. The plausible exposures are the ones the Caribbean shares: offshore financial services, and drug transit money moving through a small banking system and into property. None of that is shown here.
St. Vincent and the Grenadines.imp: Nothing documented means nothing to set against people here as a cost. The risk a small economy carries is concentration: a handful of banks and registries carry all the foreign money, so one compliance failure shows up as correspondent banks abroad pulling out and ordinary transfers getting slower and dearer for everyone. Worth watching is who can register companies here, and what they are asked to prove.

Suriname.d: Suriname's documented record is about one family and the security apparatus it ran. Dési Bouterse, who took power after a 1980 coup and was later twice elected president, was convicted in absentia by a Dutch court in 1999 of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine; with no extradition treaty the sentence was never carried out, and he was elected president afterwards. A separate Surinamese prosecution over the 1982 killing of fifteen political opponents produced a twenty-year sentence, finally upheld in December 2023. He did not surrender, disappeared in January 2024, and died in hiding later that year having served no time on either conviction. His son Dino ran the country's counter-terrorism unit, which is to say the office that would investigate exactly this. The US Drug Enforcement Administration lured him to Panama and arrested him in 2013; in New York he pleaded guilty to cocaine importation and weapons offences, and to offering men he believed were Hezbollah operatives a base in Suriname, who were in fact informants. In both cases the trafficking ran through the state's own security posts rather than being smuggled past them.
Suriname.imp: When the counter-terrorism unit is itself the problem, there is no office left to report it to, and a conviction handed down abroad changes nothing at home without an extradition treaty. Neither conviction here was ever served, which leaves the families of fifteen people killed in 1982 with a verdict and nothing else. What to watch is whether court judgments are enforced against people who still hold office.

Argentina.d: Argentina's record is thick and mostly old, and the thread running through it is a lodge. P2, a secret masonic lodge in Italy whose membership lists were seized by Italian police in 1981, turns out to have had Argentine officials on them: an interim president, a minister of social welfare whose ministry funded a death squad, a navy commander who sat on the junta, a foreign minister, an economy minister. The lodge's grand master, Licio Gelli, was given an Argentine state honour and a diplomatic post with immunity by a 1974 presidential decree. Those men are dead or convicted, but the state terror they ran is still being tried: a federal court convicted fifteen officers, including a former de facto president, of running Argentina's part in Operation Condor, the coordinated campaign among South American dictatorships against each other's exiles. What is live now is quieter. Traffickers buy judges and police commanders in the provinces, with a Santa Fe police chief and a federal judge in the north both convicted of protecting the trade. Construction and energy contractors are on trial with a former president over cash handed to officials for public works contracts. And the finance ministry and central bank are run by former JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank executives, while free-market think tanks funded through a US network claim credit for the current government's programme.
Argentina.imp: A judge who takes money from traffickers does not just free one defendant; he sets the price of every case in his court, and people in Rosario live with the homicide rate that follows. Bribes on public works are paid back through the roads and power lines that are built badly or not at all. When the people who manage the currency come from the banks that hold the debt, ordinary borrowers have no comparable voice. Watch who funds the institutes that write the policy.

Bahamas.d: Two things sit on the record here, forty years apart, and both are about banking rather than government. Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau was a subsidiary of the Italian bank whose 1982 collapse became one of Europe's largest financial scandals; the president of the Vatican Bank had been a director, and the Nassau and Luxembourg units between them accounted for about half of the $1.2 to $1.4 billion lent to shell companies in Panama. Bahamian regulators suspended its operations after the collapse. That is history, but it is why the jurisdiction appears on this map at all. The current entry runs the other way. Global banks have been cutting correspondent relationships, the accounts that let a local bank move money across borders, with small Caribbean jurisdictions faster than with anywhere else, on the grounds that the compliance cost outweighs the business. What the IMF and others found is that ordinary remittance and trade payments then move into channels that are harder to see, while the trafficking money the withdrawal was meant to address never depended on those accounts. Nobody here has been charged in either matter.
Bahamas.imp: Losing a correspondent account is not abstract: it is a family paying more to send money home, a small importer who cannot pay a supplier, a shop that can no longer take a card. A measure taken against crime has mostly been paid for by people with nothing to do with it, and the flows it targeted carried on elsewhere. Watch which banks still hold Bahamian correspondent lines, and what a remittance costs.

Bolivia.d: The documented route in here is the drug trade, and it runs through the agency built to stop it. Two successive heads of the FELCN, the national anti-narcotics force, have been convicted in American courts: one caught in a sting agreeing to protect cocaine shipments bound for Miami, the other convicted in Manhattan in 2025 of steering investigations away from allied traffickers and assigning his own armed officers to guard cocaine loads. That is not an outside force bribing its way in; the command of the counter-drug police was the inside. The older layer is the dictatorship. Luis Arce Gomez, interior minister and chief of repression after the 1980 coup, was given a life sentence by a Rome appeals court in 2019 in the Operation Condor case, the campaign South American military governments ran jointly against each other's exiles. That coup also drew a stranger visitor: a journalist's single-source account describes an aide of the Unification Church's founder meeting the new general, and claims later Bolivian investigations put church money into the coup. The map carries that as a claim, not a finding. Bolivia was added to an international financial watch list in 2025.
Bolivia.imp: When the anti-drug police are run by men paid by traffickers, every seizure becomes a business decision about which rival to remove, and the farmer or the street seller is prosecuted while the shipment moves on. The convictions in this record came from courts in Miami and New York rather than La Paz, which tells people here where accountability actually sits. Watch whether a Bolivian court ever tries a Bolivian police commander for this.

Brazil.d: Brazil carries more documented cases than almost anywhere on this map, and they run in several directions at once. Organised crime is the most advanced. The PCC, the country's largest criminal organisation, is accused not only of buying police officers but of owning parts of the formal economy: two Sao Paulo city bus operators, taken over by the city in 2024, along with a port terminal, ethanol plants and more than a thousand petrol stations held inside some forty investment funds, with methanol blended into the petrol sold to motorists. Rio's militias, which began as off-duty police protection rackets, hold territory and seats; the Supreme Court convicted a former federal deputy and his brother, an audit-court counsellor, of ordering the 2018 murder of the city councillor Marielle Franco. Churches are the second route, and a lawful one: pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God founded the party now called Republicanos, whose bishops have held ministries and the mayoralty of Rio, and a cross-party evangelical caucus in Congress runs into the hundreds of signatories and votes as a bloc. Third, companies. The Car Wash investigation exposed a construction cartel paying politicians for contracts with the state oil company, and foreign firms have since pleaded guilty in American courts to bribing the same officials. The background is the Cold War: a CIA-linked institute paid for opposition campaigns in the 1962 election, and prosecutors cite army files as evidence of Brazil's part in Operation Condor.
Brazil.imp: A criminal organisation that owns the bus company decides how you get to work and whether the fuel in the tank is real, and adulterated petrol wrecks engines belonging to people who never touched the drug trade. Bribes on oil contracts come out of a company every Brazilian part-owns. A caucus voting as a bloc on its churches' priorities writes law for everyone, including people of other faiths. Watch whether big convictions survive appeal; several have been annulled.

Canada.d:
Canada is mostly on the receiving end. Public inquiries now treat foreign governments as the main problem. Justice Hogue's final report of January 2025 calls China the most active state interfering here, working through consulates, proxies and the Communist Party's United Front Work Department, the body that builds influence among overseas Chinese communities. India is named second: Canada expelled six Indian diplomats in 2024 after the police said Indian agents had used a criminal gang to target Sikh activists, and the inquiry cited intelligence that Indian proxies may be funding candidates. A committee of parliamentarians reported that some MPs and senators were themselves witting participants, taking disguised money from foreign missions and passing colleagues' views to foreign diplomats, though Hogue found no traitors in Parliament.

Alongside that sits ordinary corruption in cargo and construction. Border services officers have been convicted of waving vehicles through, in an agency that had no independent civilian oversight body until legislation was brought forward in the 2020s. Quebec's Charbonneau inquiry heard that construction firms paid a share of Montreal public works to the Rizzuto Mafia and to political parties.

The older layer is domestic and fraternal. Toronto's city hall ran through the Orange Order, a Protestant sworn brotherhood, for a century, and four prime ministers were members. A rival Catholic order, the Ordre de Jacques-Cartier, worked by recruiting decision-makers in order to get French Canadians appointed to senior federal posts, and dissolved in 1965 after an insider published what it did.
Canada.imp: It shows up as decisions made for reasons nobody voted on. A party nomination can turn on buses organised around a consulate, and a family can be pressured here because relatives abroad are reachable. Public works cost more when a share goes to a crime family and to parties. Drugs cross a border staffed by officers who were paid to look the other way. What is new is that inquiries now name all of this in public, and that the border agency is finally getting outside oversight.

Chile.d:
Chile's current arrangements are religious and corporate rather than foreign-state. Lay Catholic movements supply people to high office. President José Antonio Kast, who took office in March 2026, belongs to Schoenstatt, a movement founded in Germany in 1914; his under-secretary of justice is a numerary, a lay member, of Opus Dei. These are memberships, not evidence that either organisation directs policy. Earlier governments drew ministers from free-market think tanks in the Atlas Network, an international network of such institutes.

Money reaches politics through campaign finance. Prosecutors established that the lithium and fertiliser miner SQM paid invoices issued by politicians, advisers and their relatives, moving money to campaigns and parties across the spectrum. The company settled US bribery charges and later signed a lithium partnership with the state copper company.

The background is heavier. A US aid scheme linked the University of Chicago's economics department to Santiago's Catholic University from the mid-1950s; its graduates wrote the plan the junta adopted in 1975 and then ran the finance, economy and planning ministries and the central bank. In the same years the intelligence service DINA convened Operation Condor, the cross-border hunt for exiles, and held prisoners at Colonia Dignidad, a German sect compound whose residents helped torture them. Courts convicted the DINA chief and indicted Pinochet, who died before any verdict.
Chile.imp: Policy can follow commitments that were never on a ballot, a minister's movement or a think tank's programme, and voters have no way to weigh them when they cannot see them. Campaign money arriving as a paid invoice decides which candidates can afford to run. Where narcotics officers resell what they seize, an arrest buys the public nothing. And the torture cases from the dictatorship still set who trusts the state here and who does not.

Guatemala.d:
The offices built to stop trafficking here have repeatedly been the ones running it. The anti-narcotics police director and his deputy were arrested during a US-funded training visit and pleaded guilty to a cocaine conspiracy. A vice-president and an interior minister were indicted in Washington. Mayors and members of Congress have been convicted since, one using official municipal letterhead to pass a shipment off as a delivery of cement.

What changed the record was CICIG, a commission set up by UN agreement with Guatemala to help local prosecutors take apart criminal networks inside the state. Its customs-bribery case brought down a president in 2015. It was also investigating the next president's campaign financing, and he ended its mandate in 2019 after deploying troops near its offices. By 2023 more than thirty judges and prosecutors who had worked those files had left the country under threat of arrest, and the cases they built no longer have a domestic forum. This is capture achieved by removing the prosecutor rather than by buying the judge.

Enforcement now arrives mostly from outside, as extraditions and as US sanctions on Guatemalan freight and trading companies holding property for trafficking organisations. The oldest entry is political: a 1970s vice-president who led the World Anti-Communist League, the network tying anticommunist governments to death squads across the region.
Guatemala.imp: When the anti-drug agency is the one moving the drugs, reporting a trafficker means telling him. The loss of the commission matters more than any single case: the prosecutors who could try powerful people are abroad, so a Guatemalan with a complaint has nowhere at home to take it, and whether anyone is tried now depends on a foreign court having jurisdiction. A municipality's own paperwork can be used to get a load through a checkpoint unopened.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is where the trade reached the presidency and was proved in court. A president who held office from 2014 to 2022 was convicted in New York of conspiring to import cocaine and sentenced to 45 years. His brother, a member of Congress, had been convicted in the same court, with trial evidence that included cocaine packages stamped with his initials and testimony that the proceeds funded the governing party's campaigns. The national police chief of that period pleaded guilty to taking payments to provide armed protection for loads crossing the country. The president received a full US presidential pardon in December 2025 and was released the same day; the conviction stands and the sentence goes unserved, and Honduras asked Interpol to act on a domestic arrest order written for exactly that situation.

Underneath the officials sits a layer of family businesses that carried the money. A former vice-president's family and their bank were designated as launderers for a trafficking organisation, and Honduran regulators put the bank into liquidation within days. Two other large networks were designated in the same period, each with a legitimate business face.

The 1980s entry is different in kind: a group headed by the armed forces commander took money from a front for the Unification Church while taking over university, labour and peasant bodies.
Honduras.imp: When the head of state is in the trade there is no office above the problem to appeal to, and police protection that should be neutral is sold by the chief. Depositors in a bank liquidated because its owners were launderers lose access to their own money while payouts are arranged. A pardon granted by a foreign president can undo a sentence Hondurans had no say in, leaving the verdict on paper and the man at liberty, which is why the domestic arrest order matters.

Jamaica.d:
Two things are documented in Jamaica, twenty years apart, and both show a government caught between a foreign demand and a domestic interest. In the 1980s most of the state's foreign-currency accounts and its US commodity financing ran through BCCI, a bank later closed worldwide for fraud. One of its officers told a US Senate committee that it handled every penny of foreign currency going into or out of Jamaica, and the Senate report lists large loans to the Bank of Jamaica and to the state oil firm. That is the whole of what is established here: one foreign bank sitting at the chokepoint of a country's hard currency.

In 2010 the government spent nine months resisting a US request to extradite Christopher Coke, head of an armed organisation based in the Tivoli Gardens district, and retained a Washington law firm to lobby against it. The security operation that followed killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York. A commission of enquiry found the operation's conduct unjustified, and the prime minister had already resigned over the affair before it reported.
Jamaica.imp: A single bank holding all of a country's foreign currency means its collapse becomes the country's problem and its records are the only account of where the money went. The extradition fight shows the other cost: a district leader who can deliver votes can buy a government's lawyers, and when the standoff finally breaks it is the people living in his district who are shot. The findings came after the prime minister had gone, which is the usual order here.

Mexico.d: Organised crime is the main outside force inside the Mexican state, and it works at every level rather than at the top alone. The method is a payroll: a police commander, a prosecutor, a judge, a prison director paid to look away or to act. Where a whole municipal force has been bought, the remedy is administrative — disarmed, disbanded or federalised — so most of it leaves no conviction behind. A sitting governor of Sinaloa and nine other state officials, among them the mayor of the capital and a serving senator, now face a New York indictment over a protection arrangement with one cartel faction; he denies it, resigned days later, and Mexico calls the evidence insufficient. Most of the record comes from US courts and US sanctions lists rather than Mexican ones, because Mexican cases against senior figures tend not to hold: federal police arrested ten mayors and other Michoacán officials in 2009, and within two years the courts had released all of them for want of evidence. Cartel money also sits inside ordinary business — tequila distilleries, gas stations, customs brokerages, a Puerto Vallarta resort whose call centres sell fake timeshare resales to its own customers. Older channels run alongside: foreign oil traders and construction firms paying officials of the state oil company for contracts, and a secret Catholic group, El Yunque, named in press accounts as placing members in party leadership and a federal cabinet — claims the party denies and no court has tested.
Mexico.imp: If the prosecutor, the judge and the police chief are on the same payroll, reporting a crime can be the most dangerous thing you do. Avocado and lime growers pay a fee per hectare and per shipment to people the state does not stop. Fuel from an ordinary station, pills from a licensed pharmacy and a timeshare contract can all belong to the same network. Watch whether cases against senior officials end in a Mexican verdict or only in a US filing.

Nicaragua.d: What is documented in Nicaragua is mostly outside states working on the institutions that deal with people directly. Russia's Interior Ministry runs a police training centre in the Las Colinas district of Managua, set up as an affiliate of the Russian ministry and attended at its opening by the president's son; it has trained Nicaraguan police and later officers from elsewhere in Central America and the Caribbean. The US Treasury sanctioned the centre in 2024, saying it teaches the Russian government's methods of suppressing civil society. The other direction is older and runs through money for politics. The National Endowment for Democracy, a foundation funded by the US government, put about $2 million into Nicaragua's civic opposition in the 1980s, roughly half of it to the newspaper run by Violeta Chamorro, who went on to win the 1990 election; Congress voted further money to boost the opposition shortly before that vote. The endowment says its grants are public and nonpartisan, and critics compared them to earlier covert operations in Chile. Banking left a mark too: a Luxembourg-held unit of Banco Ambrosiano, the Italian bank that collapsed in 1982, was licensed here and lent to both the Somoza government and the Sandinistas, until a presidential decree cancelled its licence in 1985.
Nicaragua.imp: Police training shapes how officers behave at a protest or a roadblock, so who does the training is not a technicality. Foreign money for newspapers and parties means some voices in an election are louder because a government abroad paid for them, and it hands whoever is in power a reason to call every critic foreign-funded. What to watch is which outside bodies are allowed to operate here and which get shut down.

Panama.d: Panama's position is what gets bought here: a banking system, a shipping corridor and a legal profession that can move money and goods with little trace. Offshore company formation is the clearest case. Mossack Fonseca, the firm at the centre of the Panama Papers, was tried at home and its founders acquitted in 2024, the judge citing insufficient and improperly gathered evidence. The firm that replaced it as the region's largest incorporator then turned up across the Pandora Papers, having built thousands of structures without verifying who owned them; it says it followed the law in force at the time and faces no charge. Goods move the same way through the Colón Free Zone, the largest free zone in the Americas, where cargo passes without entering Panamanian customs territory. Beneficial-ownership rules have been tightened and the volume has not fallen. The older record set the template. General Manuel Noriega held about $25 million in a bank account opened in the name of the national defence forces, and had the same bank pay off the mortgage of the man he chose as president. The current case is construction money: the Brazilian builder Odebrecht says tens of millions went to Panamanian officials, and the main laundering trial opened in 2026 with a former president taking part by video from asylum in Colombia.
Panama.imp: A system built to hide ownership hides it for everyone, so the bribe, the stolen contract and the ordinary tax dodge use the same lawyer and the same shell company. When the money goes, the road or the hospital it was meant to pay for is not built. An acquittal on procedural grounds leaves people no clearer about what actually happened. Watch whether the ownership rules now on paper change who gets registered in practice.

Paraguay.d: Paraguay sits on a cocaine corridor and at the corner of the Tri-Border Area with Brazil and Argentina, and what gets bought here is the part of the state that would otherwise stop the cargo. A laundering and cocaine investigation opened in 2022, A Ultranza Py, charged police officers, a serving prosecutor, court officials and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies, and seized hundreds of properties; several principals fled before arrest and one of the case's own prosecutors was later removed. Trade is the other channel. In the free-zone import-export business at Ciudad del Este, invoices and value move without matching cargo; Argentina froze one network's assets and the US designated its principals. In 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned a former president and the sitting vice-president for corruption, saying both had ties to members of Hizballah, the Lebanese armed movement and party, and that their representatives collected bribes at events it held in the country. The sanctions on the former president were lifted in 2025. The dictatorship left its own residue: in 1992 a lawyer and a judge found the secret police archive in a station outside Asunción, which proved Operation Condor — the coordinated hunt for exiles run by South America's military governments — had existed, and gave a later truth commission the names of 9,923 victims.
Paraguay.imp: When the prosecutor and the judge are part of the network, a seizure or an arrest is not the end of anything: the file stalls and the person charged leaves the country. Border trade nobody checks means honest importers compete with businesses whose cargo and paperwork do not match, and pay the same costs without the same margins. What to watch is whether the 2022 case reaches a verdict or quietly expires.

Peru.d: In Peru it is the courts that outside forces reach most often. Wiretaps set on a Callao trafficking group in 2018 picked up a separate network on the same lines — a supreme court judge, the president of the Callao superior court and members of the council that appoints and promotes judges, trading sentence reductions and posts. The judge fled to Spain, the court president was jailed, and the first conviction after a full trial came seven years later, with several implicated judges still sitting while under investigation. Construction money reaches the presidency: one former president is serving twenty years for taking about $35 million from the Brazilian builder Odebrecht in return for a highway contract, and another was convicted with his wife in 2025 of laundering tied to the same company. Both deny it. Religious and fraternal organisations place people openly rather than covertly. Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members seek holiness in ordinary work, has had members as production and defence minister, as a cardinal appointed a state mediator by Fujimori, and as mayor of Lima and now senator; membership is lawful and is not itself wrongdoing.
